Walpole's fund and Florence's were raided, Pitt's fund became circular, Brady locked dated Treasuries in custody, and Perry held the US "as much bound by its contracts as are individuals". The plan in one frame: payments bought and held at 1.0x cover, the gift announced and capped at the lower of two tests, and the leftover a standby called last.
sources: S2 #1-#6 (Brady, Pitt, Perry, Monte delle doti, P50/P99, overrun facility)
use: FR page "why prefund, and why Treasuries". The holder is the US Treasury, and the bonds themselves are the custody.

idea: Japan's "negative spread". Life insurers promised about 4% (5.5-6.5% pricing in 1995) on money still to be invested, while assets earned about 2% after 1990. The gap hit the whole book for a decade. Nissan Mutual failed on 25 April 1997, the first postwar life-insurer failure, and others followed.
sources: Nippon Life Research Institute report id=51079; Nogami, SOA International Section News, May 2016; Wikipedia "Nissan Life"; CEPII letter 196 (2000)
use: The coupon soft spot at full scale. Japan's gap was on 100% of the book every year; Laura's is on the reinvested coupons only, once (TNA note 1 names this risk). Laura's own size: a 2pt fall in yields costs about $21k of the $500k (IPS_number_sheet, 16 Oct; MODEL, old design). Device: a table of a 1989 insurer beside Laura, same promise length, same 2pt fall.
critique: It was not only rates: property, loan and share losses, and policy surrenders, all played a part. CEPII's "Ponzi-style" is a journalist's word. Counts differ (8 failures per Nogami; "six of the eighteen" per CEPII). Chiyoda failed probably in October 2000, not 1999. Window: Nogami says JGBs rose from 11% to 42% of life insurers' asset mix 1995-2015, which is not "the survivors then bought".
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened NLI, the SOA pdf, Wikipedia and CEPII); counts CONFLICTING
clash: Partly. S1 says the gap is "covered in about 93 of 100 paths by the order of cover in the plan". That old order leaned on the VT half, and the FINAL says no payment depends on a share price, so the FR must cover the gap from Treasuries.
where: S1 §1 l.19-68; FUSIONS §2 item 6; README l.71
note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): a 2-point fall costs about $21k is now $23,509 as written and $0 with Keel's margin (sections 2 and 6)

idea: Equitable Life's guaranteed annuity rates (UK, 1957-2000). A free option (each £100 buys £10 a year) was sold with no price and no reserve. When rates fell from 1993, the board cut payouts to those who took it. The House of Lords ruled against it on 20 July 2000, adding about £1.5bn to liabilities; the society closed to new business on 8 Dec 2000 with assets of about £34bn.
sources: Geneva Association, "Equitable Life" case study (2016) pdf; Wikipedia "Equitable Life Assurance Society v Hyman"
use: "What we announce, we own": a named failure behind the FINAL's "whatever figure you choose is money you already own". It is also the structure Caplet avoids, a guarantee resting on a share-heavy base. Device: the chain 1957-88 free option, 1993 no reserve, 2000 court, December 2000 doors close.
critique: Three things are blended: a rate option, longer lives and discretionary bonuses. It was "a promise written without a price", not "a promise too big", and also a regulatory and disclosure failure. The ten payments do not fit (no option is written on them).
verified: VERIFIED through a second-hand summary of the Geneva Association pdf (S1); not quoted verbatim

idea: Dutch funding-ratio zones and conditional indexation. A fund's one number is assets over liabilities (x100%). Below about 104% the fund must take measures; between 104% and 110% there is no indexation; at 110% or more, indexation may be granted. The Dutch abandoned the regime: under the new system "the funding ratio no longer determines whether benefits rise or fall".
sources: De Nederlandsche Bank, "pensions funding ratio" page (paraphrase); Future of Pensions Act detail UNVERIFIED (Houthoff page not opened)
use: The cliff lesson: share a fixed fraction (half the shares) rather than all or nothing at a line. A three-zone "repair / hold / share" picture for co-sponsors.
critique: The thresholds are cliffs. The ratio moved with the discount rate, so cuts came when yields fell. Indexation means inflation-linking, which Laura's nominal payments lack. The procyclicality story comes from background reading and was not re-verified.
clash: Partly. A "repair" zone implies trading in response to a ratio, and the FINAL allows only two reasons to change. Use only the "half, not all" sharing lesson.

idea: Why the cushion is thin: about 1.00x cover is right for bought cash flows, and buffers exist for unmatched risk. Laura's ~102% sits under the Dutch 104% buffer, and her 1.006x sits under a project's 1.20-1.30x DSCR; FUSIONS gives headroom of $1,139 (3.8bp, A01).
sources: DNB page (S1 #3); Renewables Valuation Institute and Forvis Mazars DSCR pages (S2 #4); Model Suite A01
use: Answers a judge's "why so little slack?": the copied part needs no cushion, and the only cushion belongs to coupon reinvestment.
critique: Stale: 102% and 1.006x used the 16 Oct curve, and cover was 1.004x on 22 Oct (Conflict 7). CLAUDE.md (6 Nov, 5 Nov curve, MODEL) puts the ladder at $302,163, so cover is now below 1.00x, which is exactly the case the FINAL's COMPLETE2028 handles.
verified: Sources VERIFIED (S1, S2); cover figures MODEL (old design) and superseded
clash: No, it fits COMPLETE2028. Never quote 102% or 1.006x.
note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): cover 102% / 1.006x / headroom $1,139 is now below 1.00x at $300,000 ($302,287); 1.07x with Keel's margin (sections 1 2 and 6)

idea: Germany's maximum guaranteed rate (Höchstrechnungszins). The regulator caps what an insurer may guarantee at a cautious portfolio's expected yield less a 40% safety margin (at least 0.4pt in low-rate phases). The rate was 4.00% from July 1994 to June 2000, 3.25% from July 2000, 2.25% in 2007-11, 0.90% in 2017-21, 0.25% in 2022-24 and 1.00% in 2025; the DAV recommends 1.0% for 2027.
sources: DAV (German Actuarial Association), "Höchstrechnungszins in der Lebensversicherung" pdf; PwC Germany insurance-news blogs (articles 240720 and 252092)
use: Answers "why promise only half?". Regulators haircut what may be promised because sellers under competitive pressure cannot be trusted to cap themselves. The top of Laura's band is her own maximum guaranteed rate, and the FINAL's kept half is her haircut: the same instinct, not the same number.
critique: It protects new customers only, and it is blunt (one rate for all). It fell to 0.25%, making guarantees almost unsellable. The 40% is a judgement. The Swiss BVG comparison was not opened.
verified: VERIFIED (S1; paraphrase of the DAV and PwC pages)
note: Insurer-cap analogy; never "guarantee" for Laura's range; the cuts 4.31% and 2.87% play the safety margin's role (NUMBERS 4)

idea: Germany's additional interest reserve (Zinszusatzreserve, since 2011): when an old guaranteed rate rises above the reference rate, the insurer must build the reserve now, not when the gap bites.
use: The regulator's version of "price the reinvestment gap and set it aside early" (the 24 Oct K-fix; Synergy B's 2031 re-measure). With Japan: every insurer that waited paid more.
critique: Costly; it was a repair for old 4% contracts.
clash: Partly, as Synergy B. It is a set-aside the FINAL does not state; fine if it comes from Treasuries or 2028 money as a pre-set rule.

idea: Ruin theory with risky investment. With the reserve in cash, the chance of ruin falls exponentially as capital grows; with the reserve in a risky asset it falls only as a power, and if 2a/sigma^2 < 1, ruin is certain.
sources: Frolova, Kabanov and Pergamenshchikov, "In the insurance business risky investments are dangerous", Finance and Stochastics 6 (2002) 227-235; arXiv 2012.05083 (intro); arXiv 1505.04331
use: "Cushion in bonds, shared upside in shares", and "you cannot buy certainty in the asset that is trying to beat you" (a short Portfolio Analysis box).
critique: The result is asymptotic and assumes an infinite horizon, random claims and premium income, none of which Laura has. Window 28 Oct: an analogy, not a theorem-backed reason. The 1-in-10 to 1-in-100 figures are illustrations only.
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened the DOI abstract and the arXiv intros)

idea: The classical Cramér-Lundberg ruin model: seems relevant, isn't, because it needs random claims and Laura's are known to the dollar.
use: One FR "considered and rejected" line.
critique: As stated

idea: Solvency II's two boxes. A cash flow that "can be replicated reliably" using instruments with an observable market value is valued at the copy's price, with no separate risk margin. Only what cannot be copied (policy options, mortality, expenses) carries a margin.
use: Ten fixed nominal $50k payments are the cleanest replicable cash flow there is, and Treasuries are the copy, so the price of the promise is the price of the ladder. Coupon reinvestment is the part not replicated "in amount and timing", and its reserve is Laura's "risk margin" (the $10k-$20k hold-back option, number sheet decision 3; MODEL, old design). Device: a two-column page, "bought" and "reserved".
critique: Art. 40 says nothing about coupon reinvestment. "Replicable" is a judgement. The risk margin's calibration is a policy number.
verified: VERIFIED (77(4) quoted from legislation.gov.uk; Art. 40 paraphrased)
clash: No: the bought box is the FINAL's LADDER and FLOOR. Any hold-back sizing is not in the FINAL.
note: Now the hold-back is the extra Treasuries, $35,894 bought Jan 2028 (NUMBERS 2); no $10k-$20k or margin. Solvency II's two boxes stand.

idea: The zero-premium stress test. Solvency II Art. 18 does not count a future premium the payer cannot be compelled to pay, so count the 2028 deposit as zero and ask "would the payments hold if it never arrived?"
sources: Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art. 18 (legislation.gov.uk); R06 and L-10 (22 Oct curve)
use: Honest answer for the FR: usually, not always. The ladder costs more than $300k in 46-47% of paths (median gap about $9.8k), filled from the 2028 deposit. A cheque breaks only if yields fall about 2pt and the deposit falls by more than about 56% (M3); with a coverage rule the cheques survive a deposit of about $40k (M5). All MODEL, old design. This ties CAREER to COMPLETE2028, since the 2028 deposit is career income.
critique: Window 28 Oct: S1's "Yes" is FALSE on Keel's own numbers. Art. 18 is an analogy, not an authority.
verified: Art. 18 VERIFIED; S1's answer CONFLICTING (corrected by the Window and FUSIONS Conflict 1)

note: VOID figure (NUMBERS.md 9 Nov): ladder over $300k in 46-47%; break if the deposit falls over 56% after -2pt is now $2,287 over now and a 53% threshold (sections 1 and 5)

idea: Deferred income annuities and mortality credits: seems relevant (a lump sum now, fixed income later), isn't. Without a mortality pool, an annuity is a ladder plus the insurer's margin, and annuities are not WInS-permitted.

Kitces's example: a ladder supports about $57.43 a year per $1,000 against about $98.86 from a pooled annuity (25 years, 3%).

idea: Brady bonds (1989). Defaulted bank loans were rewritten into bonds whose principal was locked in specially issued 30-year US Treasury zeros held at the New York Fed, while the coupons stayed exposed (some had short rolling guarantees). Ecuador defaulted on its Bradys in 1999; Mexico retired its in 2003.
sources: Wikipedia "Brady Bonds"; Susmel, University of Houston course page (bauer.uh.edu/rsusmel/7386/brady.htm)
use: "The 1989 twin": lock what must not fail in dated Treasuries, let the rest float, and tell the buyer which is which. That is the FINAL's floor fund plus VT, done at national scale, and it justifies stating the bottom and the top at different confidence levels.
critique: The protection was partial and did not prevent later defaults. The vault was bought with borrowed multilateral money. Mathematically it is just a zero plus a risky bond; the novelty was packaging and transparent pricing. The "12-18 month" rolling guarantee is UNVERIFIED. Laura is the investor, not the debtor, and her risky half is shares she owns, with price risk but no default risk.
verified: VERIFIED (S2 via fetch-tool summaries; re-check quotes before citing)
clash: No, provided the FR says Brady's vault was Treasury zeros, which Laura cannot buy (STRIPS are banned). Her vault is coupon bonds and iBonds, which carry reinvestment risk.
note: Analogy only (Treasury-backed principal); never "protected"; the plan holds Treasury funds and individual Treasuries, not zeros (STRIPS banned)

idea: The Brady "stripped yield" as a method for the 2031 range. Price the protected principal as a Treasury zero, subtract it, and read the price of risk from what is left. For Laura: strip what is owned (the floor) and quote only the leftover with a probability. Mexican pars' stripped spread went from 254bp (31 Dec 1993) to 452bp (31 Mar 1994).
sources: Susmel, University of Houston course page
use: FR co-sponsor text: quote the bottom as owned and the top as a probability-weighted leftover. Three tools, one range: Brady strips, P99 covers, the newsvendor places.
critique: None beyond row 25

idea: Pitt's sinking fund (1786): £1m a year plus its interest to buy back debt. It worked from 1786 to 1793 while there was a surplus; with war borrowing from 1793 it bought debt with borrowed money. Walpole's earlier fund was raided; Pitt's was abandoned in the 1820s. Robert Hamilton of Aberdeen (1813), not Alexander Hamilton, exposed the fallacy.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund"; Hansard, Commons, 11 Mar 1823 (a cost "equal to a perpetual annuity of 268,000l."; "voted away 324,000,000l."); econbiz full text of The Industrial Revolution (author unconfirmed: the fund "lulled the mind of the ministers"; £271m and £618m borrowed); Wikipedia "Robert Hamilton (economist)"
use: "A promise to save is not a vault": the FINAL buys the payments in January 2027 instead of scheduling savings for them. FR section "what we refused to do". Keel's analogy: paying down a mortgage from a credit card you have not paid off.
critique: The fund was mis-fed, not pointless (the 1823 defenders), so "sinking funds are fraud" is unfair. Price's "penny at the birth of Christ" and Pitt's 1792 rule are UNVERIFIED and dropped. S2 itself notes "the owned bottom is only owned once the 2028 deposit has arrived".
verified: VERIFIED in parts (S2, fetch summaries); part of the Wikipedia date chain is tagged [citation needed]
clash: Partly. S2 says the 2028 money funds "only the floor and the stocks, never the ten payments"; the FINAL says it completes the ladder if yields fall.
where: S2 §2 l.88-148; FUSIONS §2 item 5; README l.72

idea: Ricardo's test: "No sinking fund can be efficient for the purpose of diminishing the debt, if it be not derived from the excess" of revenue over spending. Ask of every dollar the plan counts on: does it exist, or is it promised?
sources: Ricardo, Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ch. 17 (marxists.org)
use: The $300k exists in January 2027; the 2028 $150k is promised (career income). The honest answer under the FINAL: the ladder is bought with money that exists, and only a gap (if yields fall) waits on the deposit, as its first call.
critique: FUSIONS Conflict 1: the test "tests the 2027 gap". The ladder costs more than $300k in about 47% of paths (MODEL, old design), so the strong form fails.
verified: VERIFIED (quote from the marxists.org text, via S2)
clash: No in the honest form; yes if stated as "no payment waits on money not yet earned".
note: Ricardo's question now: most of each payment is inked Jan 2027 from money she has; the rest waits on the 2028 deposit (CONCEIT). 47% and $2,287 void.

idea: Pitt's anti-raid rule. What Pitt got right was making the money hard to raid by law. A stated rule and a public range do the same for Laura against her own future self.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund" (Pitt's 1786 law "stopped ministers from raiding the fund in crises")
use: Backs the FINAL's "only 2 possible reasons we would change our plan" as an anti-raid rule; links to rules over discretion and commitment devices (C R02 47-49).
critique: Pitt's law did not stop the wartime circularity: a rule protects the money only while its source is real.
note: Too small or off the path for 6-8 pages; store only

idea: Perry v. United States (1935). In the one time the US rewrote a bond term (the 1933 gold-clause abrogation), the Court called the abrogation invalid as applied to the bond. But Perry recovered nothing, because he could not show a loss of buying power, so the rewrite stood: "a right with no remedy". The line "as much bound by their contracts as are individuals" is Chief Justice Waite's, from the Sinking-Fund Cases (1879), quoted in Perry.
sources: Cornell LII, 294 U.S. 330; Window 28 Oct correction; FUSIONS header correction (Felix, huddle H-003)
use: Answers "what if the government changes the rules?". The only term ever rewritten was a gold clause, and Laura's bonds are plain dollars. The risk the Court named, buying power, sits on the facility side, which is why the kept half exists. Device: "which clause broke in 1933, and does Laura's bond have one?"
critique: It is a gold-clause case, not about ordinary nominal Treasuries. The "political compromise" reading is UNVERIFIED. It says nothing about debt-ceiling delays (C R02 13). Never write that the Treasury "cannot rewrite a bond", or that terms were "broken": they were "rewritten" once.
verified: VERIFIED (Cornell LII); S2's "cannot rewrite" gloss CONFLICTING (corrected)
clash: No, if worded per the corrections. It supports "barring a US default".
note: Same Perry v. United States point as H5-041.

idea: The late Treasury bill payments of April-May 1979: some bill redemptions were paid late. With 1933, these are the only blemishes on the US payment record that the files name.
sources: Felix's correction (huddle H-003); no outside source cited
use: The honest edge of "barring a US default": the near-miss was a delay. That is one more reason each holding matures before its January (C R02 13).
critique: None recorded. It concerns bills, which Laura does not hold directly.

idea: Project-finance two-test sizing. Lenders size debt on both P50 (the expected case, at about 1.20-1.30x DSCR) and P99 (the 1-in-100 bad case, at about 1.00x) and lend the lower amount. Under a normal curve with a 10% standard deviation, P90 is about 87% of P50 and P99 about 77%.
sources: Renewables Valuation Institute, "P50 vs. P99 in Project Finance: How Lenders Size Debt"; Forvis Mazars DSCR page; edbodmer.com wind P99 page (not opened)
use: How to state two numbers at two confidence levels without contradiction: a floor defensible in the 1-in-100 case, a top defensible in the expected case, and an announced gift equal to the lower of what the two tests allow.
critique: The normal curve ignores fat tails (C R02 59). Wind years are independent and stock years are not, so a 1-in-100 year is not a 1-in-100 path. The multiples are convention. Lenders can walk away; Laura cannot.
note: Two-test sizing now runs as the cuts 4.31% and 2.87% on owned payouts (NUMBERS 4); P50/P99 debt sizing is background only

idea: The cost-overrun facility and the order of call. A committed pre-completion standby is "callable only after contingency is fully used and contractor obligations are enforced", and the sponsor funds "all or a capped portion" last. Worked example (illustrative): budget 1,000, contingency 70 (7%), facility 100 (10%).
sources: Private Equity Bro, "Cost overrun facilities in project finance"; Gowling, Mondaq and rets.ai pieces not opened
use: The FINAL's kept half ("for building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar or a co-sponsor falling short") is a capped standby, called last, after the contractor, insurance, contingency and co-sponsors. Laura's gift is a capped contribution, not a completion undertaking. Say so, because overruns arrive when costs rise (repo check: Taiwan construction cost index +6.53% y/y, Aug 2026).
critique: The contingency size is illustrative, and real overruns are larger (C R05 19). Lenders rarely accept a cap on a completion guarantee. The "cost-to-complete undertaking" label is slightly off.
note: Never 'callable after the builder's contingency' or any order (second coherence reader: a rule the IPS never wrote); Norway's owner-held reserve (Q5-018) carries the practice.

idea: Contingent support goes uncounted, so price it. "Almost without exception, sponsors' financial reports ignore completion guarantees." Proposed charge = (50% minus P(abandonment)) x mean overrun + P(abandonment) x debt; e.g. a $500m project with $300m debt, a $50m overrun and 1% abandonment gives $27.5m.
sources: IJGlobal, "Quantifying contingent support in project financings"
use: Laura's 2031 range is itself a contingent commitment, and pricing it even roughly is the knowledgeable move for the FR.
critique: One author's proposal, not a standard; the 1% is invented for illustration.
note: Pricing contingent support is apt, but her flexibility has no promised use or order; never counted or priced in the range

idea: Florence's Monte delle doti (1425). A father deposited money when his daughter was about five, and the fund paid a named sum at marriage after 5-15 years. Depositors were lending to the Commune, which in 1452 sent the interest on 549,624 florins of the fund's credits to pay mercenaries (by 1455 its cash went to war; corrected 19 Nov from "the 1480s", card Q166 row 13, Kirshner and Molho 1978, p. 438, n. 65).
sources: Wikipedia "Monte delle doti"; a Unibo article quoting Molho (1994) p.31; Market Histories (a popular site, UNVERIFIED against Molho); Molho, Marriage Alliance in Late Medieval Florence (1994), and Kirshner-Molho (1978), titles only
use: "Same promise, different holder": the instrument has barely changed in 600 years, so what matters is who holds the money. A human story hook for an FR page on why to prefund and why Treasuries.
critique: The payment date was marriage, not fixed, so ages were fudged. The issuer was also the borrower. The return was a lure (11-15%), not a match. A dowry fund had no ladder or matching, so "the same idea" stretches. It had a forfeit feature Laura lacks.
verified: PARTLY; rate CONFLICTING (11-12% against "up to 15%": quote no rate); the raid's date VERIFIED as 1452 at source (Q166-013, 19 Nov 2026)
note: Colour only.

idea: Muni escrows and yield burning. Dealers overcharged for the escrow Treasuries in advance refundings. Lehman's 1994 portfolio of $15.8m carried a 0.42% markup, and Lehman agreed to pay $450,151.62 to issuers and $4,520,857.29 to the US Treasury.
use: "Cover after costs": headroom is only real after execution cost. Illustration: 0.42% of a $298k ladder is about $1,250, about two-thirds of the 16 Oct headroom (MODEL, old design). An FR Articulation footnote on real-world execution.
critique: The cases were about tax-arbitrage rules and dealer conduct, not escrow design. WInS charges a flat $10 per bond trade, with no markup.
note: 'Headroom' is void (the ten cost more than $300,000); 2.5 states the cost as $200 of fees, in dollars only.

idea: The debt service reserve account (DSRA), a cash reserve (usually 6-12 months of debt service) for revenue disruption: seems relevant, isn't, because Laura's ladder has no revenue to disrupt. The nearest real thing is the gap between a bond's maturity and its January payment.
use: One sentence: the buffer has a name and a convention. The trap: a DSRA is often a letter of credit (someone else's promise), while Laura's vault is a bond.
critique: S2 called the buffer "about two months" (the old November-maturity design). In the locked TNA, the Feb 2037 bond covers the Jan 2038 payment, a 10.5-month gap with its own reinvestment risk.

idea: The DSCR distribution lock-up. Three zones (target, lock-up, default) give warning room before a cliff, e.g. "nothing goes to the facility while funded cover is below the lock-up level".
sources: Forvis Mazars DSCR page (1.30x lock-up and 1.10x default in the worked example)
use: Could make the 2031 gift decision automatic; S2 says fold it into the Courtroom's lock rather than add a rule.
critique: Large overlap with L-10 and the lock. The page warns that the 1.30x sizing target is not a covenant level.
clash: Partly. A cover-triggered rule adds a trigger beyond the FINAL's two reasons; acceptable only if it limits the gift, never the payments.

idea: The gift range chart and the quiet phase. The lead gift is about 10-20% of the goal; gifts halve in size and double in number down the tiers; the top gifts are raised privately before the public launch; "leadership gifts make up 60% or more".
sources: Funraise gift range chart calculator; Maine State Library campaign FAQ; Nonprofit Quarterly, "The public phase of your capital campaign, part IV"; Soapbox Engage, "Capital campaigns 101: the quiet phase"

A chart can be revised in the quiet phase, and Laura's announced range cannot. Fundraisers say a range invites co-sponsors to plan on the bottom.

idea: The Ottoman cash waqfs of Bursa (1555-1823). Founders fixed rates of about 10.8% (1555) to 13% (1823) while market rates ran higher. About 20% survived more than a century, and growing the initial capital was "an important factor"; state policy ended them.

critique: No data on capital erosion, inflation or bad debts. How much of the failure was rigidity, trustee self-dealing or the state is unknown.

idea: Taiwan's hui (合會, 標會) and Civil Code Art. 709-5, 709-6, 709-7 and 709-9. The organiser (會首) takes the first pot without bidding, must pay any contribution members fail to pay, and is jointly liable for the payments owed by members who have already won a pot. The custom was codified in 2000.
sources: legis-pedia.com article 902 (a secondary commentary; the Ministry of Justice site refused access); 月旦法學雜誌 No. 243 (2015) abstract at lawdata.com.tw; Besley, Coate and Loury (1993), American Economic Review (LSE summary); Wikipedia "Hui (informal loan club)"
use: A Taiwanese co-sponsor already knows the question to ask of any pooled promise: "who stands behind the last payment?" Laura's answer is a hui whose organiser is the US Treasury. The shares are where an organiser could come up short, which is why they are never promised. Laura is the last seat in the circle.
critique: A hui is a credit club, not an investment. Its payments rotate between people, while Laura's go one way. There are no sources for Taiwan bid rates or losses (Wikipedia's collapse examples are Vietnamese). Wharton judges may not know it.
verified: VERIFIED through secondary sources (Art. 709-1 not retrieved)
note: Tue 17 Nov evening: retired by card Q112 row 36. A hui rests on the organiser's credit and the members' good faith (Civil Code art. 709-9's legislative reason), the very risk IPS l.11 rules out, so an image of a hui organised by the US Treasury inverts l.11.

idea: Ergodicity and gambler's ruin: an average across many investors hides the fact that one investor taking a fixed $50k a year out of shares can run dry, and no later good year brings back a missed payment. So payment safety has to be built in (structural), not left to the odds (statistical).
sources: Peters, "The ergodicity problem in economics", Nature Physics 15 (2019) (coin toss: +50%/-40%; positive average, negative typical path); Doctor, Wakker and Wang, Nature Physics 2020 rebuttal (Tinbergen summary); Wikipedia "Gambler's ruin" (Pascal to Fermat, 1656); Milevsky and Robinson, "A Sustainable Spending Rate without Simulation", FAJ 2005
niche: NICHE (ergodicity framing); gambler's ruin is TEXTBOOK
use: "Laura's wealth grows by multiplication but her payments leave in fixed dollars; the only safe way out is to fix it in dollars with instruments that pay in dollars." Coin toss: the average investor gains, the typical one loses.
critique: Peters is contested ("elementary misunderstandings") and partly restates Kelly/log utility (R02 #34); cite him only with the rebuttal. Ruin here is finite (ten payments) and binary (a broken promise). Scout toy model (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), all-stock, JPM 6.7%/16.47%): about 13% of paths miss a payment (24% under 2 pt stress) while mean terminal wealth is about $0.76m and the median about $0.50m.

The twist: certainty costs Laura almost nothing, because the Treasury curve prices the ladder fairly and the unpromised money still buys shares.

idea: Bullet vs barbell (Fong-Vasicek): bonds that all mature at the payment date (a bullet) deliver in every case. Test risk payment by payment, not by the whole book's "10-year duration".

idea: Dutch book as a consistency audit: never state a probability you wouldn't bet at. Any figure that appears in both the IPS/TNA and the FR must describe the same event with the same number. "Upside for free above a guaranteed floor" is the one inconsistent promise.

idea: Two-sided refutation: name the strongest objection a professional would raise and answer it in the same text. That beats a one-sided case; naming an objection and leaving it unanswered is worse than silence.

idea: Swiss cheese and common-cause failure: count failures by cause, not by component. Laura's layers (the reinvested coupons, the 2028 deposit, the share cushion) may share one hole: a recession that lowers yields, cuts her writing income and drops shares all at once. R11 L4 adds that held-to-maturity bonds don't mind falling prices; their only weakness is yields falling for good, which usually comes with the same slump. A 2022-style year (yields up, shares down) opens a different pair of holes.
sources: Reason, "Human error: models and management", BMJ 2000;320:768-770 (PMC1117770); US NRC common-cause failure document ML082350989; Wikipedia, Fukushima (10 of 13 cooling systems lost; the one air-cooled generator survived); 10 CFR Part 50 App. A (single-failure rule; Criterion 22 on diversity) (Cornell LII); Reason 1990 (RG1)

critique: It's a metaphor, not a calculation. Redundancy arithmetic assumes independent failures. It earns its place only by naming a specific shared cause. Bond yields falling in recessions is "standard, not sourced". There is no joint probability (Jun to model).

idea: Certainty over the whole chain, not per payment: ten payments in series fail if any one fails. "99% safe per year" is about 90% over ten years (0.99^10), the same way a "100-year flood" has about a 9.6% chance in ten years. State "a high degree of certainty" for all ten payments together.

critique: Floods are nearly independent from year to year; Laura's risks share one cause. The lesson is the unit, not the formula.

Pre-commitment, in plain words: "the plan decides now what it will do in 2028, 2031 and 2033"

Once Laura names a top, the shares behind it are a quasi-bond, so she turns them into a real bond before she names it

idea: Breaking a promise costs trust, and beating it earns nothing: exceeding a promise made people no happier than keeping it, and trust is "much easier to destroy than to create". So the range is set where she can surely keep it, and any surplus stays hers and unannounced, never "more if markets are kind"

idea: The newsvendor's critical fractile: if over-promising costs k times what under-promising costs, promise the 1/(1+k) quantile (k = 4 gives the 20th percentile). A modelled top reached ~76% of the time sits near p24, implying k ≈ 3.2 ("over-promising treated as about three times worse"). Buying both ends is the limit where a miss is unacceptable. The bottom here is owned and has no quantile, so the rule applies only to the top
sources: Arrow, Harris & Marschak, "Optimal Inventory Policy", Econometrica 19(3) 1951, 250-272; IDEA_BANK rows 5, 84, 88; FACTS N5

idea: Gifts promised from a donor's own fortune fail when the fortune falls. Colleges normally expect 2-5% of pledges to go uncollected, and one recommends having 50% in hand before building ("You can't pay the contractor with a pledge"). use: Test (a wording guard): if the report gives a source for "never erase", it is Venetian writers of the 1530s-40s, not Pacioli. Its reason is proof ("you cannot prove what was there"), so the rule is about the record, not ownership
critique: A gloss, not Manzoni's Italian. Geijsbeek says Manzoni "copies whole chapters" of Pacioli, so the line may be Manzoni's wording of Pacioli's storno
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026, Geijsbeek's text); Manzoni's own words UNVERIFIED (not read)
note: Tue 17 Nov: wording guard, kept only with the right attribution: the never cross out or erase line is Manzoni's (Venice, as Geijsbeek 1914 renders his index), never Pacioli's; Manzoni's Italian not read; no CONCEIT line attributes it to Pacioli, so nothing there to fix.

idea: Pacioli's 13th inventory item is money with Venice's Camera de l'Imprestì, listed with the office's book, the page of your account, the clerk's name, and dates "put down precisely so that you know when everything falls due and what the per cent. is". Taiwan's company law still asks property accounts for 「名稱、種類、價格、數量及其存置地點」 (name, kind, price, quantity and where it is kept)
sources: Pacioli (1494), ch. 3, 13th item; ch. 17 heading ("Camera de l'Imprestì (municipal loan bank)"), in Geijsbeek (1914); 商業會計法 art. 26
use: Explain (2.0, beside Table 1): the first printed bookkeeping book lists claims on a public office by where they are recorded and when they fall due. Table 1 lists each Treasury by CUSIP and maturity, every holding at one broker (cards Q38, Q78), held for her (UCC 8-503, card Q72)
critique: Geijsbeek calls the office "a bank" and a "municipal loan bank"; whether it held Venice's public debt was not read, so never say "Pacioli's merchants held government bonds". His deposit earns a rate; Laura's ladder is matched to dated payments
note: Tue 17 Nov: store only; a charming 1494 precedent for Table 1's identifiers and dates but close to trivia (Book 18) and it serves no decision; never say Pacioli's merchants held government bonds; Taiwan's art. 26 does not bind Laura.

idea: Pacioli sorts what is owed to you by who owes it: "of good money, if the money is due from good people, otherwise you will say of bad money"; then "enter diligently every thing that you have ... even if there were ten thousand items"
use: Explain (2.0 definition, 3d): a written figure is not ink because it is written. It is ink because of who will pay it: a Treasury held to its date. A co-sponsor's pledge is owed; Laura's floor is owned (Q83 guard)
critique: Pacioli records bad money in the inventory too, so ledger ink holds doubtful claims; Laura states none. His test is a merchant's view of a person's character; hers is a Treasury held to its date
note: Tue 17 Nov: 2.0 guard evidence: a ledger's ink can hold bad money, so a written figure is not ink; supports the definition's owned, never signed; the synthesis is Q106-035 and the owed against owned point is already Q7c-035.

idea: Pacioli has a public officer's clerk "attest to the truth of everything" and "attach the seal of that office to make the books authentic for any case in court"; keeping two sets, "one to the buyer and one to the seller", is "very bad" because "they commit perjury"
use: Explain (3d): one set of figures. What co-sponsors hear is the range the report states. The seal turn (CONCEIT V2.2 3d) gains a history: a seal attests the record
critique: Supports Q83's guard: the seal proves the book is the one presented, not that the merchant can pay. Laura's ink needs no seal or officer; never "ink is a sealed figure"
note: Tue 17 Nov: store only; a notary's seal attests the book, not the money (Q83 guard); never mix with V2.2's calligraphy seal in 3d, and never ink as a sealed figure.

idea: When a scrap-book entry is carried to the journal, Pacioli strikes it with "a single diagonal line (una sola riga a traverso)", so it shows as posted and stays readable. A later writer in Geijsbeek's abstracts throws the waste book away once posted ("In Holland they do not preserve it"), while "Blotting or erasures in the journal are improper"
sources: Pacioli (1494), ch. 12; Geijsbeek (1914), abstract of a later writer (Ympyn or Stevin; not confirmed in the extract)
use: Explain (3c, 3f): the move is a posting. Half of the shares become Treasuries, and the forecast top is struck once and left readable, so the report can show the figure before rounding ($118,072) beside the stated top ($115,000, NUMBERS 4)
critique: Comics erase the pencils after inking (card Q40). Pacioli keeps the struck draft readable; the Dutch practice throws it away. The crafts split on what happens to a draft
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026); the later writer's name UNVERIFIED
note: Tue 17 Nov: struck-but-readable drafts do the job non-photo blue already does in 3c; never print the unrounded $118,072 in prose (density cut: Table 2's note); the later writer behind erasures improper is unconfirmed.

idea: Leave no empty space where a figure could be slipped in. Entries go "close under each other ... without leaving of any empty paper, to avoid suspicion of Forging any parcells betwixt them" (Dafforne 1635). Pacioli opens accounts "without leaving any space in between ... so that nobody can speak evil of you". Taiwan rules through skipped lines and stamps unused pages 「空白作廢」. UK cheque users "draw a line through all unused space so that fraudsters cannot write in extra names"
sources: Dafforne (1635), reproduced in Geijsbeek (1914); Pacioli ch. 28; 會計法 art. 68; 商業會計處理準則 art. 11; Pay.UK (2022) s. 3.2
use: Explain (3c, 3b): the space above the stated top is ruled off. About $8,476 above $115,000 joins her flexibility (NUMBERS 4), so no larger figure can be read into the gap and no stated contribution ever sits above the stated top
critique: These rules stop someone else forging; Laura's ruled line stops her own overpromise. The space above her top is not void: it is money she keeps
note: Tue 17 Nov: store; ruling off unused space maps loosely to the cap ($8,476 excess, NUMBERS 4) but the rule stops someone else forging and the space above her top is money she keeps, so trim and bleed in 3c does it better.

idea: Pacioli tells merchants to close the books every year, "especially if you are in partnership with others. The proverb says: Frequent accounting makes for long friendship"
use: Explain (3d, Table 3's sentence): an account to co-sponsors can be regular, but only of the ink (which Treasuries are held, for which dates). Whether 3d offers it is Caplet's call
critique: The parallel breaks where the conceit bites: a yearly account of the shares would put pencil in front of co-sponsors before the move. Co-sponsors are not partners in her portfolio
clash: Possible: a yearly letter is not in the IPS; offer it as wording only, never as a new rule
note: Tue 17 Nov: a yearly account to co-sponsors is a new process outside the IPS, and before 2031 it would state figures the plan states only at the 2031 meetings (SKELETON 3c, IPS l.15); the proverb is decoration.

idea: Pacioli on public loan offices: keep these accounts "very clearly and obtain good written evidence as to debits and credits in the handwriting of the clerks", because "they often change their clerks" and each blames the last
use: Test (3e, Table 3's sentence): keep the broker's written record of each Treasury held for her and check it against Table 1. Custody is where an owned figure can go astray (card Q72: SIPC caps only its own top-up; the risk above it is delay)
critique: Pacioli feared clerks' errors at a loan office. Laura's Treasuries are book entries held through a broker, where a lost record means delay, not loss (card Q72). Never "the broker's record is the ink"
note: Tue 17 Nov: store; a 1494 precedent for 3e's custody clause (checked each January against the broker statement, already in SKELETON); never the broker's record is the ink.

idea: Taiwan's Accounting Act (government books), art. 67. A writing error found at the time is ruled through by the clerk who wrote it, signed or sealed, and 「不得挖補、擦、刮或用藥水塗滅」 (no patching, rubbing, scraping or blotting out with chemicals). An error found later that changes a total needs a new voucher. Clerks are jointly liable for losses their writing errors cause the treasury
sources: 會計法 art. 67 (law.moj.gov.tw, pcode T0030001); last amended 1972 per LawPlayer
use: Explain (2.0 or 3d, in the team's sentence, never Laura's words): this is Taiwan's literal rule that a written figure is never rubbed out, and it completes Q83's turn on the arts funders' receipts
critique: It binds government agencies (and subsidised private bodies, art. 121), not Laura or co-sponsors' pledges. It is about the record, not ownership. Never legal advice (the case leaves Taiwan law out)
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; Keel translation; amendment year from LawPlayer, a secondary site)
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3d store; Taiwan's Accounting Act art. 67 (no patching, rubbing or scraping) is the national version of Q83's turn but lacks the word pencil and is about the record, not ownership; Q83-029 stays the turn; never legal advice.

idea: Taiwan's company books, 商業會計處理準則 art. 13. If correcting an error leaves the total unchanged: 「劃紅線二道」 (two red lines) through it, the correct figure above, signed or sealed by whoever corrects it, or a new voucher. If the correction changes the total, a new voucher is required. Art. 13 is untouched by the 3 Jul 2026 amendment (arts 15, 25, 26, 33-35, 45; in force 1 Jan 2028)
sources: 商業會計處理準則 art. 13 (law.moj.gov.tw pcode J0080010; law.moea.gov.tw)
use: Explain (3d or 2.0): "in a Taiwanese company's books a wrong figure is struck through twice in red and signed, never rubbed out". The correction stays visible, with a name on it
critique: A regulation under the Business Entity Accounting Act, not the Act itself; about past entries. Red here marks a correction, not a loss
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; Keel translation)
note: Tue 17 Nov: twin of Q106-010 for company books (two red lines, signed); one Taiwan correction rule is enough, and red adds a colour the conceit avoids.

idea: The official English of art. 13 has an error: both sentences say "does not affect the total"; the Chinese second sentence says 「影響總數者」 (does affect the total)
sources: Regulations on Business Entity Accounting Handling, official English, amended 2021-09-16
use: Test (a wording guard): quote the Chinese with Keel's translation, never the official English, if 2.0 or 3d uses this rule
critique: A translation fault, not a rule
note: Tue 17 Nov: guard only for Q106-011: quote the Chinese with Keel's translation, never the 2021 official English of art. 13.

idea: The Business Entity Accounting Act (商業會計法) has no "erase" article. It requires numbered pages that may not be damaged (art. 24) and punishes forging or altering (變造) books or destroying their pages with up to five years in prison or a fine of up to NT$600,000 (art. 71); destroying pages or the audit trail draws NT$60,000-300,000 (art. 76)
sources: 商業會計法 arts 24, 71, 76 (amended 18 Jun 2014; pcode J0080009); compare Pacioli ch. 6 (pages numbered against someone who "could tear out" one)
use: Test (claim 2): never "Taiwan's Business Accounting Act forbids erasing". If the Act is named, say it "forbids altering the books"
critique: Penalties for falsifying records say nothing about what stands behind a figure
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; Keel translation)
note: Tue 17 Nov: wording guard: never say Taiwan's Business Entity Accounting Act forbids erasing; if named, it forbids altering or destroying the books (arts 24, 71, 76).

idea: The same Act's art. 33: 「非根據真實事項，不得造具任何會計憑證，並不得在會計帳簿表冊作任何記錄」. No voucher may be made and nothing recorded in the books unless a real event stands behind it
use: Explain (3d): Taiwan's accounting law lets no figure into the books without a real event behind it; Laura lets no figure into her co-sponsor letter without an owned Treasury behind it
critique: Art. 33 covers events that have happened; Laura's ink is a payment still to come, backed by a security she holds now. It is a business law, not a rule for a donor's letter
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; Keel translation)
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3d store; no figure in the books without a real event behind it is a neat Taiwan echo of no stated figure without an owned Treasury, but it binds companies, not a donor's letter; Q67-043 and Q43-009 carry the point more directly.

idea: Taiwan books a company's income on the accrual basis, 「於確定應收時」: when it is certain to be receivable
use: Explain (3c): the top becomes "certain to be receivable" only after the move, so that is when it is stated. 3c's "certain" keeps the stated range as its subject (cards Q71, Q74)
critique: Accrual timing for a company's income, not a portfolio forecast; the parallel is the word 確定 (certain), not the rule
note: Tue 17 Nov: store; the parallel is the word 確定 only; 3c's certain keeps the stated range as its subject (Q71, Q74), never the figures.

idea: IAS 37: "An entity shall not recognise a contingent asset" (para 31), "since this may result in the recognition of income that may never be realised. However, when the realisation of income is virtually certain, then the related asset is not a contingent asset and its recognition is appropriate" (para 33)
sources: IFRS Foundation, IAS 37 paras 31-33 (2021 and 2024 versions); AASB 137 has the same text
use: Explain (2.0 definition, 3c, 3d): Laura's rule is the global accounting standard's rule for gains. A figure is booked once it has stopped being contingent, and the top stops being contingent at the move, when the Treasuries that pay it are owned
critique: IAS 37 covers claims from past events (its example is a lawsuit the entity is pursuing, para 32), not a portfolio's future value. Laura writes a letter, not financial statements: a parallel, never "IFRS requires"
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3c outside check, verified quotes, but IAS 37's bar is virtually certain, a likelihood, while Laura's is owned, which is stricter; never Laura's rule is IAS 37's rule or IFRS requires, never set it beside KPMG's probability is not a factor (US GAAP), never prudence or conservatism (CONCEIT 5b rank 1).

idea: IAS 37 is less strict than Laura in one place. A contingent asset is disclosed "where an inflow of economic benefits is probable" (para 34); it is "assessed continually" and recognised "in the period in which the change occurs" (para 35)
use: Explain (3d, 3b): Laura mentions none of her pencil to co-sponsors, not even a probable figure. Her flexibility (the half kept, $21,347 centrally, NUMBERS 4) is never offered as money that might come. "The period in which the change occurs" is one date: the move on the first trading day of 2031
critique: A company must tell its own investors about probable gains. Co-sponsors do not own Laura's portfolio, so saying nothing about the pencil misleads no one
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3b-3d: IAS 37 would disclose a probable gain and Laura offers none of her flexibility ($21,347, NUMBERS 4), backing never offered; the change happens on one date, the move in January 2031; a parallel, never a rule she follows.

idea: US GAAP says the same, at least since 1975: "Contingencies that might result in gains usually are not reflected in the accounts since to do so might be to recognize revenue prior to its realization". Any disclosure must "avoid misleading implications as to the likelihood of realization"
sources: FASB (1975), FAS 5 para 17(a)-(b), carrying forward ARB 50; now ASC 450-30-25-1 (as quoted by PwC)
use: Test (3d co-sponsor language): the "misleading implications" clause is the test for Laura's words. Nothing in them may suggest a figure above the stated top
critique: Written for company accounts; "realization" fits a sale. Laura's top is made real by buying Treasuries, not by receiving cash
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; ARB 50's year not read)
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3d test from US GAAP (FAS 5 para 17, ASC 450-30): Laura's words must avoid misleading implications as to the likelihood of realization, so nothing in them suggests more than the stated top; fits SKELETON 3d's no up to, no at least.

idea: KPMG: "probability is not a factor in the recognition of gain contingencies. Therefore, gain contingencies are typically recognized later than loss contingencies"; realisation "requires resolution of all uncertainties"
use: Explain and test (3c, with 3a): this is why a top that is 97% likely a month before the move is still not stated. For gains the odds do not count (NUMBERS 4 l.378: a month early, 2.9% of house paths short). The plan treats risk the way accountants treat losses, early: the extra Treasuries ($35,894) ink the interest line in January 2028 (3a), and 3e states the 1-in-20 building-cost and Taiwan-dollar limit now
critique: "All uncertainties" goes too far for Laura: after the move the funds' costs beyond the fee remain, covered by the 0.5% held back. Say "the top is owned", never "every uncertainty is resolved"
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3c's best outside answer to why not state a top early: for gains probability is not a factor (KPMG on ASC 450-30); fix: 97% is Keel arithmetic on NUMBERS 4 l.453's 2.9% (not l.378) and is said as aha row 7 words it; drop the treats losses early clause, which reads as conservatism (CONCEIT 5b rank 1).

idea: PwC: a gain is "realizable when assets are readily convertible to known amounts of cash or claims to cash", and one test is "Whether the counterparty has the ability or wherewithal to pay the amount". Deloitte traces "realized or realizable" to Concepts Statement 5, para 83
sources: PwC (2025), Viewpoint FSP 23.5; Deloitte (n.d.), Roadmap: Contingencies, 3.3
use: Explain (2.0 definition): this splits ink from pencil in accounting's own words. VT can be turned into cash quickly but not into a known amount, so it is pencil. A Treasury held to its date is a claim to a known amount from a payer that can pay, so it is ink
critique: An iBond fund pays its net asset value, not par (NUMBERS 3), so the floor's $103,178 is not known to the dollar. The rounding down and the 0.5% held back keep the stated bottom safe. Never call the fund's payout fixed
note: Tue 17 Nov: the VT mapping likely breaks: Concepts Statement 5 para 83, which Deloitte cites, counts fungible units with quoted prices in an active market as readily convertible (check at source), so VT would be realizable; split ink from pencil by payer and date, never by convertibility; never fixed for IBTM's payout.

idea: To accountants, "virtually certain" is the line for booking a gain, not a percentage; the IPCC uses it for 99-100% (card Q4c)
use: Test (3c's word): a finance judge reads "virtually certain" as IAS 37's booking line, which the top passes only after the move. 3c's word stays "certain" with the stated range as its subject (cards Q71, Q74), never "virtually certain" as a confidence label
critique: Two professions use the phrase in two ways; using it invites the other reading
note: Tue 17 Nov: keep the guard (3c says certain, never virtually certain) but drop which the top passes only after the move and not a percentage: IAS 37 leaves the bar unquantified, so where the top crosses it is Keel's inference.

idea: Negotiable Instruments Act (票據法) art. 11(3): 「票據上之記載，除金額外，得由原記載人於交付前改寫之。但應於改寫處簽名。」 Every item on a cheque or note except the amount may be rewritten by its writer before delivery, signed at the change. On 23 Mar 2026 the Taichung District Court held a promissory note void because its amount had been changed
sources: 票據法 art. 11, as quoted in 臺灣臺中地方法院 115年度司票字第2295號 (23 Mar 2026)
use: Explain (3d, in the team's sentence before Laura's words): in Taiwan's own law the amount is the one line that can never be pencil. It is written once, or the paper is void. Laura's range is her amount line, written once, after the move
critique: A note is a promise to pay, so it is owed, which Laura's ink is not. Her letter is not a negotiable instrument. Never legal advice
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; the statute read as the ruling quotes it, MOJ page not opened)
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3d candidate, Taiwan's own law fixes the amount line (票據法 art. 11, Taichung ruling 23 Mar 2026), but a note is owed, so use it only for writing the amount once, in the team's sentence, never as what makes a figure ink (owned, never signed, Q42); one Taiwan turn with Q83-029; read the statute on the MOJ page; never legal advice.

idea: Taiwan's Accounting Act tells a government accountant to refuse to sign a document whose figures or words show 「塗改痕跡」 (marks of alteration) not signed or sealed, or whose amount in words and in figures disagree
use: Store, possible 3d context: finance staff at a public co-sponsor in Taiwan work under a rule that refuses an altered amount. A figure stated once and never changed fits that habit
critique: About vouchers inside government, not pledges or donors' letters. No source read says any co-sponsor applies it
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; Keel translation)
note: Tue 17 Nov: store only; about vouchers inside government, and no source says any co-sponsor applies it; never imply co-sponsors check Laura's figures this way.

idea: The Accounting Act applies (「準用」) to private bodies that receive government subsidies, as the government's accounting office decides (art. 121). Taipei's and Taichung's arts-grant receipts are void if 「擦刮挖補塗改」 (card Q83 row 29), the same verbs as art. 67's 「挖補、擦、刮」
sources: 會計法 arts 67, 121; card Q83 row 29
use: Explain (3d, deepens Q83's turn): the arts funders' pencil rule is not a local quirk. The national Accounting Act bans scraping and patching government books in the same words
critique: The link is Keel's own reading of matching words; no source read says the grant rules derive from art. 67. Never "co-sponsors count only ink" (rater AI)
verified: UNVERIFIED (the link between the two; both texts read at source, 17 Nov 2026)
note: Tue 17 Nov: the link between the grant rules and art. 67 is Keel's reading; say the same words, never derived from, and drop not a local quirk, which implies the link; never co-sponsors count only ink.

idea: Bookkeepers wrote every entry in ink and running totals in pencil: "These footings should always be written in pencil" (1912); the total "should be entered in pencil in small figures immediately under the last regular entry, which, of course, is in ink" (1920); the trial balance in "light pencil marks, which may be erased when the work is completed" (1887)
sources: Bookkeeping: Complete course (1912); Business accounting vol. 1 (1920); Bookkeeping and accountancy (1911); Dominion Business College (1887); Teaching bookkeeping and accounting ("Pencil Footings")
use: Explain (2.0, 3c, 3a): in a ledger the pencil was the total, not the entries. The ten payments and the bottom are entries in ink; the shares' running value is a pencil total, and so is the interest cash earns while it waits until the extra Treasuries ink it (3a). Never in Table 1 itself
critique: A running total is arithmetic on known entries and is right once added; a share value is a market price that keeps moving
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; authors of the 1911, 1912 and 1920 texts not recorded)
where: This run: survivorlibrary.com; the-eye.eu; uoguelph.ca; archive.org
note: Tue 17 Nov: 2.0 or 3c, pairs with Q106-026: bookkeepers really kept entries in ink and running totals in pencil, a literal pencil and ink in the judge's own trade; close to finance (Q58 claim 4), so one clause; never in Table 1.

idea: A pencil total was inked only when the account was closed: "Rule and foot the account; write the footings in black ink" (1912); "rule the closing lines in red ink and enter the footings in black ink" (1911)
sources: Bookkeeping: Complete course (1912); Bookkeeping and accountancy (1911)
use: Explain (3c, 3d; a candidate turn): the move is the closing. Half of the shares are ruled off into Treasuries, and the top, a pencil total until then, is written in ink. The other half stays an open account in pencil: her flexibility
critique: Closing fixes a past total; the move fixes a future payment by buying Treasuries. And only half the account is closed
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3c-3b, the strongest new turn that keeps the mapping: a pencil total was inked only when the account was ruled and closed, as the top is owned only at the move, while half the account stays open as her flexibility, the pencil never inked; needs no glossary; textbook authors not recorded.

idea: Checks were made in pencil and never erased: "Use a pencil for checking, and make very small check marks. These marks should not be erased" (1912). Auditors ticked in coloured pencil: "a check mark in colored pencil should be made to the right of the amount" (Castenholz 1919, p. 156), to limit "the danger of the office force tampering with the auditor's ticks" (p. 192); "a tick in red pencil is made to the right of each account" (Peloubet 1949)
sources: Bookkeeping: Complete course (1912); Ariail & Hughes (2014), quoting Castenholz (1919); Peloubet (1949)
use: Explain (3e monitoring; said beside Table 3, never in it): monitoring is the auditor's tick beside each inked line, a check in another colour that the Treasury paying it is still held and on its date, never part of the figure. Panel 3 marked down the printing-trade words; a finance judge needs no glossary for a tick
critique: A tick confirms a past entry against a voucher; Table 3 watches future events (fund notices, the 2028 deposit)
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026); Castenholz read only as Ariail & Hughes quote him
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3e, a glossary-free alternative to registration marks (panel 3) but a coloured-pencil tick gives pencil a second meaning beside the definition; say a tick beside each owned line, never a pencil tick or a colour; Castenholz read only via Ariail and Hughes.

idea: British audits of the 1940s ticked each figure twice, "in front for a posting and behind for a voucher", and three times in the cash book; clerks used stamps "often using different colored ink"; the work was called "ticking and bashing"
use: Explain (2.0, beside Table 1): every inked figure has its voucher. Each payment ticks to a Treasury by CUSIP and date (Table 1 by CUSIP, card Q38). This also kills claim 3's "auditors worked in pencil" as a rule
critique: A voucher proves a past payment; a CUSIP proves present ownership of a future one
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; page range not confirmed)
note: Tue 17 Nov: twin of Q106-027 (ticking each figure to its voucher); the CUSIP tie is already Table 1's job (Q38).

idea: Working papers: "Some prominent firms prepare their working papers in pencil, some in ink. There seems to be little uniformity of practice". "Report drafts may be prepared in pencil, since the copy of the report itself is the permanent record. If working papers are to be examined by a third party, papers prepared in ink convey a greater impression of authenticity". An instruction in the same book prefers pencil "due to ease in correcting errors or making subsequent adjustments"
use: Explain (3d): accountants split pencil from ink by who will read a paper and whether it must last. What a third party will rely on goes in ink, and Laura's co-sponsors are that third party
critique: Peloubet's ink is about appearance ("impression of authenticity"); Laura's ink is ownership. An inked look without an owned Treasury is exactly the fault the conceit avoids
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026; who wrote the "pencil is preferred" instruction quoted in the book is not confirmed)
note: Tue 17 Nov: store; Peloubet's ink is an impression of authenticity, so the parallel breaks under its own disanalogy; useful only as the warning that an inked look without an owned Treasury is the fault the conceit avoids.

idea: Some auditors put "a special form of check-mark upon all figures upon which a correction may appear", then "look back over their work for corrections, erasures or alterations in order to see that nothing of the kind appears without the special check-mark"
sources: The science and practice of auditing (Internet Archive scan via Wikimedia Commons; author and year not confirmed)
use: Test (3e): no stated figure changes without its mark. The IPS gives only two (l.17): a missed deposit or a Treasury default; "A fall in the market is not one of them"
critique: The auditor's mark guards against someone else's change; the two reasons bind Laura's own hand
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 17 Nov 2026); author and date UNVERIFIED
note: Tue 17 Nov: store only; the two reasons are exits for when the plan cannot be carried out (Q7b-033), not marks on corrections; author and year unverified.

idea: Cheques are written in indelible ink and corrected in the open: "Use a ball point pen with indelible or permanent black or blue (preferably black) ink"; changes are "made clearly by crossing through the error", "initialling or signing the correction"
sources: Pay.UK (2022), Best practice guidelines for business users of cheques, s. 3.2
use: Explain (2.0, the definition): the most familiar money document already follows the conceit's rule. The amount goes on in ink, and a change shows
