idea: "In the red": Rollins (1907, quoted by Gary Martin): "Formerly it was customary, and is now with some bookkeepers, to make an entry of a loss in red ink, from whence arose the term 'in the red'". The OED's first "in the red" is 1926 and "in the black" 1928 (quoted by Barry Popik); Campbell's Actual Accounting (1911-12): "Enter the $266.00 of loss in red ink"
use: Test (a wording guard): no "in the red" or "in the black" anywhere in the report, and no colour for VT (CONCEIT guard)
critique: The origin story rests on two secondary pages
verified: UNVERIFIED (secondary pages read 17 Nov 2026; Rollins and the OED not read)
note: Tue 17 Nov: in the red rests on secondary pages; the guard (no in the red or in the black, no colour for VT) is covered by Q106-033 and CONCEIT's no-puns, no-colour rules.

idea: Red ink did not mean loss alone. "Enter the gain on the debit side, in red ink"; "Red ink is used commonly for rulings of all kinds, for closing entries in the ledger, and for records that require emphasis ... The use of red ink is largely a matter of custom" (1912). "The inventory and the closing entry of gain or loss are written in red ink to distinguish them from the business items" (1887). Taiwan uses red for correction lines (row 11)
sources: Bookkeeping: Complete course (1912); Dominion Business College (1887); 商業會計處理準則 art. 13
use: Test (kills claim 4's "red always meant loss"): if red ink is ever mentioned, it marked closings, transfers and corrections
critique: None needed
note: Tue 17 Nov: guard only: red ink marked closings, gains and corrections, not loss alone; the report uses no colour words.

idea: Comics and ledgers treat an ink mistake in opposite ways. The comics artist paints it out in white so the printed page looks clean (card Q40). The bookkeeper must leave it readable, struck through and signed or answered by a counter-entry (rows 1, 10, 11), because a hidden correction "will be construed as deceit" (row 2)
sources: Card Q40 (Richmond 2006; Martin); Pacioli ch. 31; 會計法 art. 67; 商業會計處理準則 art. 13; Geijsbeek (1914)
use: Explain (3d, 3c; the strongest new turn): a figure given to co-sponsors lives in a ledger, not on a comic page, so any change to it would show. That is why Laura states only what she owns, after the move, and never has to correct it
critique: Keel's synthesis of verified sources. Laura's ink is never corrected at all, so the turn explains why she waits, not how she would fix a figure
verified: VERIFIED (each source read at source, 17 Nov 2026, or by card Q40; the synthesis is Keel's)
where: This run: archive.org; law.moj.gov.tw; card Q40
note: Tue 17 Nov: 3c-3d, a witty glossary-free turn (the inker may paint a mistake out, the bookkeeper may not hide one) but fix: the will be construed as deceit quote is Manzoni's as Geijsbeek renders him, never Pacioli's; and it must not undo V2.2 3d's printed page (use one frame for co-sponsors, never lives in a ledger, not on a comic page).

idea: Where the bookkeeping parallel breaks: a ledger's ink proves what happened; Laura's ink proves what will be paid. Ledger ink can hold "bad money" (row 4) and is corrected in ink (row 1); Laura's ink is a Treasury held to its date and is never corrected
sources: Pacioli chs 3, 31; FINAL IPS l.13 ("Held to the end, these pay what they say")
use: Test (for every writer of a ledger turn): the image may borrow the ledger's visibility, never its sense of "recorded" for "owned". The definition says "owned" (CONCEIT V2.4 guard 7)
critique: Written so the 27 Nov writers stop where the parallel stops (V2.4 guard 1)
note: Tue 17 Nov: guard for every ledger turn (V2.4 guards 1 and 7): borrow the ledger's visibility, never its recorded for owned; ledger ink records the past and can hold bad money, Laura's ink is a Treasury held to its date (IPS l.13).

idea: Pacioli's three books: a memorandum (scrap book or blotter) where "any one in your family can make entries", day by day and hour by hour; a journal ("your private book"); and a ledger. "Many, on account of their small business, use only the last two"
use: Store, possible 3e: what anyone may jot down (forecasts of the top, share prices) is the memorandum. What Laura tells co-sponsors is posted from it once, by one hand
critique: All three books are in ink. The memorandum is provisional in use, not in medium, and it records past trades, not forecasts
note: Tue 17 Nov: store only; the parallel breaks under its own disanalogy, since all three of Pacioli's books are in ink and record past trades, not forecasts.

idea: Solutions found with an aha were recalled after 14 days 64.4% of the time, without one 52.4%; for correct solutions, recall matched 20.42% against 9.61% failed (dz = .61); 50 people, 34 magic-trick videos
sources: Danek, Fraps, von Müller, Grothe & Öllinger (2013)
use: The core of claim 1: an aha the judge has is worth about 12 points of recall two weeks on, the gap between reading Caplet's report and the next team's
critique: Self-generated solutions to tricks, not arguments read in a report; recall measured on solvers, not readers
verified: VERIFIED (abstract, method and results read in part, 17 Nov 2026)
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha setting, claim 1; true for magic-trick solvers who found the answer themselves, so never read the 12 points as a judge's gain or the gap to the next team's report; rows 4-5 (shown answers) are the report's case.

idea: Aha is not a truth certificate: of 329 solutions people felt with an aha, 75 were wrong (23%, Keel arithmetic on Table 1); and wrong aha solutions were remembered too
sources: Danek et al. (2013) Table 1; Danek & Wiley (2020)
use: Every aha row keeps its truth check (bond desk, coherence readers) apart from its aha score; a vivid wrong aha sticks as well as a right one
critique: Lab solvers, not readers of a checked report
note: Tue 17 Nov: register process guard: a felt aha is no truth check (75 of 329 wrong, Keel arithmetic on Danek's Table 1), so each spine row's truth check stays apart from its aha score; pairs with row 22.

idea: Across 1,863 magic-trick solutions, aha strength predicted recall a week later (d = 0.30); jointly, being right (d = .27) and feeling sure (d = .29) mattered most, pleasure a little, and a sudden "restructuring" not at all
use: Memory rides on a right answer held with certainty: each aha ends on a fact stated flatly with its number, which is what Book 19's strong true words allow
critique: Correlational within a lab task
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha setting; the certainty measured was the solver's own, not the text's tone, so the link to stating each fact flatly (Book 19) is Keel inference; say only that right answers held with certainty were remembered best and restructuring added nothing.

idea: Induced insight: a solution word shown after a brief solving attempt gave an aha on 75% of solvable riddles, and was recognised 24 hours later 48% against 39% for unsolvable controls (d = 0.96); "remember" responses 19% against 9%; N = 26
sources: Kizilirmak, Thuerich, Folta-Schoofs, Schott & Richardson-Klavehn (2016) Frontiers in Psychology 7:1693
use: The answer to Caplet's "our job": the report states the answer; the judge's only work is to hold the puzzle for a sentence; the aha and the memory gain survive
critique: Single words in a scanner; control items were nonsense, so part of the gain is "understood against not understood"
note: Tue 17 Nov: every spine row and Book 11: a shown answer after a brief attempt still gave an aha and better memory, so the report states each answer and asks nothing of the judge; never quote d = 0.96 as the aha's size (the controls were nonsense items).

idea: A shown answer after a failed attempt still gave an aha on 22% of images, and that aha raised memory a week later on its own account; finding the answer oneself raised it more (re-solved 78% against 41%), and the aha alone had "a comparably weak relationship" to memory
sources: Kizilirmak et al. (2016) Psychological Research, doi 10.1007/s00426-015-0697-2
use: Sizes what Caplet's ban costs: the report gives up the larger generation effect and keeps the smaller aha effect; it is still worth having
critique: 20 people, Mooney images; co-authors not read on the page
verified: VERIFIED (abstract, results, discussion read in part, 17 Nov 2026)
note: Tue 17 Nov: sizes what Book 11's ban costs: a shown answer keeps a smaller aha benefit, a self-found one more; supports row 4, with the aha's own link to memory weak.

idea: Shown solutions to camouflaged pictures (induced perceptual insight) were still known a week later 56-57% of the time; amygdala activity at the reveal predicted which
use: A reveal the reader watches, not makes, can still leave a mark a week on, the judge's gap between first read and panel
critique: Pictures, not arguments
note: Tue 17 Nov: same lesson as row 4 (a watched reveal still sticks) on camouflaged pictures, with no told-cold baseline; row 4 carries it.

idea: Generating an item beats reading it by d = 0.40 (86 studies, 445 effects, 17,711 people); by test type: recognition .46, cued recall .55, free recall .32
sources: Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott & McDaniel (2007) Memory & Cognition 35(2) 201-210
use: The ceiling for "reached, not told", which the report can only approach by induced insight (rows 4-5)
critique: Word-level tasks (synonyms, anagrams), not arguments
note: Tue 17 Nov: context only: the generation effect is the ceiling the report gives up under Book 11; word-level tasks, so no aha row changes.

idea: Trying and failing, then being shown, sits between only reading and finding it oneself ("generate ≤ fail-to-generate < read" in memory loss terms)
sources: Slamecka & Fevreiski (1983), as reported by Kizilirmak et al. (2016)
use: A judge who has formed even a wrong expectation is "fail-to-generate", which beats a judge who was told cold
critique: Secondary report of a 1983 paper
verified: UNVERIFIED (1983 paper not opened; read only as cited)
note: Tue 17 Nov: UNVERIFIED (the 1983 paper read only as cited); a judge's unstated expectation is not an attempt to generate, so never call the judge fail-to-generate until the original or Brod et al. 2018 is read.

idea: "Effort toward comprehension": a puzzling sentence ("The haystack was important because the cloth ripped") whose key word (parachute) came about 5 seconds later was recalled better than one with the key inside; the gain held even for sentences readers could follow unaided
sources: Auble & Franks (1978); Auble, Franks & Soraci (1979), as summarised by Zaromb et al. (2010) and Vaughn et al. (2017)
use: The sentence-scale recipe: puzzle sentence, then key sentence; even an easy aha gains from that order
critique: Spoken single sentences; Danek et al. (2013) argue cued "ahas" differ from self-found ones
verified: VERIFIED (1979 abstract read at source, 17 Nov 2026; the recall results read only as reported by Zaromb et al. 2010 and Vaughn et al. 2017)
note: Tue 17 Nov: the original of row 10's delayed-key effect, its results read only as summarised; row 10 carries the verified table.

idea: Delayed key: recall 44% (easy) and 49% (hard) against 21% and 24% with the key embedded and 28% and 18% with none; readers' judgments of comprehension and learning missed it: "subjects were not aware of this benefit"
use: Recall roughly doubles when the key follows the puzzle; and Keel's readers' strength ratings cannot detect that, so cold tests score recall
critique: Between-subjects designs weaken it (Zaromb & Roediger 2009: the effect "did not occur" between subjects)
note: Tue 17 Nov: the sentence-scale recipe for all ten spine rows (puzzle sentence, key in the next, recall about doubled for lab sentences); drop the cold-test clause: Zaromb's readers were people, and simulated readers' ratings are no evidence of the same blindness.

idea: Context before a hard passage doubled recall (8.00 against 3.60 of 14 ideas) and comprehension (6.10 against 2.30 of 7); the same picture shown after the passage gave 3.60, no gain; a "washing clothes" topic before gave 5.83 of 18, after 2.65
use: Paragraph scale: the frame comes first; a reveal held to a paragraph's end is "context after" and does nothing; 2.0's definition must come before Table 1's rows
critique: Deliberately obscure passages; Laura's report is clear without a frame
note: Tue 17 Nov: 2.0 and CONCEIT V2.1: the frame before the rows (8.00 against 3.60 of 14 ideas) and a key held to a whole passage's end did nothing, so the definition stays before Table 1 and each aha's key sits in the next sentence.

idea: An irrelevant cue made sentences harder to remember than no cue at all, because readers tried to understand them through it and stopped looking for a better one
use: A conceit turn that fits a different mapping is worse than no turn; never use a turn as an aha's key
critique: Sentence lists, not a report
note: Tue 17 Nov: conceit guard (V2.4): an irrelevant cue lowered recall below no cue, so a turn that fits a different mapping is worse than none, and a turn is never an aha's key sentence.

idea: Insight is "any sudden comprehension ... that involves a reorganization ... to yield a nonobvious or nondominant interpretation", including "comprehension of a joke or metaphor"; an impasse is not required; it is "preceded by substantial unconscious processing"
sources: Kounios & Beeman (2014) Annual Review of Psychology 65, 71-93
use: The evidence must be on the page before the turn (processing first); a conceit turn can itself be a small aha when defined first
critique: Neuroscience review; says nothing about reports
verified: VERIFIED (abstract, definition, summary points read, 17 Nov 2026)
note: Tue 17 Nov: conceit (Book 19's startling new perspective): grasping a metaphor counts as insight and needs no impasse, so a defined turn can be a small aha; drop the leap from unconscious processing to where evidence sits on the page.

idea: The aha has four marks: suddenness, ease, positive affect (not pride) and the feeling of being right; a sudden gain in processing ease explains the pleasure and the felt truth
sources: Topolinski & Reber (2010) Current Directions in Psychological Science 19(6) 402-405
use: The key sentence must be short and easy: the ease of the last step is the feeling; a key buried in a long sentence loses it
critique: Theory paper; fluency effects small and context-bound (Q14b-009)
verified: VERIFIED (abstract and section text read at source on the publisher page, 17 Nov 2026)
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha setting: the ease of the last step is the felt aha, so each key sentence is short and plain; distinct from Q14b-009 (fluency of a whole text).

idea: Curiosity is "a form of cognitively induced deprivation that arises from the perception of a gap in knowledge"; it "requires a preexisting knowledge base" and rises with knowledge, so people grow "progressively more curious about the topics that they know the most about"
use: Finance judges are most curious about gaps in finance: an aha should open a gap in something they know (confidence intervals, diversification, funding at market), and a cross-field parallel only serves one
critique: Theory and review
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha targets and the conceit: curiosity rises with knowledge, so each aha opens a gap in finance (confidence, diversification, funding at market) and each cross-field turn serves that gap, as CONCEIT V2.4 guard 2 already asks.

idea: Curiosity's triggers: (1) "the posing of a question or presentation of a riddle", (2) "a sequence of events with an anticipated but unknown resolution", (3) "the violation of expectations", (4) someone else holding the information
use: Caplet bans trigger 1 (Book 11); trigger 3 does the same job with no question: state the fact that breaks the expectation; trigger 4 is the conceit's co-sponsors who will never see the construction lines
critique: Untested ranking of the four
note: Tue 17 Nov: Book 11 answered: a stated fact that breaks an expectation (trigger 3) opens the gap with no question; drop the trigger-4 mapping, since the judge sees the construction lines co-sponsors never do, so it opens no gap for the judge.

idea: People must see a "manageable" gap; overconfidence hides gaps ("fat but happy"); "guessing combined with accuracy feedback increased curiosity"
sources: Loewenstein (1994), citing Gettys et al. (1987) and Loewenstein et al. (1992)
use: A judge sure they know the answer feels no gap: name the belief's real holder so the judge notices they share it; the gap must be one sentence wide
critique: Guessing needs an active reader; the report cannot ask for guesses
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha targets: a judge sure of the answer feels no gap, so naming the belief's real holder lets the judge notice they share it, with the gap one sentence wide (pairs with row 39).

idea: Curiosity is transient and "when curiosity is satisfied, the result is generally disappointing"
use: Keep each setup to one sentence and close it at once with a concrete figure; a long build-up to a small key disappoints (register row 3)
critique: Anecdotal evidence cited (mail, Felcher et al. 1993)
note: Tue 17 Nov: register row 3 (2.5): satisfied curiosity tends to disappoint, so a one-sentence setup closed at once by its figure; the evidence is anecdotal.

idea: Curiosity is an inverted U in confidence, peaking near 50% sure (r = .44 with uncertainty); answers to high-curiosity questions people had got wrong were recalled better 1-2 weeks later
sources: Kang, Hsu, Krajbich, Loewenstein, McClure, Wang & Camerer (2009) Psychological Science 20(8) 963-973
use: The best aha targets a belief a judge half-holds: Neyman's point (row 1) and diversification (row 2) suit it; a belief no expert holds raises no curiosity
critique: 16 people, 12 at follow-up; recall percentages only in a figure
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha targets: curiosity peaks near 50% sure, so half-held beliefs (the usual reading of a confidence level, diversification) suit spine rows 1 and 2; 16 people, figures only in a chart.

idea: Hypercorrection: errors made with high confidence are corrected more after feedback (retest 79% against 70% for low confidence; gamma .14), with more attention to surprising feedback; a replication gamma was .13, more than two-thirds of errors corrected
sources: Metcalfe, Butterfield, Habeck & Stern (2012) J Cognitive Neuroscience 24(7); Fazio & Marsh (2010) Psychological Science 21(6)
use: An expert's confident wrong belief is the best place for an aha; the cold test should record how sure the reader was of the assumption they name
critique: Small effects; feedback was the answer itself, minutes later
note: Tue 17 Nov: aha targets: confident errors are corrected more once shown wrong, so a confidently held expert belief is the best target; drop the cold-test field, since a simulated reader's stated confidence is not a person's.

idea: One week on, correction fell from 86% to 56%; hypercorrection held (gamma .19), but confident errors were more likely to return when the correct answer had been forgotten
sources: Butler, Fazio & Marsh (2011) Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 18, 1238-1244
use: Tie each aha's fact to one concrete figure, and let that figure recur once plainly (a table cell, a later sentence) so the judge's old belief does not return by panel day
critique: Trivia questions; a week, not a judging season
clash: strains the register's "told once" only if the recurrence is a second aha; a plain figure is not
note: Tue 17 Nov: the register's told once: confident errors returned when the fact was forgotten, so each aha's figure may recur once plainly (a table cell, a later number), never as a second aha.

idea: Solving an anagram inside a claim raised its truth rating (d = .61; aha trials d = .63), for false claims as much as true ones; the authors' "Eureka heuristic" works only when prior knowledge is valid

critique: Online sample (268); the between-subjects test was only marginal (p = .069)

sources: Laukkonen, Webb, Salvi, Tangen & Schooler (2022) Scientific Reports

note: Tue 17 Nov: every spine row: g = 0.33 for university readers, and it works only on a misconception really held, so each aha names a belief someone real holds (a rule, a court, an industry figure), never a straw one.

critique: Science misconceptions, students and public

idea: Fair play in detective fiction: "The reader must have equal opportunity with the detective for solving the mystery"; "The truth of the problem must at all times be apparent--provided the reader is shrewd enough to see it"; "no literary dallying with side-issues"

where: MOI order 台內國字第1130801422號; NLMA regsearch/175
note: Guard: never say the code was tightened after Hualien 2024 (last revision 1 Mar 2024, a month before).

idea: What followed Hualien: evaluation subsidies (preliminary up to NT$15,000, detailed up to NT$400,000); weak-storey retrofit for red- or yellow-tagged homes up to NT$15m a building (six floors or fewer NT$7.5m), at most 85%; tagged buildings may go straight to 危老 rebuilding; 50 weak-storey cases approved in Hualien within a year
use: Aid targets homes; the general weak-storey subsidy covers buildings at least half residential, so an arts building is mostly outside (as read; eligibility is a legal question, out of scope)
critique: Housing programme; Hualien-specific rules
where: MOI press releases 11 Apr 2024, 31 Mar 2025; 作業規定 (11 Jun 2024, amended 21 Aug 2025); EY briefing
note: Store only.

idea: Strengthening comes in stages: New Taipei's slides note a weak-storey retrofit cuts collapse risk sharply, but meeting the design earthquake "未來仍需進行整幢完整補強" (later still needs full retrofit of the whole building, art. 77-1). One 2019 job: NT$1,732,532 with one design change adding NT$80,000 (4.6%, Keel arithmetic) and 6 days; a Hualien building NT$8,316,676
sources: 新北市政府都市更新處 (2024)
use: A partial fix may not end the question; an owner of an older building can face a second round
critique: Housing cases; never a figure for Laura's building
where: NTPC Urban Renewal Office slides, May 2024
note: Store only.

idea: Renewal-maintenance subsidy schedule: seismic retrofit NT$4,000 per square metre, up to 55%; facade repairs NT$1,500 per square metre, up to 50%
sources: 新北市政府都市更新處 (2024)
use: Shows public money exists for older-building works, mostly for housing and renewal schemes
critique: Eligibility and scope not checked (legal)
where: NTPC slides, "中長期重建協助措施"
note: Subsidy schedule.

idea: New-build code cost in Taiwan: NCREE says the 2022 near-fault provisions raise new buildings' seismic capacity 20-30% "而工程造價成本僅增加約5%" (while construction cost rises only about 5%); buildings with isolation or damping rose from 80 (2009) to over 1,000 (2022); the chance of a magnitude-7 quake within 50 years "可能高達三成" (may be as high as 30%)
use: For a new small building the code adds a few percent at most; the seismic cost question is about old buildings (claim 2)
critique: Near-fault sites; NCREE is the code's author
note: Store: new-build code cost about 5% (NCREE).

idea: US evidence on new-build code cost: today's model codes add "only about 1%" to construction cost over 1990 standards (earthquake design: $0.6bn a year of cost for $7bn of benefit); one 1976 steel building: seismic design added 2.8%
use: Same order as NCREE's 5%: code cost is small on a new building
critique: US codes and prices
verified: VERIFIED (fact sheets and report pages read)
where: NIBS Mitigation Saves; MIT report No. 28
note: US evidence.

idea: Retrofit cost as a share of a new building: FEMA's UCSB North Hall, $11.76 per sq ft against about $60 to replace (about 20%); estimating heuristics use 12% and 20% of replacement value; reinforcing costs are "higher for older buildings, smaller buildings and historic buildings", and Los Angeles replaced school buildings once reinforcing passed 70-80% of new
sources: FEMA (2021); Fung et al. (n.d.); Larrabee & Whitman (1976)
use: The order of magnitude for an older building: a tenth to a fifth of new, more if small, old or historic; never a figure for Laura's building
critique: US and Greek cases; no Taiwan figure found (gap)
where: FEMA case study; NIST manuscript; MIT 1976
note: Store: retrofit about 12-20% of a new building.

idea: A retrofit pulls in other work: total cost includes non-seismic work the job triggers (disability access, asbestos removal, system upgrades), design fees and permits
use: The route by which a building's age becomes cost is a chain, not one item; an "overrun" in an old building is often triggered work
critique: FEMA 156 itself not read; Taiwan's triggers are legal questions
note: A retrofit pulls in other work.

idea: Importance factor (code fact): a building used only for assembly needs I = 1.25 only if its total floor area is 1,000 m² or more; mixed use: assembly under 1,000 m² gives 1.0, 3,000 m² or more 1.25, and 1,000-3,000 m² 1.25 only if assembly is 20% or more of the floor area. Section 8.3: an existing building, after detailed evaluation or retrofit, must reach the 475-year design earthquake times I, or a stated performance target
use: A small residency probably sits under the 1,000 m² line, so the code's extra margin for assembly would not apply (Keel inference; whether its rooms count as assembly is an engineer's call)
critique: Code fact only; no advice on any building
where: MOI order of 1 Mar 2024, sections 2.8 and 8.3
note: Store only.

idea: Hidden conditions in old-building repair: the Control Yuan's own heritage building (roof and facade) was planned at NT$74.0m and 640 days; after three design changes for work found during the job (rotten roof trusses found beam by beam) it cost NT$90.627m and took 877 days: +22.47% cost, +37.03% time; the first tender failed for too few bidders
use: The clearest Taiwan record of the overrun IPS l.15 names; the risk sits in the building, not the index
critique: A national heritage building; much larger than a residency
where: LY Control Yuan final-accounts assessments, 2018 and 2019 accounts
note: The Control Yuan's heritage repair.

idea: The PCC warned beforehand: "如屋頂未拆解前，無法詳細預估桁木損壞數量" (until a roof is taken apart, the number of damaged timbers cannot be estimated), so design changes would follow
sources: PCC letter of 31 Mar 2015, quoted in LY Budget Center (2020)
use: Old-building overrun risk is known in advance and cannot be sized in advance: the case for money promised to no one rather than a sized contingency (CANON A31)
critique: One agency's letter on one building
note: Store quote: until a roof is taken apart, damage cannot be counted (PCC); pairs with Q5d-010.

idea: Small heritage repairs struggle to draw bidders: the Tamsui house (淡水木下靜涯舊居) failed three tenders before award on 30 Dec 2019; it and Tainan's 三山國王廟 both changed total budget and schedule during works
use: For a small old building, delay arrives before cost; a 2033 opening carries time risk
critique: Budget changes not sized in the report
note: Store: small heritage repairs struggle to draw bidders.

idea: Treasure Hill's build time: an artist-village idea in 1999, listed 2004, works from late 2006, opened 2 Oct 2010 "following a four-year-long renovation and rebuilding project"; no cost figure found in what was read
sources: Ministry of Culture (2015); Taipei Artist Village (n.d.)
use: Four years of works and eleven from idea to opening for an arts conversion of old self-built houses; Q9c has its budgets and contract, this row adds the time
critique: A whole settlement, not one building
note: Store only.

idea: Both Taipei city residencies were re-used buildings: Taipei Artist Village was a four-storey former maintenance-office building re-used in 2001 (閒置空間再利用); its site went to urban renewal and it left at the end of 2023 (closure in Q9c row 22)
use: In Taiwan an older building is the usual home of a residency, so site and age risk is the norm, not the exception (Keel inference from two cases plus Q9c's five)
critique: Small sample
note: Store: both Taipei residencies reused buildings; adds to card Q9c's site losses.

idea: Synthesis for claim 3: the national index at 3% adds about 19% over six years (1.03^6, Keel arithmetic), and the plan already shows it (NUMBERS 8d; Table 3 row 7); the parts no national rate shows are at least as large in single cases (a 5-point city gap in one month, row 15; a 22.47% heritage overrun, row 35; repeated failed tenders, rows 18 and 37)
use: Rewrite claim 3 without "mostly": the risk the plan cannot show comes from the site and the building's age and condition
critique: No measured shares; cases are larger buildings
note: 3e limit: the national rate is the part the plan shows; site, age and timing are at least as large and no national rate shows them.

idea: The village grant is for an "art village" that "常態性辦理" (regularly runs) residencies, with operating staff who have an arts background (pt 2). Any legally established or registered body may apply (pt 3): no individuals, and no minimum years
use: A new residency is not yet an "art village" in the grant's sense, so public running money follows the building and a first season
critique: A definition, not a years rule. How "regularly" is judged in review is not written
note: Store: who the village grant is for.

idea: What an applicant must file (pt 8): an operating-funds estimate (營運經費概算); its financial position (財務運作狀況); a residency of at least one month paying at least NT$800 a day; proof of ownership or right of use of the site; proof it can run residencies, or an affidavit (切結書); proof of other bodies' resources; its registration certificate; and, after more than 3 straight funded years, a self-improvement plan
use: The first things a Taiwanese public funder reads are owned money, the site and the running plan. 3d can carry all three
critique: Adds the financial position, affidavit and registration items to Q9c row 3
note: What an applicant files.

idea: The terms (pts 4, 9-15): one year, from approval to 30 Nov; competitive; amounts "depend on the legislature's budget", and the Ministry may cut or stop them; receipts by 30 Nov; a contract at NT$1.5m or more; any surplus returned in proportion to the grant; no second public grant for the same work; grantees must host foreign residents and the Ministry's exhibitions (pt 13(5)); a two-year bar after a revocation; equipment belongs to the village's owner
use: A public co-sponsor's next year is never promised. The money is reimbursement, and it carries duties to the funder
critique: Q9c rows 1 and 7 cover the one-year rule, the budget clause and double funding. This row adds the hosting duty, the proportional refund and the bar
note: 3d or 3e: Taiwan's residency grant is one year at a time and its amount depends on the legislature; public money comes after the building, never in place of it.

idea: The 2009 text (行政院文化建設委員會補助藝術村營運扶植計畫作業要點) paid only for hardware improvement (capital), up to NT$2m. Applicants: government-registered foundations, associations, studios or companies (工作室（或公司）), and villages. The site had to be owned or held on a "二年合法管理使用租約" (two-year lease). No staff or admin costs. Work done by 20 Dec 2009; applications to 31 Aug 2009; a signed contract
use: The programme began as money for the building's fabric of private villages. It has since moved to running money
critique: One version. Hardware improvement is not construction
note: Store: the 2009 grant paid only for capital.

idea: In 2013 the programme had two categories, "駐村計畫" (residency plan) and "硬體改善" (hardware improvement). Applications ran to 15 Jun for the same year
use: Capital money for villages lasted at least to 2013
critique: A local news repost of the call
note: 2013's two categories.

idea: Multi-year money came and went. Aug 2021: bodies funded more than 3 years running could ask for a cross-year plan of at most 2 years; cities and counties joined as applicants (Ministry share 50%-90% by fiscal tier); NT$500 a day; at most 3 cases and NT$5m a year per applicant. Nov 2023: cap "每一申請案每年" NT$3m; the 3-case cap dropped; contract threshold NT$1.5m. Dec 2024: cross-year plans removed; "常態性辦理" and professional staff added; NT$800 a day. Oct 2025: cities removed
use: The longest public promise a private village ever had here was two years, and it lasted three rounds. Laura's ten years of operating money owned (CANON A4, A33) has no public counterpart
critique: Whether any village used a cross-year plan was not found
verified: VERIFIED (2021, 2023 and 2024 versions read in full; the 2024 call quotes the 2-year option)
note: Store: the two-year option came (2021) and went (Dec 2024).

idea: Thirteen versions in 17 years (30 Jul 2008 to 28 Oct 2025): about one change every 16 months (Keel arithmetic). The name changed in Dec 2024
use: Today's rulebook will not be the 2032-34 rulebook. 3e can name "programme rules change" as a limit
critique: Counting versions says nothing about which way rules will move
note: 3e limit: the rules changed 13 times in 17 years, about every 16 months; a co-sponsor's terms can change before 2032.

idea: Application windows moved around: 2013 to 15 Jun (same year); the 2022 and 2023 rounds 1-30 Nov of the year before; 2024 round 4 Dec 2023 to 3 Jan 2024; 2025 round 18 Dec 2024 to 17 Jan 2025; the 2026 list published 29 Jan 2026
use: For a residency's year Y: apply Nov of Y-1 to Jan of Y, hear in late Jan, get paid after receipts by 30 Nov of Y. Set against the floor fund's payout on or about 15 Dec 2032 (CANON C8), public village money cannot come before Laura's
critique: Windows can move again (row 7)
verified: VERIFIED (county notices read in part; the 2026 list in full)
note: Application windows moved.

idea: The 2026 list: NT$13.5m to 11 grantees, each NT$0.7m to NT$1.8m. None near the NT$3m cap. Mean NT$1.23m, about $37,450; the total is about $412,000. Seven judges named. Note on the list: "本案補助金額需俟立法院預算審議結果而定" (amounts depend on the legislature's budget review)
use: A typical grant is about a third of the $115,000 central contribution (NUMBERS 4) for one year, if won. The cap (about $91,550) is about four-fifths of it (Keel arithmetic)
critique: A year's grant is running money. Laura's contribution is one-off capital. Comparing them is about scale, not use
note: Scale for 3d: the whole 2026 village programme was about $412,000 to 11 grantees, a mean of about $37,000; needs a NUMBERS entry before print.

idea: Who won in 2026. Six private or independent grantees took NT$6.4m: 利澤國際文化有限公司 (a company) 1.7; 曉劇場 0.7; 超級浪 0.7; 橋仔頭白屋股份有限公司 (a company) 1.5; 空場 1.0; 絕對藝力 0.8. Five public or city-linked grantees took NT$7.1m: 新北市美術館 1.0; Kaohsiung's city foundation (Pier-2) 1.8; Taipei's (Treasure Hill) 1.7; Tainan's (Soulangh) 1.8; 國立臺北藝術大學 0.8
sources: 文化部 (2026e); Keel arithmetic; split by Keel from the names
use: Private residencies, companies included, win grants of the same size as public ones. This supports Q9c row 8
critique: The private/public split is Keel's reading of names
note: Store only.

idea: The same names come back. Treasure Hill, Lize, 橋仔頭 and Soulangh were funded in 2023, 2025 and 2026. Makotaay (a company) was funded in 2023 and 2025, and Grand View (a family foundation, Q9c row 32) in 2025. Neither is on the 2026 list
use: An established public-linked village is renewed most years. A private one can be in one year and out the next. This is the shortfall that is actually seen
critique: Why the two are absent is not published; they may not have applied. The 2023 and 2025 lists are excerpts, not full lists
note: Store: incumbents win most years.

idea: 2023 and 2025 lines, often paid in two parts. 2023: Soulangh via Tainan NT$1.9m (0.2 + 1.7); Treasure Hill 1.9 (0.7 + 1.2); Lize 1.5 (0.3 + 1.2); Makotaay 1.0; 橋仔頭 1.6 (0.8 + 0.8). 2025: Treasure Hill 2.0 (0.7 + 1.3); Lize 2.0; 橋仔頭 1.5 (0.9 + 0.6); 絕對藝力 0.5; Soulangh 1.8; Pier-2 1.5; plus Q9c's Makotaay and Grand View at 0.9 each
use: Grants of NT$1.5m-2.0m a year are what a funded village gets. One is roughly Laura's $50,000 a year in NT$ (NT$1.64m, Keel arithmetic)
critique: Excerpts only. The 2023 and 2025 totals were not found
verified: UNVERIFIED (search excerpts of annexes and the written report)
note: Store only.

idea: Scale: the village programme's NT$13.5m in 2026 is about 0.05% of the Ministry's proposed 2026 budget, NT$29.6bn (Keel arithmetic). NCAF is paid to evaluate it (12 villages visited in 2024; about NT$1.24m a year budgeted for 2026-27)
sources: 文化部 (2026e; 2026g); Q9c row 10; 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2026c)
use: A line this small survives or dies by policy choice, not by the size of the budget
critique: Keel arithmetic across two documents
note: Store: the programme is about 0.05% of the Ministry's budget.

idea: NCAF's 2027 standards say who may apply: ROC nationals, foreigners with a permanent-residence card, and private legal persons, institutions or groups registered with the ROC government. Excluded: government bodies and organisations whose main shareholder or donor is government, parties, schools, and work for a degree. The Q&A: permanent residence needs 5 years' lawful residence with more than 183 days a year. Companies are private legal persons: 2025 grantees include 游擊文化股份有限公司 and 你哥影視社有限公司
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2026a), 壹 and Q&A 1; (2026b)
use: Who may apply turns on registration and residence, never on capital. Whether Laura or a facility of hers qualifies is a legal question, out of scope
critique: The standards are for 2027 and are revised every year (31 revisions since 1996)
verified: VERIFIED (standards read in part; annual report in part)
note: Store only.

idea: NCAF timing and payment. 2027-1: apply 1 Jan-1 Feb, results 15 Apr, projects from 1 May. 2027-2: apply 1-30 Jun, results 16 Sep, projects from 1 Oct. Outbound exchange has six rounds a year. Grants are paid "原則上於計畫結束" (in principle when the plan ends), within 14 working days of receipts, or by instalments set in a contract. The board allocates within that year's budget, and a category may go unfunded. At most 2 grants per applicant, round and category. One plan funded by both NCAF and the Ministry must pick one ("擇一接受"). "獨家贊助" (exclusive-sponsorship) plans are barred
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2026a), 參, 柒, 玖, Q&A 4 and 16
use: NCAF project money for late 2032 could be decided before Laura pays (2032-2 round, Sep), but it is paid after the work. 3d: name which funder pays which part
critique: Q11d row 3 has the 14-day rule. This row adds the windows, the single-sponsor bar and the pick-one rule
note: Store: NCAF pays at a project's end.

idea: NCAF has no residency-operations item in its regular grants. The arts-environment "專業服務平台" (professional service platform) is for groups only: up to three straight years, each a one-year grant reviewed yearly, with no non-consumable equipment, rent or utilities. Visual-arts exhibition grants may pay foreign artists' airfare, with no venue hardware. Outbound exchange pays airfare and up to three months' living costs for competitions or selections
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2026a)
use: NCAF pays for what happens in a residency, not for the residency
critique: Q11d row 5 has the platform rule; this row adds the foreign-artist and outbound items
note: No residency-operations item.

idea: The only two-year NCAF residency item found is "駐團藝術工作者" (artists in residence with a troupe). It is taken only in round 2, for "次二年之全年度計畫" (the next two calendar years; 2027-2 covers Jan 2028-Dec 2029). It is limited to groups inviting outside guest artists (ROC nationals or permanent residents)
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2026a)
use: Taiwan's public funder does fund two-year residencies, but inside performing troupes, not for a residency building
critique: Music, dance and theatre categories only
note: Store only.

idea: NCAF's "視覺藝術組織營運補助專案" (operating grants for visual-arts organisations). Open to non-profit foundations, associations or groups "許可登記或立案滿一年且具固定專職人力一人以上" (registered at least one year, with at least one full-time staff member). It pays a calendar year's full-time salaries, admin costs and "場所租金" (venue rent). One round a year, 1-30 Nov, for the next Jan-Dec. 5-7 judges and a presentation. Amounts "需俟立法院預算審議結果而定" (depend on the legislature) and may be reduced or stopped. Receipts and report within one month of the plan's end, then payment, under a contract. Not paid where the Ministry funds the same case. Surplus returned
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2023)
use: The one public grant found that pays a private space's staff and rent, and it wants a year's existence and an employee first. This is the mild form of claim 3's "track record first"
critique: Visual-arts organisations only. A residency of another kind may not fit
note: Correction: the written tests are legal form, a site right, a running residency and staff (NCAF: one year registered, one full-time employee), not private capital.

idea: Its size. It was moved from the Ministry to NCAF in 2018, and the Ministry donates its budget. 2020: 24 applied, 17 funded. 2025: 27 applied, 21 funded, NT$15m. 2026: 26 applied, 23 funded, NT$15m. Each grant is NT$350,000-900,000 (about $10,680-$27,470). The 2025 and 2026 calls ran 1 Nov-2 Dec 2024 and 1 Nov-1 Dec 2025; results came on 7 Mar 2025 and 13 Feb 2026, two to three months into the funded year. Two 2026 villages hold both grants: 超級浪 (village NT$0.7m, NCAF NT$0.35m) and 絕對藝力 (NT$0.8m and NT$0.7m)
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2021; 2026d, with the 2025 notice; n.d.-c); 文化部 (2026e)
use: Running money is known only after the year has begun, so the space must carry itself to February or March. Stacking the two programmes is possible when they fund different items (Keel reading of rows 3 and 18)
critique: The 2025 list was seen as a page excerpt
verified: VERIFIED (2026 notice and the programme page read; 2020 final accounts in part); 2025 UNVERIFIED (excerpt)
note: The operating grant's size.

idea: Taiwan's 2008-09 recession: the Council for Cultural Affairs' spending was NT$5.31bn in 2008 (+0.9%), NT$6.86bn in 2009 (+29.1%), NT$8.40bn in 2010 (+22.5%) and NT$10.75bn in 2011 (+28.0%), then NT$9.55bn in 2012 (-11.2%, the year the Council became the Ministry). The grants-and-subsidies line was NT$1.68bn in 2008, NT$2.89bn in 2009 (+71.6%) and NT$2.70bn in 2010. Figures to 2012 are audited final accounts
sources: 立法院預算中心 (2017); Keel arithmetic
use: In Taiwan's deepest modern recession the central culture budget rose, and its grants rose most
critique: Some stimulus money may be inside (not separated). The 2012 fall is the reorganisation year; its cause was not read. These are national totals, not residency lines
verified: VERIFIED (report read in part: the table)
clash: risk: IPS l.9 "co-sponsors cut their budgets" (CANON B4) does not describe Taiwan's central culture budget in 2008-10
note: Coherence guard (CANON B4): Taiwan's central culture spending rose in 2009-10 and with COVID money in 2020-21, so the report never says Taiwan's government cut arts money in a recession; IPS l.9's co-sponsors are private and US funders (card Q4b).

idea: The Ministry's budget 2013-2024 (DGBAS figures on the Ministry's statistics site): 2015 NT$16.74bn; 2016 NT$16.53bn (-1.3%); 2019 NT$19.81bn; 2020 NT$19.49bn (-1.6%); 2021 NT$17.74bn (-9.0%); 2022 NT$17.77bn; 2023 NT$21.02bn (+18.3%); 2024 NT$25.92bn (+23.3%). Spending ran at 90-99% of budget
use: Small dips in 2016 and 2020, a 9% fall in 2021, then two large rises
critique: The cause of the 2021 fall was not read. Budget, not grants
note: The Ministry's budget 2013-2024.

idea: COVID: the Ministry's share of the special budget was NT$0.8bn (2020), +NT$3.22bn (1st addition), +NT$0 (2nd), +NT$4.549bn (3rd, June 2021) and +NT$1.61bn (4th, Sept 2021): NT$10.18bn in all, about 52% of its 2020 regular budget (Keel arithmetic). Relief rounds 1.0 and 2.0 approved NT$2.886bn to 23,422 businesses and individuals. NT$4.77bn had been paid by the end of Aug 2021
use: In the 2020-21 shock the state added money on top, and fast
critique: Relief went to working arts businesses and workers. A residency not yet running would have got nothing. The Audit Office found late payments and mismatches
note: COVID relief.

idea: NCAF grants by year: totals NT$357.3m (2019), NT$356.5m (2020, -0.2%), NT$364.1m (2021, +2.1%), NT$382.3m (2024), NT$433.7m (2025, +13.4%). Regular grants NT$149.8m (2019), NT$133.3m (2020, -11.0%), NT$140.0m (2021, +5.0%), NT$181.1m (2025). Outbound exchange went from NT$24.2m (2019) to NT$13.2m (2020) and NT$8.0m (2021). The 2018 jump is the Ministry's troupe grants moving to NCAF; the 2022 peak of NT$610.0m was not explained in what was read
sources: 文化部 (n.d.-d); 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2021; 2022; 2026b)
use: NCAF's total held flat through COVID. The fall in regular grants was closed borders. This extends Q4b rows 26-29 to 2019-2025
critique: Totals mix the Ministry's donated projects with NCAF's own money
verified: VERIFIED (statistics table; reports read in part)
note: Store: NCAF grants by year.

idea: NCAF's next budgets. Government money for basic operations is NT$267.157m in 2026, the same as 2025 (2024 actual NT$217.157m). The 2027 budget has grant spending of NT$460.547m against NT$453.484m in 2026 (+1.56%), financial income of NT$292.5m against NT$267.7m, and total spending of NT$603.3m against NT$584.4m
sources: 財團法人國家文化藝術基金會 (2025b; 2026c)
use: NCAF now has a yearly government grant beside its fund income, so its grants rest less on markets than in 2011-15 (Q4b rows 26-28)
critique: Budgets, not actuals. The government line is itself voted
note: Store only.

idea: 2025: the Ministry proposed NT$29.0bn. The legislature cut NT$1.1bn and froze NT$3.4bn, the Ministry's "史上最高" (highest ever). The cuts included NT$0.59bn across the board, all NT$59.43m of media spending, NT$243m from public TV and TaiwanPlus, and NT$1.65m of grants to private groups and artists. 30% of operating expenses (業務費) was frozen at the Ministry and its museums. The whole central budget was cut 6.6% that year, against about 1.04-1.25% before
sources: 文化部 (2025d); 中央社 (2025); 行政院主計總處 (2026a)
use: Public arts money in Taiwan now carries a political risk with no link to the economy
critique: Grants to groups were barely cut. The freeze hit running costs, not grants

idea: In a 40,000-letter field test, donation rates were 3.36% (control), 4.75% (seed announced), 4.41% (1:1 match) and 8.55% (overhead covered by a lead donor); seed alone lifted the rate about 41% over control (Keel arithmetic) and beat the match

(2014) "Avoiding overhead aversion in charity", Science 346(6209): 632-635, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25359974 ; rates from Harvard Business School Working Knowledge (30 Nov 2015), https://www.library.hbs.edu/working-knowledge/donors-are-turned-off-by-overhead-costs-here-s-what-charities-can-do

idea: Why lead gifts persuade: a lead gift signals quality, but "the leader must give an unusually large amount to convey a credible signal"; the wealthiest move first because signalling costs them least
sources: Andreoni, J. (2006) "Leadership giving in charitable fund-raising", Journal of Public Economic Theory 8(1): 1-22, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9779.2006.00250.x ; https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jpbect/v8y2006i1p1-22.html

idea: Leading by example raises giving only when followers do not know the project's value ("the follower mimics the action of the leader"); it "has no effect on total contributions and earnings when such returns are commonly known"
sources: Potters, J., Sefton, M. & Vesterlund, L. (2005) "After you: endogenous sequencing in voluntary contribution games", JPubE 89(8): 1399-1419, https://sites.pitt.edu/~vester/endogorder.pdf ; (2007) "Leading-by-example and signaling in voluntary contribution games: an experimental study", Economic Theory 33(1): 169-182, https://sites.pitt.edu/~vester/jet2007.pdf

critique: Lab games, small groups; institutional co-sponsors may do their own checks (Keel inference)

idea: Who stands behind the first money matters when the name carries expertise: a match named as from the Gates Foundation raised more than an anonymous match, most among past donors to poverty charities, and the effect lasted after the match ended; revenue per letter $0.28 vs $0.15

critique: Contrasts with row 9 (naming did not matter for the opera); Gates is an expert in the cause, Laura is the founder

idea: The refund rule in theory and lab: provide the good if pledges cover its cost, refund otherwise; undominated perfect equilibria "implement the core". Lab tests with a money-back guarantee supported efficient outcomes; larger groups did worse, especially early
sources: Bagnoli, M. & Lipman, B.L. (1989) "Provision of public goods: fully implementing the core through private contributions", Review of Economic Studies 56(4): 583-601, https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/restud/v56y1989i4p583-601..html ; Bagnoli, M. & McKee, M. (1991) "Voluntary contribution games: efficient private provision of public goods", Economic Inquiry 29: 351-366, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1465-7295.1991.tb01276.x

critique: Group-size point from Ledyard's survey, http://www.dklevine.com/archive/ledyard.pdf (secondary); the efficient outcome is not the only equilibrium

critique: Theory with known values and costs

The authors compare it to deposit insurance, never paid in equilibrium
sources: Cason, T.N., Tabarrok, A. & Zubrickas, R. (2021) "Early refund bonuses increase successful crowdfunding", Games and Economic Behavior 129: 78-95, https://business.purdue.edu/research/working-papers-series/2021/1326.pdf

idea: Funded projects run late and some never deliver: over 75% of funded Kickstarter projects delivered late; about 9% failed to deliver (possible range 5-14%); 65% of backers agreed rewards came on time

idea: All-or-nothing vs keep-it-all: of 22,850 Indiegogo campaigns (2011-2013), 5.2% chose all-or-nothing; they set bigger goals (mean $31,397 vs $20,478) yet succeeded twice as often (34% vs 17%), reached 64% vs 42% of goal and drew 189 vs 76 backers; all-or-nothing is "a costly signal of commitment"; keep-it-all suits "small, scalable projects"; every verified non-profit used keep-it-all

(2020) "Crowdfunding models: keep-it-all vs. all-or-nothing", Financial Management 49(2): 331-360, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/fima.12262 ; working paper https://leeds-faculty.colorado.edu/bhagat/crowdfundingmodels-keppitall-allornothing.pdf

idea: Support rises as a goal comes near and drops once it is reached; over a campaign it is U-shaped
sources: Kuppuswamy, V. & Bayus, B.L. (2017) "Does my contribution to your crowdfunding project matter?", Journal of Business Venturing 32(1): 72-89, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jbvent/v32y2017i1p72-89.html

critique: Kickstarter backers, not institutions
note: Support drops once a goal is reached, so overruns arrive after funders relax.

idea: Gifts that complete a project are over twice as large; this pull to completion added over $15m, about 16% of donations on DonorsChoose; few projects expire close but not complete; a project at 50% or more after one week has at least an 85% chance of completing

critique: Classroom projects with small budgets
note: Funders like to complete a project; a large owned floor brings that moment closer.

idea: Goal gradient in helping: funds close to their goal received more, on Kiva and in a field test; the reason is perceived impact
sources: Cryder, C.E., Loewenstein, G. & Seltman, H. (2013) "Goal gradient in helping behavior", Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 49(6): 1078-1083, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022103113001364

critique: Micro-loans and small appeals

idea: Uncertainty about how much is needed breaks group funding; uncertainty about the size of the benefit does not. Threshold known: catastrophe avoided in 18 of 20 groups (8/10 with known impact, 10/10 with uncertain impact). Threshold uncertain: catastrophe certain in 16 of 20 groups and at least 80% likely in the other 4
sources: Barrett, S. & Dannenberg, A. (2012) "Climate negotiations under scientific uncertainty", PNAS 109(43): 17372-17376, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3491499

critique: A climate game with 10 equal players avoiding a loss; the facility cost itself stays uncertain and is outside scope (case p.4)

idea: The width of the uncertainty has a sharp cut-off: threshold known at 150, 80% of groups avoided catastrophe; uncertain over 100-200, 135-165 or 140-160, none did; over 145-155, 40% did. A later replication: 90% vs 42%, and a warning that narrowed the uncertainty to within 10% raised it to 61%
sources: Barrett, S. & Dannenberg, A. (2014) "Sensitivity of collective action to uncertainty about climate tipping points", Nature Climate Change 4: 36-39, as reported in Hurlstone et al. (2025), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11898102
use: The cut-off lies between ranges about 7% and 13% of the threshold wide (Keel arithmetic: 10/150 and 20/150); narrow beats wide by far more than intuition suggests
critique: The 2014 numbers read only in a secondary account; lab climate games
verified: VERIFIED: Hurlstone et al. 2025 full text; Barrett & Dannenberg 2014 UNVERIFIED at source
note: A sharp cut-off in tolerable uncertainty, but the 2014 figures were read only in a secondary account.

idea: Ambiguity (an unknown spread) is worse than known risk, and "Early and credible commitment helps groups to cope with uncertainty"; in theory more ambiguity lowers the largest number of contributors
sources: Dannenberg, A., Loschel, A., Paolacci, G., Reif, C. & Tavoni, A. (2015) "On the provision of public goods with probabilistic and ambiguous thresholds", Environmental and Resource Economics 61(3): 365-383, https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/57121/ ; Kishishita, D. & Ozaki, H. (2020) "Public goods game with ambiguous threshold", Economics Letters 191, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/ecolet/v191y2020ics0165176520301282.html

critique: Lab and theory
note: Ambiguity is worse than known risk and early credible commitment helps; a stated confidence turns one into the other.

idea: The counter-case: in theory, when a good is valued highly, wider threshold uncertainty can raise contributions because each giver feels more likely to be the one who tips it; the lab gave "only limited verification", and wider uncertainty "will sometimes, but not always," hinder collective action
sources: McBride, M. (2006) "Discrete public goods under threshold uncertainty", JPubE 90(6-7): 1181-1199, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272705001568 ; McBride, M. (2010) "Threshold uncertainty in discrete public good games: an experimental study", Economics of Governance 11(1): 77-99, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/49p8c2jv

critique: Weak lab support

idea: The uncertainty effect: people value a risky prospect below its worst outcome (over 1,000 participants); a replication put it at about 65% of the worse outcome, shown by at least 62% of people
sources: Gneezy, U., List, J.A. & Wu, G. (2006) "The uncertainty effect: when a risky prospect is valued less than its worst possible outcome", QJE 121(4): 1283-1309, https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/121/4/1283/1855222 ; Simonsohn, U. (2009) "Direct risk aversion: evidence from risky prospects valued below their worst outcome", Psychological Science 20(6): 686-692, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19422629
use: A bare range can be valued below its own bottom; a bottom presented as owned money gives the listener a sure thing to anchor on (Keel inference)
critique: Contested: Keren & Willemsen (2009, JBDM 22: 301-317) found it nearly vanished with clear instructions; Rydval et al. (2009, Experimental Economics 12: 473-487) questioned it; neither read at source
verified: VERIFIED: QJE and PubMed abstracts; critiques UNVERIFIED
note: The uncertainty effect is contested by later studies that were not read; cite only with the doubt stated.

idea: People use risk "as an excuse not to give": when money for themselves is traded against money for a charity, a risky impact lowers giving more than it should
sources: Exley, C.L. (2016) "Excusing selfishness in charitable giving: the role of risk", Review of Economic Studies 83(2): 587-628, https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/Excusing%20Selfishness_Published_d8e096a8-ca8c-42ed-a8d4-f3b0b993ded1.pdf

critique: Individuals in a lab; institutional budgets follow other rules

idea: Numeric ranges cost little trust: five experiments (n = 5,780, including a BBC field test) found a numeric range "does not substantially decrease trust"; vague verbal uncertainty cost more
sources: van der Bles, A.M., van der Linden, S., Freeman, A.L.J. & Spiegelhalter, D.J. (2020) "The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers", PNAS 117(14): 7672-7683, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205438
use: A numeric range is safe for Laura's credibility; vague words are not
critique: About uncertain facts (such as unemployment figures), not promises or forecasts

idea: Forecasts that state their uncertainty improved decisions, raised trust and softened the damage when a forecast was wrong
sources: Joslyn, S.L. & LeClerc, J.E. (2012) "Uncertainty forecasts improve weather-related decisions and attenuate the effects of forecast error", Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 18(1): 126-140, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21875244

critique: Weather forecasts; student participants
note: Forecasts with stated uncertainty kept trust when they missed.

idea: The preference for ranges peaks at a narrow width and falls as ranges widen: readers want forecasts "as precise as warranted ... but not more"; the form of a forecast changed investors' confidence, not their estimate
sources: Du, N., Budescu, D.V., Shelley, M.K. & Omer, T.C. (2011) "The appeal of vague financial forecasts", Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 114(2): 179-189, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2010.10.005 ("Shelley" is right: the publisher's erratum, OBHDP 115(1): 143, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2011.01.005, corrects the article's "Shelly"; REFERENCES_APA row 47); SSRN abstract https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3499375 ; Hirst, D.E., Koonce, L. & Miller, J. (1999) "The joint effect of management's prior forecast accuracy and the form of its financial forecasts on investor judgment", Journal of Accounting Research 37 (Supplement), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=145610

critique: Investors in experiments, earnings forecasts

sources: AFP Career Center, "Capital Campaigns: How They Work, Timeline, Gift Table (2026)" (28 May 2026), https://careers.afpglobal.org/career-resources/on-the-job-7/capital-campaigns-a-practical-guide-for-fundraising-117 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Narrows store H2-054's 40-100% to a modern 60-80%; Laura's whole announced figure is owned at the meetings, the extreme end of the rule
critique: A secondary page on a job-board site summarising AFP 2021 and Capital Campaign Pro; AFP's 2021 note not read
note: Campaigns launch with 60-80% secured; a secondary page, and the AFP note was not read.

idea: Large gifts concentrate further: in a 2026 sector report, donors giving more than $50,000 were "0.4% of all donors" but "53.3% of all dollars"
sources: Shattuck, S., Capital Campaign Pro (25 May 2026), "2026 Nonprofit Sector Research for Capital Campaign Fundraising", https://capitalcampaignpro.com/2026-nonprofit-sector-campaign-fundraising (underlying report not named in the excerpt) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Co-sponsor money depends on a few large givers, so one cut budget moves the total a lot (context for IPS l.9)
critique: US annual giving, not campaigns; underlying report UNVERIFIED; it does not show budgets falling in a recession, so CANON B4's co-sponsor half still needs a source
verified: VERIFIED: search excerpt of the article; underlying data UNVERIFIED
note: Same concentration point as Q11b-031 with weaker sourcing (annual giving, underlying report unread).

idea: Inequality made a threshold harder: 5 of 10 equal groups reached the target against 2 of 10 unequal groups; failing unequal groups also wasted more (EUR 15 more invested, p = 0.039)
use: Unequal co-sponsors are a harder table than equal ones; Q11a's equal-group results do not carry over untested
critique: Groups of 6 students, a loss-avoidance game, 10 rounds, EUR 120 target; 10 groups per treatment
verified: VERIFIED (full main text, PNAS article page)
where: This run; answers Q11a Gaps (group size)
note: Background for 3d: unequal groups reached a target less often (2 of 10 against 5 of 10); small lab groups, and Q11c-005 finds the opposite.

idea: Non-binding pledges tripled success under inequality, 2 of 10 to 6 of 10 (one-sided p = 0.085), close to the 7 of 10 of equal groups; players kept their word (EUR 31.8 given against EUR 32.6 pledged)
use: Written intentions help unequal funders coordinate even before they bind; the 2031 round of statements is the cheap repair
critique: Anonymous students; marginal significance; pledges cost nothing to break
note: 3d: non-binding pledges took unequal groups from 2 to 6 of 10 and were kept, so an early written statement is the cheap repair (p = 0.085).

idea: Early signals by the rich decided success: the rich gave EUR 3.17 in round 4 in successful groups against EUR 2.06 in failing ones (EUR 9.83 against 6.67 over rounds 4-6); "the poor are not willing to compensate for the rich's inaction"
use: A large funder's early signal matters, and small funders will not fill a gap a big one leaves
critique: The "rich" are players with more tokens, not a donor holding an owned contribution
note: Background: large players' early signals decided success and small ones did not fill their gap; tokens, not funders.

idea: Fairness views are self-serving: 90% of the poor but 62% of the rich agreed the rich should give more; 75% of the rich in successful groups against 53% in failing ones
use: Each co-sponsor will think a larger one should carry more; an ask that names no shares avoids that argument
critique: Post-game questionnaire
note: 3d: each funder thinks a larger one should carry more, so the ask names no shares and conditions only on the facility's total.

idea: Unequal wealth alone did not hurt coordination (53.9% against 50.0% with equal wealth) and helped when members preferred different projects (56.7% against 34.4%)
sources: Corazzini, Cotton, Longo & Reggiani (2024), J. Public Economics 238
use: Unequal size is not the problem; disagreement on what to fund is
critique: Groups of 4 students online, 8 candidate projects, 12 rounds
note: Counter-result to Q11c-001: unequal wealth alone did not hurt; disagreement on what to fund did.

idea: The wealthiest member's favourite becomes the focal point: successful unequal groups funded it "around 96% of the time"; 49 of 60 groups (81.67%) never switched once they had coordinated
use: A large co-sponsor may steer what the residency becomes, and the first agreement sticks
critique: Lab projects differ only in who gains; a residency's design is negotiated over years
clash: risk: a dominant funder's terms could narrow the "financial flexibility as the project develops" (case p.3) that the kept half protects (A31)
note: Risk to record: a dominant funder's choice tends to become the project, which could narrow Laura's flexibility; lab labels, not a residency.

idea: Unequal groups split costs progressively: the high-endowment player gives more than its head start (30.18 to 33.76 extra tokens against a 28-token advantage, in the scattered-majority treatments)
sources: Corazzini, Cotton & Longo (2025), WP 1542, Table 4; Corazzini et al. (2024) section 5.4
use: A large funder carrying the largest share is the normal pattern, not a favour
critique: Tokens; real funders work to caps and formulas (rows 19, 21)
note: Large lab players paid more than their head start; no part of the report needs it.

idea: Moving in sequence beats moving together: 47.8% simultaneous against 75.6% when the star moved first (others scattered), and 58.9% against 79.4% when the star moved last (others agreed); "Sequential" +0.189 (p < 0.01), organisation alone not significant
use: Commitments in a known order, not one simultaneous ask of everyone in 2031
critique: 15 groups of 4 per treatment; one star of 76 tokens, three of 48; working paper, not peer reviewed
note: 3d order: moving in sequence beat moving together (47.8% to 75.6% or 79.4%); extends Q11a-004 to unequal funders; working paper.

idea: The design rule: "lead when unorganized, anchor when already organized"; seed money focuses attention, matching or last money gives assurance to donors already agreed
use: Laura's dated, owned figure organises the table; once the others agree, the largest funder does best coming last
critique: The star is the richest player; Laura may not be the largest funder
note: 3d order: lead when the table is scattered, anchor when it is organised, so Laura's owned figure goes first and the largest funder may come last.

idea: Who picks the project depends on organisation: with a scattered majority the star's project wins (60.0% against 15.6% when the star leads); with an agreed majority theirs wins (60.6% against 18.9% when the star anchors; the star's project never funded when all move at once)
use: If Laura's plan is clear before a big funder moves, the residency stays hers; on a scattered table the big funder's version wins
critique: Lab "projects" are labels with fixed payoffs
note: 3d background: on a scattered table the big funder's project wins; Laura's plan stated first keeps the residency hers.

idea: No first-mover advantage and no last-mover penalty; the order that maximised success also maximised everyone's payoff and fairness (majority over star payoff 0.953 when the star led a scattered group)
use: Laura going first costs her nothing in share terms; the big funder going last costs it nothing
critique: Lab
note: Background: no first-mover cost or last-mover penalty in the lab, so Laura going first costs her nothing.

idea: Older lab result: unequal groups were less successful than equal ones, and members gave the same share of their endowment whatever its size
use: Sides with row 1 against row 5: the literature is mixed
critique: Paywalled
verified: UNVERIFIED (abstract; summary in Corazzini et al. 2024, section 2.1)
note: Older lab result that inequality hurts; abstract only and the literature is mixed.

idea: Coordination is hardest when endowments are "large enough that no one person is critical"
use: A few large funders, each needed, are easier than many middling ones
critique: Paywalled
note: A few large funders, each needed, coordinate more easily; abstract only.

idea: Sequential moves beat simultaneous for a given refund rule; a full refund helped simultaneous play but not clearly sequential play
sources: Coats, Gronberg & Grosskopf (2009), J. Public Economics 93
use: Once order is used, refund terms matter less
critique: Paywalled
note: Sequence beats simultaneity and refunds matter less once order is used; abstract only.

idea: Not knowing the others' values did not lower success; a higher "step return" (the good's value against its cost) raised contributions
sources: Marks & Croson (1999), Public Choice 99; Croson & Marks (2000), Experimental Economics 2
use: Co-sponsors respond to the facility's value to them against its cost, not to disclosure of each other's shares
critique: Paywalled
where: This run; answers Q11a Gaps (Croson & Marks not searched)
note: Funders respond to the project's value against its cost; abstracts only and no part needs it.

idea: Kresge: "It's not a match; it's a reward for getting to the end by a deadline and is paid in full only when the campaign succeeds completely"

critique: The 2011 guide says the challenge grant is "no longer the centerpiece" of Kresge's work and used "on occasion"

where: This run; Q11b row 27 had only the next sentence
note: Same Kresge all-or-nothing challenge as H7-071; adds Kresge's own words, 'paid in full only when the campaign succeeds completely', which SKELETON 3d cites.

idea: Kresge's terms: a challenge grant is "Money pledged by Kresge that will be paid when grant conditions are met"; the deadline is "the day by which you will have raised your goal and met the first condition"; the goal is the whole campaign; it "typically" funds "8% to 10% of the private fundraising amount"
use: A small last slice with a hard date conditions everyone else's raise; the condition is the total, not each donor's amount
critique: The guide does not say what happens on a missed deadline; "paid when conditions are met" implies not paid
note: Same Kresge challenge grant as H7-071; adds the 2011 guide's terms (the condition is the whole goal; typically 8% to 10% of it).

idea: Kresge wants other money "committed, imminent or backstopped", warns "A request with several pending government grants is not likely to receive a Kresge grant", advises backstopping expected government money, and wants pledges committed "before the general public ever hears about the campaign"
use: Pending public money is the weak link private funders fear, and someone is asked to cover it; Laura's kept half is the obvious candidate and must not be offered
critique: Q18 row 12 already holds the backstop definition; new here are the pending-grants warning and the quiet-phase rule
clash: risk: offering the kept half as a backstop makes it promised (IPS l.15 "promised to no one"; A30, D12)
note: 3d never-offered list: private funders fear pending public money and ask someone to backstop it; the half kept is never that backstop (A30).

idea: Arts Council England capital: 100% of partnership funding "confirmed in writing" is a condition of the first payment, "otherwise, the initial payment will be withheld"; "No, 100% of the funding must be confirmed before the project can begin"; partnership minimum 5%, 10% or 15% by grant size

use: A big public capital funder is last money by rule; Laura's figure must exist in a form the residency can show in writing
critique: England only, lottery and government money; Round 1 closed
verified: VERIFIED (partnership-funding, payment and FAQ sections of the guidance page)
where: This run; Q22 rows 1-5 have the earlier CIP and MEND rules
note: 3d ask: a public capital funder withholds its first payment until 100% of other funding is confirmed in writing, so Laura's figure must exist in writing; adds to Q22-003 and Q22-005.

idea: The same funder: "we cannot provide additional capital or revenue funding if the project costs increase"; the final 10% is paid only after completion, with an accountant's statement

critique: Q22 row 3 has the CIP Round 2 version
clash: risk: the IPS names overruns as a kept-half use (A31), which co-sponsors could read as an offer
note: Same Arts Council England overrun rule as Q22-003 (no extra money if costs rise), from the newer fund.

idea: Washington State's Building for the Arts pays up to 33% of eligible costs (maximum $2,000,000), by reimbursement only; "you may start drawing down funds only after all other money needed to complete the project has been raised"; "the entire amount of non-state matching funds must be committed"

critique: A US state programme; the residency is in Taiwan
note: 3d ask: a state arts capital fund pays at most a third, and only after all other money is raised, the second case of 'last money by rule'.

idea: What counts as match there: "cash on hand, documented pledge commitments", land, in-kind, a letter of credit or "binding loan commitment"; top-ranked applicants have usually raised "more than 50 percent"; the formula gives 0.25 points per percent raised (up to 25 of 100)

critique: As row 21
note: Same point as Q22-018 (only committed money counts); Washington counts documented pledges, never intentions.

idea: When the condition fails there: unspent funds "will lapse unless reappropriated", which the legislature "generally" does "but only once"; Commerce "reserves the right to rescind any Authorization"; the facility is held 10 years
use: Public money runs on a clock; a conditional chain that misses it loses its anchor
critique: As row 21
note: 3e background: public capital money lapses on its own budget clock, so a conditional chain can lose its anchor.

idea: The NEA uses a proportional match, not all-or-nothing: 1:1 non-federal cost share, and "if your FFR shows you did not meet the required cost share ... the NEA will require you to return any NEA funds you drew down but could not match"

critique: US federal project grants; the NEA does not fund construction (Q22 row 8)
verified: VERIFIED (cost-share, declining-an-award and closeout sections of the handbook)
note: A third conditional form: a proportional match that shrinks with a shortfall; background for 3d, not in the passage.

idea: Three recognised forms (all-or-nothing challenge, last-money capital grant, proportional match); in each the funder sets the condition, its money is never at risk before it, and the applicant carries the gap and overruns
use: "Conditional on the facility's total" is co-sponsors' own practice; Laura need not invent a mechanism
critique: Keel synthesis
note: 3d: the three forms funders already use all put the condition on the total and leave gaps and overruns with the applicant, so Laura invents no mechanism.

idea: Deadlock: two funders cannot both be last money. Arts Council England and Washington count only money "confirmed in writing" or "committed", and CASE counts a conditional pledge only once its condition is expected to be met (Q11b row 32), so mutually conditional pledges need one anchor and one close date
use: Ask the others to condition on the facility's total (which includes the anchor's award) and let one funder be last
critique: Keel inference from the rules; no source discusses the deadlock itself
verified: VERIFIED (the rules); the deadlock is Keel inference
note: 3d ask, adopted in SKELETON: two funders cannot both be last money, so conditions rest on the facility's total by one close date; the deadlock is Keel's inference from the rules.

idea: Tabarrok's bonus is paid "from the entrepreneur" and must be enforceable: "The entrepreneur pays the fee for the same reason that lotteries pay out the prizes" (note 8)

critique: Theory
clash: clash if adopted: the only unpromised money is the half kept (IPS l.15; A30)
note: Same Tabarrok contract as Q11a-016; adds that the bonus is the designer's own enforceable promise, which Laura could pay only from the half kept.

idea: The "always provided" result needs complete information and identical values, by the author's own criticism; with private, differing values the best threshold is (N+1)/2 and the good is provided with probability 1/2, so the bonus is paid half the time

critique: Theory with uniform values
clash: no (corrects the scope of Q11a row 16's quote)
note: Corrects Q11a-016's 'always provided': with differing values the good comes half the time, so a bonus would often be paid.

idea: Pivot principle: with the threshold at all N, "every agent is 'pivotal' ... no free riding is possible"; a plain all-must-agree contract has "over 33 million" equilibria with 25 agents, and "negative beliefs are self-fulfilling"
use: A handful of named co-sponsors, each needed, are already pivotal; the danger is pessimism, which an owned lead figure answers
critique: Theory
note: With a few named funders each is already pivotal, and the danger is pessimism, which an owned lead figure answers.

idea: Zubrickas: the bonus is "promised by the mechanism designer from own budget", who needs "a credible capacity of raising the money promised"; a lead donor can fund it by dividing his own gift among the others if the raise fails; under uncertainty a unique outcome needs cost plus bonus at or below the lowest value; "nuisance costs" make the level matter
use: For Laura the lead-funded variant means her contribution goes to co-sponsors if the raise fails
critique: A four-page theory note
clash: clash if adopted: the floor promised "without doubt" (IPS l.15; A22, C5) would become payable to co-sponsors, not the facility (D12)
note: Zubrickas's lead-funded bonus would pay Laura's contribution to co-sponsors if the raise fails, breaking IPS l.15 (A22, C5, D12); kept as the reason 3d never offers a bonus.

idea: A large bonus backfires: with a 75% bonus five-player groups were funded in 23% of rounds by round 60, against 70% with a 25% bonus
use: There is no generous version to fall back on
critique: Groups of 5 students, 60 rounds
note: A 75% bonus cut lab success to 23%, so there is no generous version; no part needs it.

idea: A small bonus helped unequal and larger groups late (65.5% against 52.0% of rounds with five unequal players; 37.5% against 30.0% with ten), but not five equal players late (60.5% against 79.0%, not significant, 25 subjects)
use: Honest counterpoint: with unequal funders a modest bonus can work; the objection for Laura is who pays, not whether it works
critique: Fixed groups in repeated play
note: Honest counterpoint: a 25% bonus helped unequal groups late; the objection is who pays, not whether it works.

idea: The bonus is not free: from Q11a row 17's counts, failed campaigns that paid it were 87 of 220 (39.5%) with a 20% bonus and 76 of 230 (33.0%) with the early bonus
sources: Cason, Tabarrok & Zubrickas (2021) via Q11a row 17; Keel arithmetic
use: A third or more of the time the money would go to co-sponsors, not the facility
critique: Lab crowdfunding groups of 10
verified: VERIFIED (Q11a row 17 read the working paper; arithmetic here)
note: Corrects Q11a-017's 'never paid': its own lab counts paid the bonus in 33.0% to 39.5% of campaigns (Keel arithmetic, checked).

idea: Counterpoints read only as abstracts: a bonus can signal quality (strong projects expect to pay fewer bonuses); in land assembly with a few pivotal owners it raised sales 35% and nearly doubled how often the threshold was met
sources: Cason, Tabarrok & Zubrickas (2025), Management Science 71(7); Cason, Tabarrok & Zubrickas (2026), J. Urban Economics 156

critique: Landowners sell an asset and are paid; co-sponsors give

use: The IPS's hedge extends to co-sponsors: Laura's owned figure is the one commitment that does not shrink when their budgets do
critique: Keel inference; B4's co-sponsor part is PARTLY verified; Taiwan's NCAF grants held steady (-1% to +5%, Q4b)
verified: VERIFIED (the sources); the chain effect is Keel inference

sources: 文化部 (2025). 文化部推動文化藝術扎根補助作業要點 [Rooting culture and arts subsidy directions]
use: Public co-sponsors can carry the residency's programmes; Laura's contribution is the only capital in sight

idea: Multi-year work under that grant is approved "逐年核定" (year by year) and cut to the legislature's budget; grants of NT$1.5m or more need a signed contract; local-government foundations self-fund at least 20%
use: A public co-sponsor's later years are never promised; Laura's floor is owned money (A22, A32)

note: 3d and the 3e assumption, adopted in SKELETON: the Ministry of Culture approves multi-year work year by year, cut to the legislature's budget; extends H9-116.

idea: NCAF pays "原則上於計畫結束" (in principle after the project ends), within 14 working days of the report; the board allocates inside that year's budget and a category may go unfunded if money is short

idea: People read values most accurately as positions on one shared scale, then on separate scales, then as lengths, directions and angles, then areas, then volumes and curvature, and worst as shading or colour: "1. idea: Plain words make the writer look cleverer, not simpler: Buffett, "Write as this handbook instructs you and you will be amazed at how much smarter your readers will think you have become" (p. 1).
