note: Mon 16 Nov: Plain words read as more intelligent (Buffett's preface; Oppenheimer).

idea: Government statisticians' rules for a table inside a report: "Demonstration tables are used to reinforce a point made in the text"; use one when "you want users to compare values", to show "percentages", "totals", or "values of very different sizes"; "Charts should be used when you want to show patterns, trends and relationships". idea: Knight v Knight (1840): for words to make a trust, Lord Langdale required "First, if the words are so used, that upon the whole, they ought to be construed as imperative; Secondly, if the subject of the recommendation or wish be certain", and thirdly certain objects; no trust was found and the brother took absolutely
sources: Knight v Knight (1840) 3 Beav 148, 49 ER 58, at 173
use: The oldest test of when a promise about property becomes property held for someone: the second certainty is "which property?"
critique: About wishes in a will; Laura declares no trust; the three certainties are a gloss in later textbooks

note: Thu 19 Nov: store only; the three certainties are background, and the only usable part of Knight (the own-use test) is row 2's.

idea: Knight's second certainty fails when the holder may use the property for himself: "Any words by which it is expressed or from which it may be implied, that the first taker may apply any part of the subject to his own use, are held to prevent the subject of the gift from being considered certain"
use: Laura may use her Treasuries as she likes (store Q3b-033), so they are hers, not held for the residency or co-sponsors; 3d's guard: ink is what she owns, never "set aside for co-sponsors"

critique: The case turned on "ascertainment"; securities law later removed that need for brokers' customers (rows 30-32)
note: Thu 19 Nov: store; drop the 2028 deposit from the mapping (her own money to come, no seller's promise); its reasoning is the identified test the card kills for Laura, so never quoted as her rule.

critique: Goldcorp concerns a dealer's trading stock, not a custody account
note: Thu 19 Nov: same test as row 25 and row 2 (a stock its holder may deal in holds nothing for you); Pearson is the closer, commercial twin.

note: Thu 19 Nov: 2.0 or 3e aha store; quote checked at source, but the card's best five says twenty years later, which is false: Revised Article 8 was approved in 1994, the year of Goldcorp, in another country's law; say the same year, never later.

idea: Idle public money. Money Pliny had collected risked lying "otiosae" (idle). There was almost no land to buy, and nobody would borrow from a city at 12% ("duodenis assibus"), the rate private lenders charged. He proposed a lower rate and, failing that, loans forced on the councillors. Trajan: lower the rate, but forcing loans on the unwilling "non est ex iustitia nostrorum temporum" (is not in keeping with the justice of our times)

idea: The order Pliny reached later. Sinope needed water from 16 miles away. Trajan: bring the water "si modo et viribus suis assequi potest" (Firth: "provided that it can bear the expense alone"). Amastris asked to cover its sewer on the same terms (10.98-99)

idea: Taiwanese companies want the plan in writing and check amount and timing against their own budget: 98% of large firms said an arts group must finally submit a written plan, about 70% a detailed one; one firm: 你提出你的工作計劃、進度表、經費運作方式，核可就是撥錢 (give your work plan, timetable and how the money is run; approval means payment). idea: Telling givers that the running costs are already covered by someone else raised giving most: in a one-page letter test, the overhead-covered letter ("a donor had given a $10,000 grant to cover all of the overhead costs") had an 8.55% donation rate against 3.36% for the control, 4.75% seed and 4.41% match

idea: In 2022 the UK's liability-matched pension books broke through their financing, not their gilts: the 30-year gilt yield "rose by 160 basis points in just a few days", a four-day move "more than twice as large as the largest move since 2000", and leveraged LDI funds could not meet the collateral calls

idea: DMSS: each goal ("mental account") states a threshold and the chance of missing it, which implies a risk aversion. Misjudging one overall risk aversion costs 2.5 to 44 basis points (Table 3)

use: Answers the professor's "is goal-by-goal efficient?". It costs almost nothing, and clients state goals better than risk aversion

sources: Synthesis of S5, S11, S15, S16

idea: The study usually cited for "a wide range softens the blow when the result falls inside it" is retracted (2015): its data could not be produced

use: Never cite it for Laura's range; the brief listed it (and as JAR; it is TAR)

where: This run: Crossref API, repository pages
note: Refused as a source: Libby, Tan and Hunton (2006) was retracted in 2015 (Retraction Watch 16323); kept for the record so it is never cited, with Han and Tan (2007) cited instead.

idea: A second Hunton co-authored guidance study, on how analysts read early warnings, is retracted too (19 May 2015)
sources: Tan, H.-T., Libby, R., & Hunton, J. E. (2002). *Journal of Accounting Research, 40*(1), 223-246. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679X.00045; notice https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679X.12084

critique: The 2010 CAR paper by the same three (track record of bias) was not matched to a Crossref record today
verified: VERIFIED (Crossref record: "Retracted:", two retraction entries, Retraction Watch record 5444)
note: Refused as a source: Tan, Libby and Hunton (2002) was retracted in 2015 (Retraction Watch 5444); kept for the record so no store claim rests on it.

idea: A narrower form raised investors' confidence only when the company's past forecasts had been accurate; with an inaccurate record, form made no difference; form never moved the estimate itself
sources: Hirst, D. E., Koonce, L., & Miller, J. (1999). *Journal of Accounting Research, 37*(Suppl.), 101-124. https://doi.org/10.2307/2491347
use: Laura has no forecasting record, so narrowing her range would not buy confidence; owning both ends does that work
critique: Lab study, 126 individual investors; earnings, not a pledge; Q11a r33 had it at abstract level
verified: VERIFIED (as reported in Han 2013, read in full, its Table 1 and section 5.1.1; the paper itself paywalled, abstract read; Crossref: no notice)
note: Store only: a narrower form raised confidence only after an accurate record, and Laura has none, so owning both ends does that work; read through Han (2013).

idea: A result that falls in the lower part of a range (under the midpoint, above the bottom) is read more kindly than the same result against a single figure
sources: Han, J., & Tan, H.-T. (2007). *The Accounting Review, 82*(2), 521-543. https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2007.82.2.521
use: Supports the first half of claim 1: inside is read as met. For Laura it is a spare protection: the contribution lands at the top
critique: Lab study; re-estimates of earnings, not trust in a person
verified: VERIFIED (as reported in Han 2013, Table 1, read in full; the paper paywalled; Crossref: no notice)
note: Store: a result low inside a range is read more kindly than against one figure; for Laura a spare protection, since the contribution lands at the top.

idea: Knowledgeable readers judge a range against its implied midpoint as well as its ends; a stated best figure inside a range becomes a third benchmark, and a result under it reads worse than under a bare range
use: A finance-trained co-sponsor may count $105,000 (the midpoint) unless told what each end means; once Laura says she intends the top, the top is the benchmark
critique: Same as row 4; the "MID" condition is a range plus a point
clash: risk: naming the top as intended makes a shortfall under it visible; at fund costs of 0.75% the top is missed by at most $429 (NUMBERS 8l), inside the range but under the named figure
note: Tests 3d's 'she intends the top': a named figure inside a range becomes a benchmark, so the top's one exception (fund running costs above 0.5%, at most $429 short) travels with it, as SKELETON 3d plans.

idea: Ranges are "elastic": readers who want a good outcome read a range more hopefully than a single figure, and good news more than bad
sources: Han, J., & Tan, H.-T. (2010). *Journal of Accounting Research, 48*(1), 81-104. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-679X.2009.00350.x
use: A keen co-sponsor drifts toward the top, a doubtful one toward the bottom; saying what each end means removes the room to drift
critique: Investors' long or short positions, not funders' hopes
verified: VERIFIED (abstract at RePEc and Han 2013's summary, read in full; the paper paywalled; Crossref: no notice)
note: Store only: hopeful readers stretch a range toward the top, so saying what each end means leaves no room to drift.

idea: Repeated beats are not discounted: firms that had met or beaten in at least 75% of the previous 12 quarters earned a larger premium for a new beat, not a smaller one
sources: Bartov, E., Givoly, D., & Hayn, C. (2002). *Journal of Accounting and Economics, 33*(2), 173-204 (REFERENCES_APA row 133)
use: Counters claim 2's "readers learn": markets did not mark down habitual beaters
critique: 64,872 firm-quarters, 1983-1997; Q25 r7-8 already hold H3 and the walked-down beat
verified: VERIFIED (full text, author-posted PDF; Crossref: no notice)
note: Store only: markets did not mark down firms that beat repeatedly, which counters 'readers learn' in claim 2.

idea: Claim 1's asymmetry (a miss costs more than a beat earns) is a property of promises, not of market forecasts; and for Laura no result can land above the top
sources: Keel synthesis of Q25 rows 1-4 (Gneezy & Epley 2014, not re-carded), Q25 r7 and r9 (Bartov et al.; Skinner & Sloan), NUMBERS 4 "One definition"
use: Treat the bottom as a promise (a miss is fatal) and the top as a stated intention that is kept; never argue from market "beats"
critique: Gneezy and Epley's subjects judged people, not funds
verified: VERIFIED (Keel synthesis; sources as listed, each verified in its card)
note: Store and the framing of 3c and 3d: the bottom is treated as a promise and the top as a stated intention kept, since nothing can land above Laura's top.

idea: Readers discount optimism they can predict from the speaker's motives, and speakers bias more where bias is hard to detect
sources: Rogers, J. L., & Stocken, P. C. (2005). *The Accounting Review, 80*(4), 1233-1260. https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2005.80.4.1233
use: Laura wants co-sponsors to join, so a forecast of hers would be discounted; an owned bottom is not a forecast and can be checked, so there is nothing to discount
critique: 955 firm-years, 1996-2000 (445 point, 510 range); a market, not a funder
verified: VERIFIED in part (2002 working paper, Rodney L. White Center 07-02: introduction, hypotheses, sample, the two market-response tables and conclusions read; the 2005 TAR version paywalled, abstract read)
where: This run: Wharton Rodney L. White Center PDF
note: Supports 3d's proof on request: readers discount optimism they cannot check, and an owned bottom shown by a custodian statement can be checked.

idea: Bad news is believed at once and good news is checked: the market took bad-news forecasts at face value, though they were no less biased (mean errors 0.018 against 0.015)
sources: Rogers & Stocken (2005), as row 9 (working paper, Table on market response: good-news bias term t = -2.54, bad-news t = -0.87)
use: A 2031 range lower than co-sponsors hoped (say $80,000 to $100,000 if yields fall before January 2028, NUMBERS 4) is believed without proof; a high top is what invites the custodian statement
critique: Firm forecasts; Laura's figures are owned, not forecast
note: Store only: bad news is believed at once, so a lower range after a fall in yields needs no proof, while a high top invites the custodian statement.

idea: Credibility has four sources: the speaker's incentives, the speaker's record, assurance from others, and the statement's own features (precision, timing, plausibility, support)
sources: Mercer, M. (2004). How do investors assess the credibility of management disclosures? *Accounting Horizons, 18*(3), 185-196. https://doi.org/10.2308/acch.2004.18.3.185
use: Laura has no record, so her range rests on assurance (a custodian statement on request, SKELETON 3d checklist) and on the statement's support (each end named by what pays it)
critique: Review essay; abstract only
note: Store only and UNVERIFIED (abstract only): credibility comes from incentives, record, assurance and the statement's own support.

idea: Without feedback, confident advisers win; once feedback arrives, confident ones who were wrong lose more: credibility fell from 4.00 to 2.23 for confident advisers and from 3.67 to 2.84 for unconfident ones (accurate to inaccurate); people bought feedback less often on confident advisers (35% against 53%)
sources: Sah, S., Moore, D. A., & MacCoun, R. J. (2013). *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 121*(2), 246-255. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2013.02.001; with Tenney et al. (2007), REFERENCES_APA row 109, Q18 r24
use: Co-sponsors get one piece of feedback, in December 2032; a confident range is safe only because both ends are owned after the move
critique: Weight-guessing tasks (N = 184 and 377); one-shot advice, not a pledge
verified: VERIFIED (full text, eScholarship PDF; Crossref: no notice)
note: Supports 3c's confidence: confident advisers lose most when shown wrong, and co-sponsors get one check in December 2032, which is safe because both ends are owned after the move.

idea: Investors read a company's range as its top, not its midpoint: results landed above the top 41.4% of the time and at it 16.2% (57.6% at or above; 61.6% in 2002-2010); "the upper bound rather than the midpoint better represents investors' interpretation"
sources: Ciconte, W., Kirk, M., & Tucker, J. W. (2014). *Review of Accounting Studies, 19*(2), 628-660. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11142-013-9259-2
use: A corporate co-sponsor's finance staff may read Laura's top as her real figure; for Laura that reading is correct after the move
critique: 30,106 quarterly range forecasts, 1996-2010; Q11a r34 holds the cluster near the top, not the investor reading or the shares below
verified: VERIFIED (full text, author-posted PDF; Crossref: no notice)
note: Supports saying she intends the top: investors read a company range at its top, which for Laura is correct after the move.

idea: Professionals barely learn a convention even when it is the norm: analysts undid only 9.1% of the pessimistic bias in company ranges (0.110 of 1.204)
use: Learning a speaker's bias is slow even over many repeats; Laura gives no repeats, so co-sponsors bring a habit, not a lesson
critique: Analysts' quarterly revisions
note: Store only: analysts undid only 9.1% of a known bias, so a one-time speaker teaches readers nothing.

idea: Whether a range is met depends on the measure both sides count: on GAAP earnings instead of the measure guided, results fell below the range 58.5% of the time
use: One definition of the facility contribution, used everywhere (NUMBERS 4; CANON D12); never show the funds' modelled payout ($123,476), which would become a second measure the contribution then falls short of (SKELETON 3d)
critique: Accounting measures, not dollars paid
note: Tests the one-definition rule (CANON D12; lead call Tue 10 Nov 19:37): a range is missed when the reader counts a different measure, so co-sponsors never see the funds' modelled payout ($123,476).

idea: Stock returns were not clearly negative after a range unless its top fell below the analysts' prior figure: the expectation set earlier is the bar
use: Backs the plan's rule that no figure is stated before the move (NUMBERS 4: a top stated 1, 3, 6 or 12 months early is not yet owned in 2.9% to 10.7% of simulated futures)
critique: Market returns, not trust
note: Supports the rule that nothing is stated before the move: the expectation set earlier becomes the bar.

idea: Ranges became the usual form of company guidance: 46.9% of forecasts in 1996-2001 and 80.5% in 2002-2010 (quarterly); 36.5% in 1996 and 92.1% in 2011 (annual)
sources: Ciconte et al. (2014); Tang, M., Zarowin, P., & Zhang, L. (2015). *Accounting, Organizations and Society, 42*, 48-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aos.2014.12.005
use: A range is the form a corporate co-sponsor's finance staff already reads; the case's demand for a range costs Laura nothing in familiarity
critique: Company earnings; Taiwanese foundations' habits not tested
verified: VERIFIED (Ciconte full text; Tang 27 May 2014 working paper read, Table 1 described in text)
note: Store only: ranges are the usual form of company guidance, so a range costs Laura nothing in familiarity.

idea: Analysts put 73% to 77% of the weight on the bottom of a range when they revise
use: Professional readers count mostly the bottom, as both funders did with $95,000 (SKELETON 3d)
critique: 10,989 annual range forecasts, 1996-2011; "weight" is not "distance": revised forecasts still sat in the upper half of the range 33.8% of the time
verified: VERIFIED (full working paper, 27 May 2014, capana.net; published version paywalled; not behavioural, no notice in Crossref)
note: Cited for 3d: analysts put about three quarters of their weight on the bottom of a range, which is why the bottom is the one figure to count and both ends are labelled.

idea: The weight on the bottom grows with doubt: earlier forecasts, wider ranges, more disagreement, more volatile shares, and a range wider than last time (t = -7.95)
use: Laura's range is wide by company standards (row 30), so readers will lean on the bottom even harder; the remedy is saying what the width is (row 31), not narrowing it
critique: Analysts' ambiguity aversion ("max-min"), not funders'
note: Supports explaining the width in 3c: readers lean on the bottom more when a range is wide or doubtful.

idea: Leaning on the bottom was also the accurate thing to do: revisions with perfect foresight of actual earnings put more weight on the bottom too
use: Counting the bottom is not timidity in a co-sponsor; Laura's plan makes the bottom the figure that cannot fall short
critique: Company earnings fall short of ranges often; Laura's contribution does not
note: Store only: leaning on the bottom was also the accurate weighting, so a co-sponsor who counts $95,000 is not being timid.

idea: Analysts learn from a company's past ranges only weakly: after a year that landed nearer the top, the weight on the top rose to 0.283 (t = 1.73), still under half
use: Even repeated speakers barely teach readers their habit; a one-time speaker teaches nothing, so claim 2's "in time" never arrives for Laura
critique: 7,617 forecasts with a comparable forecast a year earlier
note: Store only: analysts learned a firm's habit only weakly (t = 1.73), so claim 2's 'in time' never comes for a one-time speaker.

idea: Firms more exposed to a miss (transient owners, implicit claims, earnings that matter to price) are more likely to meet or beat, by managing earnings up and guiding expectations down

critique: Archival; abstract only
note: Store only and UNVERIFIED (abstract only): walking expectations down needs repeats, which Laura does not have.

idea: A manager's forecasting record matters more to readers when uncertainty is high
sources: Yang, H. I. (2012). *Journal of Accounting and Economics, 53*(1-2), 167-184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacceco.2011.08.003
use: Laura has no record as a forecaster; ownership stands in for a record
critique: Abstract only, seen in a search result
verified: UNVERIFIED (abstract in search only; Crossref record for the citation)

idea: Say plainly that she intends the top, beside the bottom as the figure to count: true by construction after the move, and a kept stated intention beats a met expectation
sources: Keel call on NUMBERS 8l (iii), SKELETON 3d, Q25 r3 (Gneezy & Epley Experiment 4, not re-carded), van der Bles et al. (Q18 r20: "numerical ranges with a point estimate")

idea: People prefer a narrow estimate that misses to a wide one that holds: 80% chose "$18 to 20 billion" over "$20 to 40 billion" for a true $22.5 billion; "Judges presumably consider the risk of losing credibility if they claim greater precision than is warranted by their ultimate accuracy"
sources: Yaniv, I., & Foster, D. P. (1995). *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 124*(4), 424-432 (REFERENCES_APA row 249)
use: Width reads as uninformative, not as honest; Laura's width needs a meaning, not a defence
critique: Trivia estimates by students (studies of 20 to 60); Q19 r24 had it at abstract level with a second-hand example

note: Supports explaining the width in 3c: 80% preferred a narrow range that missed to a wide one that held, so width needs a meaning, not a defence; full paper, no retraction.

idea: Match the form to the uncertainty: one figure is more credible when uncertainty is low (4.98 against 4.43), a range when it is high (4.40 against 4.08); precision did not move confidence
sources: Rupar, K. K. (2011), Cornell dissertation; published as Rupar, K. (2017). *Contemporary Accounting Research, 34*(2), 849-870. https://doi.org/10.1111/1911-3846.12279
use: After the move nothing about either end is uncertain, so a bare range can read as mismatched; naming what each end is and which one she intends puts the form back in line
critique: About 120 participants, one positive-news forecast; dissertation numbers, the 2017 paper not read
verified: VERIFIED (full dissertation, Cornell eCommons; 2017 paper paywalled; Crossref: no notice on either record)
clash: risk: a range in a setting with no uncertainty left reads less credible than one figure; the case asks for a range (case l.115-118) and IPS l.15 speaks of a band, so the remedy is meaning, not form
note: Store and 3c: one figure reads better when nothing is uncertain, but the case asks for a range, so the remedy is naming what each end is, not a single figure.

idea: Managers choose precision to suit themselves (before insider sales, more where investors cannot judge what managers know); precise forecasts moved prices more; "The more precise the forecast, the more likely it is to be proven wrong"
sources: Cheng, Q., Luo, T., & Yue, H. (2013). *The Accounting Review, 88*(5), 1575-1602. https://doi.org/10.2308/accr-50506
use: Width chosen by the speaker invites suspicion; Laura's is set by a rule she states, which shuts that reading without a word of defence
critique: 10,799 forecasts, 1999-2006 (79.77% ranges); company incentives, not a founder's
verified: VERIFIED (full text, SMU open-access version; Crossref: no notice)
note: Supports a rule-set width: readers suspect a width the speaker chose, and Laura's comes from the rule's one sentence.

idea: Company ranges are narrow: width over midpoint has mean 0.117 and median 0.053 (95th percentile 0.462); Laura's central range is about 0.19 (Keel arithmetic: $20,000 over $105,000), about 3.6 times the median

note: Used in 3c: Laura's width is about 0.19 of its midpoint against a company median of 0.053; Keel arithmetic, so the numbers owner adds it to NUMBERS before 27 Nov.

idea: Precise numbers read as confident, and people choose advisers who give them: confidence 6.26 against 5.76 on an 8-point scale (d = 0.34); adviser choice d = 0.69
sources: Jerez-Fernandez, A., Angulo, A. N., & Oppenheimer, D. M. (2014). *Psychological Science, 25*(2), 633-635. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613504301
use: Laura's ends are round by design (rounded down to $5,000); the rule's sentence already says "rounded down", which makes the roundness a margin rather than vagueness; no new words
critique: Trivia and price-guessing (N = 187 and 163); a precise figure in a pledge could also read as false precision
verified: VERIFIED (full text, a mirror of the publisher PDF; Crossref: no update notice)
note: Store only: precise numbers read as confident, and the rule's 'rounded down' makes round ends a margin, not vagueness.

idea: The width is what the shares moved into Treasuries add to the floor: after the move both are owned, so the width is money, not a margin of error

idea: Metaphor against plain wording: r = .07 (corrected .073), 29 studies, 38 effect sizes, N = 3,945; "metaphor use diminished persuasiveness in almost 40% of the cases" (15 of 38 negative)
use: The image must earn its place by organising the rule, not by charm; a part with no natural fit gets none
note: CONCEIT 5b/6, SKELETON conceit: the effect is small (r = .07), so at most five images, each organising the rule; never claimed as persuasive.

idea: Metaphor showed "no demonstrable impact on competence (r = -.01) or character (r = -.02)"; a small rise in dynamism (r = .06); CIs on competence include zero, power about .60
use: No evidence that an image makes the team look less competent, and none that it looks more; the "patronising" fear is unshown either way
note: Store: no evidence an image makes the team look less competent; answers the 'patronising' worry.

idea: Initial source credibility: low r = .116, high r = .023
use: Readers who already trust the writer barely move. Judges reading a school team may start with low expectations (inference, untested on judges); not a reason to add images
note: Store only.

idea: Extended metaphors .088 (k = 14) against non-extended .048 (k = 24), intervals overlapping, and the order reversed once number and position were controlled. The best case, r = .42, was "a single, nonextended metaphor" that was novel, about a familiar topic, used early; it rests on 3 studies, N = 197
use: Carrying the image through the report gives no proven extra gain; the conceit's case rests on organisation and voice, not on extension
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 4: carrying the image through adds no proven gain; one mapping, few uses.

idea: Number of metaphors: one .076; two to eight .063; nine or more .017. Extended, two to eight .101 (k = 6, N = 519); extended, nine or more .035 (k = 4, N = 414)
use: Supports a cap below nine; five sits in the band that worked; more would fade toward zero
note: CONCEIT 6 and SKELETON: cap of five image sentences (two to eight worked; nine or more fade).

idea: Position: introduction only .123; body only .067; conclusion only -.063; first appearance in the introduction .103 against body or conclusion .022. For extended metaphors position barely mattered (.084 against .092). Best-supported theory, superior organisation: "Position at message start acts as 'title' to facilitate coherent organization of remaining message"
use: The defining use must come before what it organises (3.0 first; nothing earlier). An image saved for the end is the one placement that measured worse than none
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 3: never the last line (evidence); definition first in 3.0; image before or with its number.

idea: Novelty: novel metaphors .118 against stock ones .006 (significant); a familiar topic .065 against unfamiliar .059
use: A fresh mapping can work; a stock phrase does nothing. "Pencilled in" and "inked a deal" are stock
note: CONCEIT 5: stock phrases ('pencilled in') do nothing; the 3.0 definition carries the novel mapping.

idea: Crime framed as a "beast" or a "virus": 74% against 56% chose enforcement (Exp. 1); only 15 readers (3%) named the metaphor as a reason. A one-word frame as a short report's first sentence changed what information readers sought (Exp. 4); the same word as its last sentence did nothing (69% against 64%, p = .59; difference between the two, χ² = 5.45, p < .05). Metaphors were "most effective when they were presented early", helping "organize and coerce further incoming information"
use: Inside a part, the image comes before or with its number, never as the closing gloss on it
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 3: a one-word frame worked first, not last.

idea: Readers named the crime statistics, not the metaphor, as their reason; those with stronger prior views moved less (49% of Republicans' responses matched the frame, against 63% of Democrats' and Independents'); the frames still moved opinion more (18-22 points) than party or gender did (8-9)
use: Readers credit numbers, not images: each image sentence must carry its number (guard 1)
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 1: readers credit numbers, so each image sentence carries its number.

idea: Four experiments, one over 1,000 people, found no frame effect and no effect of supporting metaphors; prior preference dominated (Exp(B) = 7.46 and 14.22); frame memory improved in 2 of 4 experiments without changing choices. The "metaphor processing termination hypothesis": metaphor matters only when it is needed to understand the topic
use: The effect is fragile; where readers already understand the subject, the image adds little. Judges understand Treasuries
note: Store: the frame effect is fragile where readers already know the subject (the judges).

idea: Reanalysis of Reijnierse et al. (2015), N = 715: support for the frame rose with the number of consistent extensions (r = .105, p = .005), not with inconsistent ones (r = -.005); recall 84.6%, unaffected by extension (p = .31); a frame "should be presented early in a stream of processing"; "metaphor frames do not seem to reshape representations that have already been established"; typical effects .07-.15
use: Extension helps only when it is the same mapping; it does not make content more memorable; set the frame before the reader has formed a view of the numbers
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 4: extension helps only within one mapping.

idea: N = 1,000, ten issues: frame-consistent choices 54.9% with a consistent extension, 51.3% with none, 50.1% with an inconsistent one (F[2,18] = 4.011, p = .036); specific extensions 58.9%; an inconsistent extension removed the frame effect (consistent against inconsistent χ² = 10.41, p = .001); strong prior attitudes reduce it. Title example: a sports reader hears "home runs" and "fumble" as a mixed metaphor
use: Each image sentence must extend the one mapping (pencil = not yet owned; ink = owned in Treasuries that will pay it). A second mapping, even from the same craft, cancels the first
note: CONCEIT 5b and 7 guard 4: one inconsistent use cancels the gain; drop two-thirds, ranks 10-11, and trim/bleed unless it wins the blind read.

idea: Reading a passage's last sentence was faster when it extended the passage's metaphor than when it switched ("A debate is a race" against "a war"); "this result held only for novel metaphors and not for conventional metaphors", which seem stored as word senses. Related: time sentences answered faster when consecutive sentences kept one metaphor system (about 4,228 against 4,799 ms)
sources: Gentner, Bowdle, Wolff & Boronat (2001); Gentner & Markman (1997); Gentner, Imai & Boroditsky (2002)
use: Pencil-and-ink for Treasuries is novel, so it is processed as a mapping and switching costs. Ordinary finance metaphors (ladder, floor) are conventional and do not clash
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 4: switching mapping costs the reader.

idea: Novel figurative statements were read faster and preferred as similes ("A mind is like a kitchen") than as metaphors; after two novel similes on the same base, people preferred the metaphor form. Conventional ones were faster as metaphors
sources: Bowdle & Gentner, as reported in Gentner et al. (2001); Bowdle & Gentner (2005)
use: Define the conceit once as an explicit comparison in 3.0 ("as in a comic, where only the inked line prints"); after that, bare "inked" works
note: CONCEIT 6 (3.0) and 7 guard 5: define once as an explicit comparison.

idea: Analogy maps relations, not attributes ("Discard attributes of objects"; "Try to preserve relations"); systematicity: connected systems of relations are mapped; "mere appearance matches ... their explanatory power is sharply limited"; people rated as most apt the analogies they read most relationally
use: The conceit must carry a relation (owned, so it may be stated; a correction stays visible), not a surface likeness. 2.1's size ratio is the nearest thing to an attribute match in the plan
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 8: the image carries a relation (owned, so it may be stated), not a surface.

idea: "Candidate inferences are only guesses: Their factual correctness must be checked separately ... Any process capable of producing novel true inferences is also capable of generating false inferences." Differences tied to the shared structure (alignable differences) are the ones people notice: 9.0 listed for similar pairs against 3.9 for dissimilar ones
use: A good analogy makes its own differences obvious to an expert. The most alignable one here: ink cannot come off, a Treasury can be sold. The report must say the ink holds because each Treasury is held to its payment date
note: CONCEIT 8: ink holds because each Treasury is held to its date (an expert knows a Treasury can be sold).

idea: Nine kinds of analogy-induced misconception, among them carrying over a source property the target lacks, and the common-language meaning of a term. "It is not enough merely to tell people what the limitations of an analogy are ... The analogical core is what is retained." Antidotes: explicit warning of the pitfall and integrated multiple analogies, each patching the last ("alteration")
use: The exception must travel inside each use (guard 5), not in a separate caveat. "Painted over, the correction stays" and the fallback "one sealed envelope per payment" are patches of the right kind
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 5: the exception travels inside each use; 'inked' read as 'signed' is the common-language trap.

idea: Six steps from 43 textbooks and 10 exemplary teachers (86% rater agreement), step 5 "indicate where the analogy breaks down"; "Analogies are double-edged swords ... every analogy breaks down"; a textbook's sink-and-drain analogy left a misconception despite the authors' caveat; sketchy analogies dropped after one line promote misconceptions. Descriptive; it does not test outcomes
use: Supports section 8 ("the report says the limit where it uses the image"); a one-line image never developed is the riskiest kind
note: CONCEIT 8 kept: the report says the limit where it uses the image.

idea: "Explicating the conditions for each analogy reduced the incidence of alternative conceptions" (their 1993 and 2000 studies); teachers forgot the six steps, so the FAR guide asks for LIKES and UNLIKES; analogies "all break down somewhere and they usually break down sooner than later"; several analogies at once confuse readers who expect one answer
use: Section 8 is the UNLIKES list; one main mapping, at most one patch
note: CONCEIT 8 is the 'unlikes' list; one mapping.

idea: Analogy in a text "improves accurate inferencing, but at the expense of factual learning"
use: An image may help readers apply the rule while costing recall of exact figures: the number is stated literally in the same sentence and tables stay image-free
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 1: figures stated literally, since analogy can cost factual recall.

idea: Agent metaphors in market commentary ("the Nasdaq climbed") raised investors' expectations that a trend would continue (64 undergraduates; commentator-focused rating F(1,104) = 16.06, p < .001); the effect worked through what readers took to be the commentator's view (Sobel z = 4.18); it appeared when prices were shown as a graph, not as a table of numbers (t = 1.39, 0.00, 0.50, all ns)
use: In finance, metaphor shifts expectations and is read as the writer's conviction; numbers in plain form damp it. "Inked" will be read as the team's confidence, so it may never say more than the numbers (guards 1, 2, 5)
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 8 and WORDS: in finance, metaphor shifts expectations; numbers in plain form damp it. Investing-literature reference candidate (Morris et al. 2007).

idea: Expertise reversal: techniques "highly effective with inexperienced learners can lose their effectiveness and even have negative consequences when used with more experienced learners"; integrated explanatory notes "were difficult to ignore"; additions meant to make a text more coherent helped only low-knowledge readers (McNamara et al., 1996, as reviewed)
use: An image that explains a finance fact to finance judges is redundant and costs them attention; the image may carry only the team's own rule. It is not a study of analogies
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 8: expertise reversal; the image never explains finance to finance judges.

idea: With knowledgeable learners, "analogy facilitated learning when the targets were presented to discourage contact with prior knowledge. In contrast, analogy decreased performance when the same targets were presented to facilitate contact with prior knowledge"
use: Judges' knowledge of Treasuries is engaged throughout section 3: an analogy about how Treasuries work could cost them. Keep it to the rule about stating figures
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 8: analogies about how Treasuries work could collide with judges' knowledge.

idea: A sports metaphor raised scrutiny and sensitivity to argument strength among readers who like sports, and lowered both among those who dislike sports
use: Craft terms (trim, bleed, safe area, non-photo blue) resonate only with print-minded readers; pencil and ink are everyone's, so they carry the conceit (guard 4)
verified: Abstract only (plus Landau et al., 2018, secondary)
note: CONCEIT 5b rank 3: craft terms reach only print-minded readers; trim/bleed conditional.

idea: Analogies "can lead to poor relative metacomprehension accuracy for students who fail to use situation-model-based cues": readers relying on surface cues judged their understanding worse with analogies, even in an experiment where the analogies raised test scores
use: The writers' and readers' sense that a passage "reads clearly" is unreliable here. Test by repeat-back and by applying the rule to a new figure, not by preference
note: CONCEIT 10 and voice README: score restatement and one applied question, not preference.

idea: Recoded with current attitudes, the crime-metaphor effect returns; a German replication reproduced the frame effect and found no difference between metaphor and simile forms
use: The effect is real but small and depends on the audience; simile form costs nothing
note: Store: the effect is real but small and audience-dependent.

idea: Review: metaphors are "most effective when they draw on knowledge that is shared between speakers and listeners"; "unlikely to affect people who have strong ideological commitments"
use: Use the shared core (pencil, ink), not specialist craft; expect little movement in readers with fixed views
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 4: use the shared core (pencil, ink), not specialist craft.

idea: Conventional metaphors are understood by retrieving a stored figurative sense; novel ones by comparison; comprehension moves from comparison to categorisation as a metaphor becomes familiar
use: Readers will first read "inked" in its stored sense ("signed"). The 3.0 definition has to replace that sense with "owned in Treasuries", and the repeat-back test checks that it did
note: CONCEIT 7 guard 5, WORDS ink row, CONCEIT 10: 'inked' is read in its stored sense (signed); 3.0 says 'owned'; the repeat-back scores 'owned'.

idea: OMB Principle 1: "Budget authority sufficient to complete a useful segment of a capital project ... must be appropriated before any obligations for the useful segment ... may be incurred"
sources: OMB (2025), A-11 App. J, section C
use: The ten payments and the bottom are each a complete segment, bought before anything is promised on them
critique: Budget authority is legal permission, not money held; OMB applies it to whole assets
note: 3a/3d idea only (complete segment bought before anything is promised); never 'full funding' for the facility (WORDS).

idea: The cost of not doing it: funding in increments "without certainty if or when future funding will be available" brings "poor planning, acquisition of assets not fully justified, higher acquisition costs, cancellation of major investments, the loss of sunk costs, or inadequate funding to maintain and operate the assets"

critique: Laura's share is one piece of the building's money; her rule does not make the building fully funded
note: 3d store: the costs of funding a building in yearly pieces.

sources: OMB (2025), App. J, sections B and planning item 7

critique: OMB's test is about a usable asset; Laura's bottom is a usable promise
note: 3b: the deletion test in public-budget form (VT at zero still leaves a one-figure range).

idea: Advance appropriations "may bias tradeoffs in the budget year in favor of the proposed asset because with advance appropriations the full cost of the asset is not included in the budget year"; GAO: "Although OMB considers advance appropriations as consistent with full funding, the practice could be viewed as a form of incremental funding"
sources: OMB (2025), App. J, Principle 2; GAO (2001), GAO-01-432R, enclosure p. 8
use: Jan 2027 to Jan 2028: the ladder relied on the 2028 deposit for its top-up (IPS l.13; $2,388 today, MODEL). That year was "full funding with an advance appropriation": full by OMB, incremental by GAO. The ten payments are inked in Jan 2028 (CONCEIT 3)
critique: The deposit is Laura's own money (CANON D8), not a future vote
clash: risk: never say the payments were all owned in Jan 2027; CONCEIT 3 and NUMBERS 5 already say Jan 2028 and "at today's rates"
note: Store.

idea: "full funding ensures that the full estimated costs of decisions are recognized at the time that the commitment is made"; incremental funding "erodes future fiscal flexibility" and gives "an incentive to 'low ball' the estimate at the beginning"
use: The cost of Laura's promise is fixed and known when she makes it; nothing later is pulled into it
critique: GAO's subject is the Navy and civilian agencies, not donors
note: Store; the phrase 'full funding' is banned for the facility (WORDS).

idea: DOE: "one project received only about 60% of the $155 million expected during the first 3 years of a 5-year construction cycle ... the construction schedule was extended 3 years and the total construction costs rose from $236 to $313 million, an increase of $77 million"; two others funded at 40% and 43% "went over original cost estimates and were years behind schedule"
use: Measured cost of building on promised but late money: +33% and 3 years. Fits 3d's case for a capital pledge whose condition is the facility's total being reached by one close date (Q11c)
critique: Agency officials' account, three projects, large federal science buildings
note: 3d: measured cost of building on promised but late money (+33%, 3 years; DOE via GAO).

idea: Incremental funding "Reduces cost consciousness because increases in cost can simply be added to subsequent increments"; "Increases financial risk to the contractors and/or increases cost risk to the government for cancellation costs"; it can force a later choice "between having an unusable asset and continuing project funding for years, even after priorities may have changed"
use: Why Laura's contribution does not rise with overruns (SKELETON 3d): a promise that grows with cost is the incremental pattern GAO warns about
critique: Laura is a funder, not the builder
note: 3d: why her contribution does not rise with overruns.

idea: The exception: for high-technology projects "funds already invested are not necessarily wasted if no additional funding is provided because knowledge is likely to have been gained"
use: A building is the opposite case: half a building is worth little, so its funders want money in hand
critique: none needed
note: Store: half a building is worth little, so funders want money in hand.

idea: "the law is violated not just when there are insufficient funds in an account when a payment becomes due. The very act of obligating the United States to make a payment when the necessary funds are not already in the account is also a violation" (B-300480, 2003); appropriations law in one line: the Act and related statutes "[restrict] in every possible way the expenditures and expenses and liabilities of the government ... to the specific appropriations for each fiscal year" (Wilder's Case, 1880)
sources: GAO (2006), Red Book 3rd ed. Vol. II, ch. 6; GAO (1992) 2nd ed. p. 6-13 has the same sentence
use: The best fit for "no figure stated before the move" (SKELETON 3c): the wrong is the promise made before the money is there, not only the payment missed
critique: The test is "funds in the account" (an appropriation), not owned assets; the US can borrow to refill an account, Laura cannot
verified: VERIFIED (sentence read in both editions; ch. 6 read in part)
note: 3c/3d: the Antideficiency Act's 'very act of obligating' when funds are not in the account is Laura's rule's nearest public parallel (GAO Red Book 2006); one clause at most, investing-literature references first.

idea: "the Customs Service violated the Antideficiency Act by obligating against anticipated receipts from future sales of seized property"; the Air Force "violated the Antideficiency Act by overobligating its Industrial Fund based on estimated or anticipated customer orders"
use: Pencil in public-law words: the 2028 deposit before it arrives and VT before the move are "anticipated receipts". A top stated 1, 3, 6 or 12 months before the move is not yet owned in 2.9%, 6.3%, 8.7% or 10.7% of simulated futures (NUMBERS 4)
critique: Customs and the Air Force had no fixed claim on the receipts; VT's value moves daily
note: Fri 20 Nov, attack day (ATTACKS.md D20; bond 21, professor 15, plain 26): the Antideficiency Act concerns appropriations; "US law forbids an agency to commit money Congress has not yet appropriated", or nothing.

idea: A "subject to appropriation" promise is still a burden: GAO said such an indemnity, "even though it would impose no legal obligation unless or until funds are appropriated, it would impose a moral obligation"; on contracts outrunning their funds, "the failure by Congress to appropriate the money might be viewed as a serious breach of faith ... another example of a type of 'coercive deficiency' the Antideficiency Act was intended to prohibit"
use: Why "ink only goes one way": a conditional figure still binds in practice. The case's "she could damage her credibility" is the donor's version of the moral obligation
critique: Congress can be coerced into paying; co-sponsors cannot make Laura pay
note: Fri 20 Nov, attack day (ATTACKS.md D20): as Q43-010.

idea: Indemnity is allowed "where the potential liability of the government was limited to a definite amount known at the time of the agreement, was within the amount of available appropriations"
use: The cap: contribution = min(what the funds pay, the stated top), a definite maximum known when stated ($115,000 at the model's figures)
critique: Laura's lower bound is not fixed to the dollar (iBonds funds pay NAV), hence the 0.5% cut
note: 3c: the cap, a definite maximum known when stated.

idea: "Even if the initial obligation was well within available funds, the Antideficiency Act can still be violated if upward adjustments cause the obligation to exceed available funds"
use: The one exception to the top being reached: the funds' own costs above the 0.5% cut (at 0.75%, about 1 path in 17 falls short of the top by at most $429; SKELETON 3c)
critique: Laura's obligation does not rise; her money can shrink slightly
note: Fri 20 Nov, attack day (ATTACKS.md D20): as Q43-010.

idea: The SST case (B-159141, 1967): the FAA "each year budgeted for, and obligated, sufficient funds to cover potential termination liability. The appropriations committees became concerned that unnecessarily large amounts were being tied up this way, especially in light of the highly remote possibility that the SST contracts would be terminated", and cut the reserve
use: The honest cost of certainty, with a public example. The extra Treasuries ($35,894) are Laura's reserve against a remote event; unlike the SST's, most comes back (about $45,500 in 2033 money if rates hold; NUMBERS)
critique: The SST reserve covered contract termination, Laura's covers falling yields
note: Store: SST reserve against termination liability, a public example of the price of certainty.

idea: "The financing approach known as full funding has broader requirements than those found in these two acts and is enforced by policy rather than statute"; Army: "The DOD full funding policy is not statutory. Violations of the full funding policy do not necessarily violate the Anti-Deficiency Act"
sources: GAO (2003), GAO-03-1011; TJAGLCS (2026), Fiscal Law Deskbook, ch. 3
use: Two levels: a legal floor (no promise without money) and a stricter policy (pay for the whole thing first). Laura's rule is the first, kept by her own policy
critique: Laura has no auditor or statute; the rule holds by the plan and by showing holdings (H5-064)
note: Store only.

idea: The price of paying up front: "The requirement that the full cost of a project must be absorbed in the annual budget ... can make capital acquisitions seem prohibitively expensive. This has led some to suggest that the result is a bias against capital"
use: Laura's version: a smaller top. Each $5,000 more of stated top costs about $5,300 of what she keeps (NUMBERS 8o)

The median payout rate of 979 endowed foundations was 5.4% (2007), 5.8% (2008) and 6.4% (2009) while their assets fell about 24% in 2008. sources: Foundation Center, "Foundation Payout" (2012), https://foundationcenter.issuelab.org/resources/14076/14076.pdf ; 2009 highlights (row 2 URL) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Smoothing is why the lag exists: grants follow an average of past asset values, not this year's price
critique: A higher rate on a smaller base still means smaller grants a year or two later
note: Foundations smooth grants on average past asset values, which is why the lag exists.

idea: US law builds in the lag. The 5% minimum is figured on asset values set "on a monthly basis" over the year. A foundation has until the end of the following year to pay it before a 30% tax, and excess payouts carry forward
use: A crash in one year lowers the required grants mostly in the next two years, so a US foundation met in 2031 pays a 2033 pledge partly from earlier, higher asset values
critique: US private foundations only. The rule is a floor and many pay more. Taiwan's rules for foundations were not checked (gap)
verified: VERIFIED (statute text); the lag in years is Keel inference
where: This run: Cornell LII statute page
note: US payout law builds in a lag of up to two years; Taiwan rules not checked.

idea: Community foundations kept granting while gifts into them fell: grants were up 15% on 2006 while gifts received were down 22% (2009 survey)
sources: Council on Foundations, 2009 Columbus Survey results, https://cof.org/sites/default/files/2023-08/04-08-10_2009%20Columbus%20Survey%20Results_29221_0.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Pass-through funders run down their balances to keep grants up for a year or two
critique: Partly at odds with row 3 (-7.1% in 2009 against 2008); different base year and sample
note: Conflicts with Q4b-003 on a different base year; do not use either figure alone.

idea: 2022, the last big share fall: the S&P 500 fell 19.4% (-25.4% real). Foundation giving rose 2.5% to $105.21bn (-5.0% real), corporate giving rose 3.4% to $29.48bn (-4.2% real), individuals fell 6.4% (-13.4% real), and arts giving rose 2.9% current
sources: Giving USA 2023 press release, Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, https://news.iu.edu/philanthropy/live/news/51591-giving-usa-total-us-charitable-giving-declined-in (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: When shares fell alongside high inflation, institutional givers held their budgets in money terms, and their real cuts were small
critique: One year. Inflation, not the market, did most of the real cut
note: In the 2022 share fall institutional givers held their budgets in money terms.

idea: The lag year after 2022: foundation giving fell 2.3% real in 2023, to $103.53bn from $105.99bn (2023 dollars). 22% of foundations cut their payout rate in 2022, and for 2023 more expected to cut (27%) than raise (23%), the first time in the survey's history. 79% of 546 said inflation did not change their 2022 grants, several because grants "are based on the average market return of assets over multiple years"
sources: Giving USA 2024 via BWF, https://www.bwf.com/giving-usa-2024-report-insights/ ; Candid, https://candid.org/blogs/foundation-giving-and-payout-in-2022-what-changed-whats-next ; https://candid.org/blogs/how-inflation-affects-grantmaking-decisions-foundations ; https://candid.org/blogs/foundation-giving-data-in-2023-expected-grantmaking-in-2024 ; Chronicle of Philanthropy, 29 Jun 2023, https://www.philanthropy.com/news/many-foundations-are-taking-a-step-back-after-2-years-of-steep-increases-in-grants-budgets (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The foundation cut came one year after the share fall, while shares were recovering. This is the same shape as 2008-09
critique: Candid's own sample shows 2023 grants up 1.7% ($25.8bn to $26.2bn; median +0.3%; median payout of independent foundations 5%, mean 7.5%). Giving USA's real figure and Candid's nominal figure differ
verified: CONFLICTING on size (Giving USA -2.3% real; Candid sample +1.7% nominal); timing agrees
where: This run: BWF page, Candid blogs, Chronicle article
note: Sources disagree on the size of the 2023 cut; only the one-year timing agrees.

idea: Arts giving held through the 2022 share fall. In 2023 dollars, arts, culture and humanities giving was $23.55bn (2019), $22.70bn (2020), $23.49bn (2021), $23.70bn (2022) and $25.26bn (2023, +6.6% real)
sources: Giving USA 2024 table as given by BWF, https://www.bwf.com/giving-usa-2024-report-insights/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The worst recent year for US arts giving was the 2020 shutdown (-3.6% real, Keel arithmetic), not the 2022 share fall
critique: US totals, mostly from individuals. This is not building co-sponsorship. Read through BWF, not the Giving USA report
verified: VERIFIED (BWF's table); Giving USA report itself not read
note: US arts giving held through 2022 and its worst recent year was the 2020 shutdown; read via BWF.

idea: Foundations do not act counter-cyclically. Their payouts after financial shocks show "retrenchment" or "independence", not more giving when need rises
sources: Calabrese, T.D. & Ely, T.L. (2022) "How US Private Foundations Change Payouts Based on Financial Shocks: Revealed Publicness or Revealed Privateness?", Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 32(1): 166-182, https://academic.oup.com/jpart/article/32/1/166/6277840 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Do not assume a foundation co-sponsor will step in when others cut
critique: US data. Abstract only
note: Foundations do not step up when need rises; abstract only.

idea: Foundations respond asymmetrically. "A 10 percent asset shock raises payout rates by 10 to 16 basis points for positive returns but decreases them by 31 to 39 basis points after negative returns". They "do not increase aggregate spending in periods of elevated need". Founder-family foundations cut 102% more after losses. Peers crowd each other out (elasticity -0.22). Median grant payout is 4.84%, and the correlation between foundations' returns is 0.44
sources: Lu, Y. & Malliaris, S. (2026) "Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations", Journal of Financial Economics 185, 104377 (open access), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X26001480 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Foundations still run by the founder's family are the likeliest to cut. Because their returns move together, shortfalls tend to come in clusters
critique: Rates, not dollars. In 2008-09 the aggregate rate rose (row 4) because grants lagged falling assets. US only
clash: yes, partly: supports the cluster risk in Q9 row 30 (risk to note)
note: Founder-family foundations cut most after losses and foundations' returns move together, so co-sponsor shortfalls can cluster; a risk to note.

idea: University endowments cut payouts below their own policy after losses but do not raise them after gains ("endowment hoarding"). A later study found symmetric responses
sources: Brown, J.R., Dimmock, S.G., Kang, J.-K. & Weisbenner, S.J. (2014) "How University Endowments Respond to Financial Market Shocks", American Economic Review 104(3), https://consensus.app/papers/details/7831f601f303581cb3e87906847e0fab/ ; Rosen et al. (2019), Journal of Higher Education (via Consensus search) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A partner university or other endowed body protects its endowment first
critique: Universities, not arts funders
note: Two studies disagree on whether endowments cut asymmetrically; low direct use.

idea: Million-dollar gifts from foundations "tend to be countercyclical". Corporate million-dollar giving is less tied to the economy. Million-dollar gifts to the arts go with good economic conditions
sources: Osili, U. O., Ackerman, J. & Li, Y. (2019) "Economic effects on million dollar giving", Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly 48(2): 417-439, https://doi.org/10.1177/0899764018800791 (issue year 2019, online first 2018; REFERENCES_APA row 98); abstract read at https://consensus.app/papers/details/d558d16e83195cf6b31f8d6f98a7f6b8/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Big single grants from foundations may be the steadiest co-sponsor money. Big arts gifts from individuals are the least steady
critique: US. Abstract only
note: Big single foundation gifts may be the steadiest co-sponsor money; abstract only.

idea: Donations respond more to booms than to busts (US aggregate data, 1968-2007)
sources: List, J.A. & Peysakhovich, Y. (2011) "Charitable donations are more responsive to stock market booms than busts", Economics Letters, https://consensus.app/papers/details/a1e6b1a3c8aa562990811edb9db34cf9/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: For all giving, the fall in a crash is milder than the rise in a boom. This matches rows 1-2
critique: Mostly individuals. For foundations the opposite asymmetry is found (row 11)
note: Giving rises more in booms than it falls in busts; mostly individuals.

idea: In the Great Recession, giving fell more than shocks to income or wealth explain; attitudes changed
sources: Meer, J., Miller, D. & Wulfsberg, E. (2017) "The Great Recession and charitable giving", Applied Economics Letters 24(21): 1542-1549, https://doi.org/10.1080/13504851.2017.1319556 (REFERENCES_APA row 94); abstract read at https://consensus.app/papers/details/1142ead87f7951f5ac624ebb5bf70307/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A crash can cut giving through mood as well as money, so a co-sponsor's balance sheet is not the whole story
critique: Household (PSID) data, not institutions
note: Giving fell more than income in the Great Recession, through mood as well as money.

idea: Corporate giving follows profits, not share prices, and the previous year's profits at that. "Corporate giving is tied more closely to corporate profits than stock market performance". Giving as a share of the previous year's pre-tax profit was 1.02% (2007/2006), 0.99% (2008/2007) and 1.21% (2009/2008), and "previous-year profit is related to current-year giving"
sources: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, Econ Focus Q2 2010, https://www.richmondfed.org/-/media/RichmondFedOrg/publications/research/econ_focus/2010/q2/pdf/feature3.pdf ; CECP, Giving in Numbers 2010, https://intranet.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GivinginNumbers2010.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A corporate co-sponsor's 2033 budget is set from its 2032 profits, which builds in a one-year lag
critique: Large US companies (CECP members)
note: Corporate giving follows last year's profits, a built-in one-year lag; a timing clash with 'same period' to note.

idea: Corporate giving held in 2008, fell in 2009, and switched from cash to goods. Giving rose or held for 63% of companies in 2007-08 while profits fell; it fell for 57-59% in 2009. Cash giving was $4.63bn (2007), $4.53bn (2008) and $4.29bn (2009) for 96 firms (-7.3% over two years, Keel arithmetic). "Many companies compensated for fewer cash grants with product donations". Giving USA: corporate giving rose 5.5% in 2009, driven by in-kind gifts
sources: CECP Giving in Numbers 2012, https://cecp.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/GIN2012_finalweb.pdf ; 2013, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GIN2013_Web_Final.pdf ; 2010 (row 16 URL); Giving USA 2010 Executive Summary, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/GivingUSA_2010_ExecSummary.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In a downturn a corporate co-sponsor may offer materials, equipment or services instead of cash. That helps a residency but does not fill a cash pledge
critique: Large US companies. The arts share in GIN 2013 fell through smaller gifts; the exact share was not captured
where: This run: CECP PDFs, Giving USA summary
note: Corporate cash giving fell in 2009 and shifted to goods, which do not fill a cash pledge; a timing clash to note.

idea: Business support for the arts fell 14% from 2006 to 2009. The share of businesses giving to any cause fell from 70% to 52%, and to the arts from 43% to 28%. Arts sponsorship dollars rose slightly in 2009 but fell after inflation, and the arts' share of sponsorship fell from 6% to 5%
sources: Business Committee for the Arts 2010 survey, as reported by Americans for the Arts, https://intranet.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/pdf/get_involved/advocacy/research/2011/business_support11.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: After a crash, fewer companies give to the arts at all. The pool narrows; the cheques do not just shrink
critique: Survey design and firm sizes not checked
note: After a crash fewer companies give to the arts at all; a timing clash to note.

idea: UK business money for culture fell four years running while trusts and foundations rose. Business: £157m (2008/09, -6%), £144.1m (2009/10, -12%; Third Sector says -11%), £134.2m (2010/11, -7%, "fourth consecutive annual fall", below 2004/05). Trusts and foundations: £135m (2008/09, -7%), £154.6m (2009/10, +11%), £170.3m (2010/11, +10%). Individuals: £382.2m (2010/11, +6%). "Corporate money is a discretionary spend". In 2009 Arts & Business warned "the worst may be yet to come, with 2010-11 being the low-point"
sources: Arts & Business figures via WalesOnline, https://www.walesonline.co.uk/business/business-news/arts-picture-private-investors-wales-1939961 ; Museums Association, 2011, https://www.museumsassociation.org/museums-journal/news/2011/02/01032011-coprorate-giving-to-museums-falls/ and 2012, https://www.museumsassociation.org/museums-journal/news/2012/02/28022012-corporate-giving-falls/ ; Third Sector, https://www.thirdsector.co.uk/corporate-giving-arts-down-11-per-cent/fundraising/article/1051947 ; A&B Private Investment in Culture 2010/11, https://www.leanarts.org.uk/app/uploads/artsandbusiness-private-investment-in-culture10-11.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Over 2008/09 to 2010/11, business money fell 14.5% and trusts and foundations rose 26% (nominal, Keel arithmetic). Corporate arts money hit bottom two to three years after the share trough, the longest lag here, while a mix of funder types offset part of it
critique: UK only, one cycle. A&B's percentages may be real while the £ figures are nominal. Read through press reports, except the 2010/11 growth table (business: rise, fall, fall, fall, fall; trusts and foundations: rise, rise, fall, rise, rise; 2006/07 to 2010/11)
verified: VERIFIED (press reports and the A&B 2010/11 table)
clash: yes, partly: the IPS's "during that same period" does not fit a cut that lasted until 2011 (risk to note)
where: This run: news pages and A&B PDF
note: UK business money for culture bottomed two to three years after the share low while trusts rose; press reports; a timing clash to note.

idea: Match money softened the fall. Scotland's £1-for-£1 incentive limited the sponsorship fall to 7% over 2009-10, against 17% for the UK
use: Laura's committed lead gift works a little like match money: co-sponsors giving alongside a fixed lead may cut less
critique: One programme. The match effect on Laura is Keel inference
where: This run: Culture & Business Scotland page
note: Match evidence; Laura offers no match on her range, so use only as what co-sponsors' own funders do

idea: US federal arts money first rose and was cut later. NEA appropriations: $144.7m (2008), $155.0m (2009, plus $50m Recovery Act money), $167.5m (2010), $154.69m (2011), $146.0m (2012), $138.4m (2013, sequestration), which is -17.4% from 2010 to 2013 (Keel arithmetic). In the pandemic, the NEA received $75m (CARES, 2020) and $135m (ARP, 2021)
sources: National Endowment for the Arts, Appropriations History, https://www.arts.gov/about/appropriations-history (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Public money can rise in a crash through stimulus, then be cut two to four years later in austerity, after shares have recovered
critique: US federal. This is politics, not markets. Recovery Act money is not in the yearly figures
note: US federal arts money rose in the crash and was cut two to four years later; a timing clash to note.

idea: US state arts agencies cut deepest and latest. Legislative appropriations: $354.1m (FY2008), $328.8m (FY2009), $291.8m (FY2010), $272.6m (FY2011), $260.2m (FY2012, "a low point"), $277.8m (FY2013), $306.5m (FY2014), $350.6m (FY2015). That is -26.5% over FY2008-12 (Keel arithmetic; NASAA says 27%). FY2012 is the year to June 2012, about three years after the March 2009 share low. The earlier cycle ran from $449.5m (FY2001) to $279.9m (FY2004), -37.7%
sources: NASAA, FY2016 revenues news release, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/NASAAFY2016SAARevenuesPressRelease.pdf ; FY2016 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/NASAAFY2016SAARevenuesReport.pdf ; FY2026 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/FY2026-State-Arts-Agency-Revenues-Report_final-updated.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A public arts budget is the latest and deepest cutter: it falls for about three years after shares bottom and takes about six years to come back
critique: US states, driven by tax revenue, not share prices
note: Public arts budgets cut deepest and latest, about three years after shares bottomed; a timing clash to note.

idea: NASAA says why: "a built-in recovery time lag: due to the structure of public finances, state budgets take longer to rebound". After the early-1990s and early-2000s recessions, "the decrease in SAA appropriations continued several years after the recession had ended". FY2017 was still 6.7% below FY2008 in real terms. The early 2010 snapshot: state arts appropriations -10%, local government support -8%, private giving to the arts -6.5% (Americans for the Arts testimony). GIA: 2010 state -6.9%, local -8.1%, NEA up
sources: NASAA FY2017 report, https://www.nasaa-arts.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/NASAA-FY2017-SAA-Revenues-Report.pdf ; Americans for the Arts testimony, 13 Apr 2010, https://www.americansforthearts.org/sites/default/files/pdf/news/press/RobertLynch_AADTestimony.pdf ; Grantmakers in the Arts, "Public Funding for the Arts: 2010 Update", https://www.giarts.org/article/public-funding-arts-2010-update (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Three cycles have had the same shape: public arts money keeps falling after the recession ends
critique: The testimony's line that arts groups run about "a year behind business trends" was seen only in part (UNVERIFIED wording)
verified: VERIFIED (NASAA report, testimony figures, GIA page)
where: This run: PDFs and GIA page
note: Three cycles show public arts money falling after recessions end; a timing clash to note.

idea: Taiwan's corporate arts sponsorship hit a record in the edition covering the crash. The 10th Wenxin Award (文馨獎, 2010) recognised about NT$2.2bn of company giving, the highest of any edition in the award's 12 years (the Executive Yuan, in Chinese) and nearly double the 1st edition's NT$1.15bn. Its 176 winners included 21 that funded rebuilding after Typhoon Morakot. The 16th (2023, covering the pandemic years) recognised NT$1,870,506,685
sources: Executive Yuan news, 7 Aug 2010, https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/9277F759E41CCD91/600a82fb-fe45-495c-9012-3e600e2cc717 ; NCAF news, 2 Oct 2023, https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/news_detail.html?sid=670 ; rules of the 14th award (two-year counting window, award since 1998, every two years from the 7th), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/official/%E7%AC%AC14%E5%B1%86%E6%96%87%E9%A6%A8%E7%8D%8E%E5%BE%B5%E4%BB%B6%E8%AA%AA%E6%98%8E%E6%9C%83%E7%B0%A1%E5%A0%B1%E8%AA%AA%E6%98%8E.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Company money for the arts in Taiwan did not visibly shrink in 2008-09, even with the TAIEX down 46% in 2008
critique: Award totals count only givers who apply and give at least NT$500,000, so this is not a census. That the 10th edition covered 2008-09 is Keel inference from the two-year rule of the 14th. The 9th (2008) total was not found
verified: VERIFIED (EY and NCAF page text, the 14th's rules PDF); window is Keel inference
where: This run: search excerpts of the EY and NCAF pages; rules PDF
note: CANON B4 guard: never say Taiwan's government cut arts money in a recession; quote as data on one funder only

idea: Early Wenxin editions recorded corporate arts sponsorship of over NT$1bn every year ("每年皆超過十億元"), so Taiwan's corporate arts money is a steady, sizable pool
sources: 陳以亨, 林瑩滋 & 李星美 (2004) 企業贊助藝文活動的動機因素之研究, 輔仁管理評論 11(1): 33-52, https://www.management.fju.edu.tw/zh-tw/down.php?hFFile=tw_books_caty01331169529.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: It gives a base for row 24's record. 60% of large firms surveyed had sponsored the arts
critique: Before 2004. Survey of large firms
where: This run: search excerpt of the PDF
note: Taiwan's corporate arts sponsorship has been a steady pool above NT$1bn a year; pre-2004 data.

idea: The cause and year of NCAF's 41% income fall, now settled: 2015, a weak market led by Taiwan shares, after a strong 2014. Financial income was NT$283,520,045 in 2014 (88.9% of revenue) and NT$150,522,150 in 2015. The return was 2.42% against 3.59% expected, with investment losses of NT$75.6m and unrealised losses of NT$173.7m. The TAIEX fell 10.41% in 2015. Total income went from NT$318,803,033 to NT$188,860,003
sources: NCAF Annual Report 2015 (English), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/publishBookEn/20200623/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc.pdf ; CBC Annual Report 2015, https://www.cbc.gov.tw/en/public/Attachment/661517483371.PDF (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Taiwan's main public arts grant-maker lives on market returns. Its fund is about NT$2bn each in deposits, shares and fixed income
critique: One foundation. This answers Q9 row 34's critique: 2014 was ordinary investment income, not a one-off
where: This run: NCAF and CBC PDFs
note: Taiwan's main public arts funder lives on market returns (income -41% in 2015); carries Q9-034.

idea: ...but NCAF's grants ROSE that year. Grant expenses went from NT$153,598,721 (2014) to NT$160,462,639 (2015), +4.5%, and regular grants from NT$109,988,100 to NT$112,538,905, +2.3%. It ran a NT$54.7m deficit, drawn from an accumulated surplus of NT$66.1m at the end of 2014
use: Taiwan's own arts funder shields its grants from market swings with money it set aside. This is the same idea as Laura's kept half, on the funder's side
critique: The reserve was thin (NT$66.1m), and the deeper 2011 fall used it up (row 28)
note: Top-40 candidate: NCAF kept grants rising in a bad market year by drawing on money set aside, the kept half's idea on the funder's side.

idea: NCAF in 2011: investment income was NT$14m, "more than 200 million less than projected", and total income NT$37.8m against NT$191.4m in 2010 (-80%). Yet grant-related expenses held at NT$147.7m (NT$149.1m in 2010, -0.9%), and regular grants were NT$117.5m (NT$122.5m, -4.1%). The deficit was NT$183.4m, the Council for Cultural Affairs added NT$38m, and the accumulated surplus went from NT$56.8m to -NT$126.7m. The TAIEX fell 21.18% (UNVERIFIED at TWSE)
use: Even an 80% fall in income cut NCAF's grants by only 1-4%, because government stepped in
critique: A private co-sponsor has no government to top it up
verified: VERIFIED (annual report); TAIEX figure UNVERIFIED at source
note: An 80% income fall cut NCAF's grants only 1-4% because government stepped in, a backstop private co-sponsors lack.

idea: NCAF through 2008-09: regular grants were NT$112.9m (2007), NT$108.8m (2008, -3.6%), NT$105.7m (2009, -2.8%) and NT$122.5m (2010, +15.9%), while the TAIEX fell 46.03% in 2008 and rose 78.34% in 2009 (UNVERIFIED at TWSE)
sources: NCAF Annual Report 2011, five-year table (row 28 URL) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Taiwan's deepest modern crash cut NCAF's regular grants by about 6% over two years (Keel arithmetic), and they came back above the pre-crash level in 2010, one year after shares rebounded
critique: Regular grants only; the 2008 and 2009 income statements were not read
verified: VERIFIED (grants table); TAIEX UNVERIFIED at source
note: CANON B4 guard: never say Taiwan's government cut arts money in a recession; quote as data on one funder only

idea: Corporate foundations and corporate giving differ in a downturn. US corporate foundations gave +3.9% (2008) and +2.6% (2009), while CECP companies cut cash giving in 2009
sources: Rows 3 and 17 (Foundation Center 2011 highlights, https://carolinapublicpress.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/Foundation-Center-yearbook-2011.pdf ; CECP 2012, https://cecp.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/GIN2012_finalweb.pdf) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In Taiwan many large firms give through their own foundations (Fubon and Taishin, for example, appear among Wenxin winners through their groups and foundations: Fubon news, 5 Dec 2017, https://www.fubon.com/financialholdings/en/news/news_1171207_616451.htm ; row 24 NCAF URL). A pledge from the foundation may be steadier than one from the company's marketing budget
critique: Keel inference for Taiwan. Whether Taiwan corporate foundations hold endowments or are funded yearly by the parent was not checked (gap)
verified: VERIFIED (US figures); Taiwan point is Keel inference
note: A pledge from a company's foundation may be steadier than one from its marketing budget; the Taiwan point is inference.

idea: The largest funders can give more in a crash. The Gates Foundation's assets fell about 20%, to $38.7bn, yet it raised its giving to $3.8bn for 2009 from $3.3bn in 2008
use: A very large endowed funder may raise its giving when others cut
critique: An outlier with a living donor topping it up
note: The largest funder raised giving in 2009, an outlier.

idea: In 2020 large foundations borrowed to give more. Ford, MacArthur, Mellon, Kellogg and Doris Duke committed "more than $1.7 billion within the next three years", as "new funding above the previously approved budgets", with arts and culture among the named areas, raised by "using funds from their endowment or issuing long-term debt". Ford sold $1bn of social bonds (including a 50-year bond) to pay out over 10% of its endowment in 2020-21. The Council on Foundations pledge of 19 Mar 2020 drew more than 700 signatories to loosen grant terms and pay faster
sources: MacArthur Foundation press release, 11 Jun 2020, https://www.macfound.org/press/press-releases/five-foundations-commit-18-billion-nonprofit-organizations-wake-pandemic ; Ford Foundation, https://www.fordfoundation.org/news-and-stories/news-and-press/news/ford-foundation-announces-sale-and-pricing-of-landmark-1-billion-social-bonds/ ; Council on Foundations, http://cof.org/news/call-action-philanthropys-commitment-during-covid-19 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Large endowed foundations are the funders most able to act counter-cyclically, and the arts were included
critique: A short crash with very cheap borrowing; not like 2008
where: This run: MacArthur, Ford and CoF pages
note: In 2020 large foundations borrowed to give more; a short, cheap-money crash.

idea: Q9 row 30, checked against the lags: the kept half is hit first and recovers first, and co-sponsor shortfalls come one to three years later. After the 2008 fall of 36.55%, the S&P 500 rose 25.94% and 14.82% while US foundation giving dipped (2009-10), UK business arts money fell to 2010/11, and US state arts money hit bottom in FY2012.
