use: A board's confidence is a count of opinions about money not yet given; Laura's is a holding she can show
critique: Polls test the tested (high) goal, not the recommended one; the 39% benchmark's basis is not published
where: This run: CCS St. Andrew report, Holy Spirit letter, Gibbes deck, AFP Ready Reference
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c/3d: a board's confidence is a poll of opinions about money not yet given; one clause at most beside row 3.

idea: The tested goal is set high on purpose, then cut: "The tested fundraising goal is always set as a high bar" (Williston); recommended goals were 33%-106% of the tested figure (Keel arithmetic: Sacred Heart 33-42%, Spooner 37-52%, Williston 43-57%, Rappahannock 46-62%, Ventura 48%, Holy Spirit 50%, Elk Rapids 57-71%, Community Library 74%, Wild Center 88%, Howard County 100-106%); Giddings: modify by "Reducing the goal by 20-40%"; several call the result a "working goal" (Wild Center $35M; Community Library $9M; Memphis $600M)
sources: CPG Enterprises (2025); GRACE (2026); BrandRaise (2024); Rappahannock (2025); Ventura College Foundation (2023); Strebler (2026); Elk Rapids (n.d.); Campbell & Company (2024; n.d.); Schultz & Williams (2017); Giddings Consulting Group (2026); University of Memphis (2020)
use: Fundraisers find their range by asking high and cutting down; Laura finds hers by buying the bottom first and moving the top into Treasuries, so nothing needs cutting once said
critique: A "working goal" can still move in private (H9-129, Q11b); Laura's readers are not asked for a gift (Q22 r34)
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: ask high, then cut; close to H9-129's working goal.

idea: A board's goal is mostly money no one has offered yet: Rappahannock "Approximately 10% of Potential Goal Was Identified"; Williston interviewees "might range from $420,000 to $800,000" against a $1.5M bottom (28-53%, Keel arithmetic); Gibbes interviewees "$2.4 million to $3.4 million" against "$10 million ... inclusive of all sources" (24-34%)
sources: Rappahannock (2025); CPG Enterprises (2025); Capital Development Services (2025)
use: The pencil-and-ink contrast in numbers: a board's range is about three-quarters pencil; after the move every dollar of Laura's range is ink (owned in Treasuries that pay it on its date)
critique: Interviews cover only the top prospects; campaigns raise more from people not interviewed (Hotchkiss, row 16)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d beside aha 8: at feasibility a board has only 10-53% of its goal offered, so most of its range is money not yet given; the conceit's contrast in numbers (CONCEIT V2).

idea: Nashua's goal came from two rules and was rounded down: "The largest gift to a campaign should total 20% of the campaign goal"; indicated gifts should be "at least 40% of the goal"; $1.1 million indicated, so "likely to achieve a $2.5 million goal" ($1.1M / 0.4 = $2.75M, rounded down; Keel arithmetic); 56% would give, 22% maybe, 22% no
use: A stated figure from a written rule, rounded down, is the fundraisers' own method; Laura's range rule also rounds each end down to $5,000 (NUMBERS 4)
critique: The campaign's outcome was not found (Gaps); the 40% rule is one firm's
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: fundraisers also round a stated goal down; matches NUMBERS 4's rounding to $5,000.

idea: A baseline and a stretch, checked before going public: "We recommend the parish set a baseline campaign goal of $1.2 million with a stretch goal of $1.5 million"; the first 10-15 asks are "quiet", then "reassess the campaign goal ... before taking the campaign 'public'"
use: Same order as Laura's: a baseline fixed first (her bottom, Jan 2028), a stretch settled privately, and nothing public until it is settled (she states nothing before the move; a top stated 1-12 months early is not yet owned in 2.9%-10.7% of house paths, NUMBERS 4). The difference: her stretch is bought before she speaks
critique: One parish report; width 22.2% (row 2)
where: This run: Sacred Heart Parish report (GRACE)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c/3d: a real report's baseline and stretch, reassessed before going public, is Laura's order (2.9-10.7% checks with NUMBERS 4); one parish, so one clause.

idea: Counsel uses floor words when the top is unknown: CCS "has the capacity to raise a minimum of $4.5 million (and potentially more)" when all-source indicated gifts were $4,569,321-$4,849,821 (floor 98.5% of the low end; Keel arithmetic); CCS case study: "a goal of at least $2.5 million", which raised $3.8 million (152%, Keel arithmetic)

verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 16 Nov 2026; the 2014 report via a document-sharing copy)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d wording: 'at least' is counsel's word while the top is unknown; supports rows 31-33 against NUMBERS 4 option D.

idea: A published excess rule: Elk Rapids set its private goal at $3.5M (above the feasible $2.0-2.5M), matched by a $3.5M bond levy, and promised "Every dollar raised beyond the $3.5 million goal will be allocated to approved future investment areas"; Phase I was later "fully funded"
sources: Elk Rapids District Library (n.d.); Northern Express (n.d.)
use: A stated top plus a public rule for anything above it is how a library talks; Laura's rule does the same: what the funds pay above the stated top joins the half kept ($8,476 centrally, NUMBERS 4)
critique: Funding included grants and a public levy; Laura's excess is hers to decide, not pre-allocated (CANON D12)
clash: no (NUMBERS 4: the excess joins the half kept)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3b/3d: a public rule for money above the stated top; Laura's excess ($8,476) joins the half kept (NUMBERS 4; CANON D12).

idea: A feasible bottom can still be missed: Williston's study called $1.5M "doable and feasible"; the library "has raised around $600,000" (40% of the bottom; Keel arithmetic); a $13.9M bond passed 1,262 to 1,215, then failed by 60 votes on a revote; the addition was cut from about 11,500 to under 7,000 square feet, and a new bond of at most $9M went to a 3 Nov 2026 vote; the first pledges were "$125,000 pledges in the first week"
sources: CPG Enterprises (2025); WCAX (2026a, 2026b); Town of Williston (2026); Williston Selectboard (2026); Dorothy Alling Memorial Library Board of Trustees (2025)
use: A board's bottom is a forecast that public votes and donors can undo, and when it fell short the building shrank; Laura's bottom is a Treasury fund bought in Jan 2028 that no vote can shrink
critique: The 3 Nov 2026 result was not found (Gaps); the shortfall is mostly the bond vote, not the gifts

idea: One report, three ranges: Spooner's readiness study states "$2.5M-$3.5M", "$2.75M - $3.5M" and "$2.75M-3M" for the same campaign (widths 33.3%, 24.0%, 8.7%; Keel arithmetic) against a $6.76M tested campaign beside a $4.25M state grant; by Sep 2026 the campaign had not launched and the project was a "$12.8m conceptual cost"

note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: three ranges in one report read as soft; also why row 2's 'narrower than every range' needs care.

note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: a leader's hopes push a figure up; a letter to parishioners, not co-funders.

idea: Goals are set to be beaten: Capital Campaign Pro's surveys: 2023, average 108% of goal (high 170%, low 75%, "Only 5 out of 32 was under 100%"); 2024-25, average 106% (high 156%, low 75%); 2026, "an average of 116%" (high 175%), success "around 95%"

where: This run: Bloomerang and NLC slide decks
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: the sample shapes the lesson; not causal.

critique: Old (2005), local, small; correlation only
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: a smaller goal against what is in hand matters more than a study; 2005 and local.

sources: Chicago Tribune (2002); Los Angeles Times (2002); Philanthropy News Digest (2002)

critique: A bequest-style trust gift, not a co-funded building; paid over 30 years
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c: the setup for row 23, a floor and a range hung on one share price.

idea: The floor sat in one share and fell: the trusts were funded on 18 Jan 2002 "entirely" with Lilly stock (about $286 million); "By March 2002, National City had formulated a draft Investment Policy Statement"; an internal e-mail: "We still have at least 75 percent of the portfolio in one stock (RISK!)"; "a $102 million decline for 2002" (36%; Keel arithmetic); the charities sued; the court held the trust let the bank hold the stock "despite any resulting risk", and the bank was not liable

use: An investment policy on paper did not protect a floor kept in a falling asset; Laura's bottom is a Treasury fund from Jan 2028, and her plan changes only for a missed deposit or a Treasury default
critique: Trust law and a bank trustee, not a family plan; the stock recovered (row 24)

sources: Indianapolis Business Journal (2005); Chronicle of Philanthropy (2003); Chicago Tribune (2003); Philanthropy News Digest (2007); Encyclopedia of Indianapolis (n.d.)

idea: Taiwan's largest private medical gift needed a top-up: Kuo's foundation pledged NT$150億 to NTU in 2007, mainly for a cancer hospital (the gift's "第一期建物", its first-phase building, was the 永齡生醫工程館, built 2011-2014); in 2019 he said "150億元是不夠的" because of equipment changes and inflation, and gave NT$50億 more; in 2020 the hospital, open since July 2019, lacked operating money (an ordered MRI could not be installed), the university had raised NT$10億 from others, and NT$38億 of the further 50億 had been paid

note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: a fixed donor figure while the state carried the rise; in Taiwan the founder pays first and grantees carry overruns (row 30), so never suggest co-sponsors carry hers.

critique: A billionaire with new income each year; a university, not a residency
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: a fixed founder figure, then more as a separate choice (CANON D12).

use: A promise written as a share of what one might have later is pencil, and was kept 8 times in 22 (36%; Keel arithmetic); a figure owned before it is said is ink and cannot drift
critique: An advocacy think tank's report; the pledge is moral, not legal
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d conceit contrast: promises stated as a share of future wealth were kept 8 times in 22; an advocacy think tank's count, so name it.

idea: In Taiwan a public grant stays uncertain until it is paid, and the grantee carries overruns: the MoC's private-space programme pays in two halves (start and completion) and overruns from design changes are "由獲補助單位自行籌應"; the local-revitalisation rules let the MoC "酌減或取消原核定補助，獲補助者不得請求補償或賠償"
sources: Ministry of Culture (n.d.-a); Ministry of Culture (n.d.-b)
use: A Taiwanese public co-sponsor's figure is pencil until paid and can be cut with no remedy, which is why Laura keeps flexibility for "a co-sponsor falling short" (IPS l.15)
critique: Same idea already carded for other programmes (Q11d r8, Q11e r16, Q5d r28, Q10d r9); this adds two programmes and the no-compensation clause
note: Mon 16 Nov: Twin of Q11e-016 (overruns borne by the grantee; multi-year grants cut with the budget); the no-compensation clause can be added there.

idea: "At least" makes listeners doubt even a true figure: in Geurts and Nouwen's Dutch experiment, from "Beryl had three sherries", most accepted "more than two", but "only about half accepted 'Beryl had at least three sherries'"
use: Half of readers resist "at least n" when n is exactly known; Laura after the move knows exactly what she owns, so "at least $115,000" would read as hesitant
critique: Dutch students and sherries, not co-funders and dollars
verified: VERIFIED for Cummins & Katsos's report (read at source, 16 Nov 2026); Geurts & Nouwen (2007) itself UNVERIFIED (not read)

note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d wording: 'at least n' leaves about half of readers doubting an exact n; Geurts and Nouwen read only through Cummins and Katsos.

critique: Whether the doubt is part of the word's meaning or a pragmatic inference is debated (row 33)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d: from a speaker who knows, 'at least' signals ignorance and hints at money CANON D12 keeps outside; argues against NUMBERS 4 option D.

idea: The plain number says "exactly": "At least three and more than two do not trigger an 'exactly three' implicature, in contrast with the bare numeral three"; "at least" is often taken to signal ignorance, "more than" less so; whether "at least" signals ignorance depends on the question being answered (a "how much at minimum?" question licenses it)
sources: Cremers, Coppock, Dotlačil & Roelofsen (2022); Westera & Brasoveanu (2014); Kennedy (2015)

note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d: the bare figure says exactly; 'at least' fits only a how-much-at-minimum question asked before the top is known.

idea: Counsel shows its record to the board: Interkom's St. Catharines deck listed past campaigns against goal ($5M goal / $7.5M raised; $3M / $3.3M; $5M / $5M)

critique: A firm's chosen examples, not a full record
note: Mon 16 Nov: store only: counsel shows its record; Laura's is the rule's record (both ends owned in every history window after the move, NUMBERS 4).

idea: A private equity fund must give investors "at least ten (10) Business Days" before called money is due
sources: ILPA (2020a) Model LPA s.6.2.1; ILPA (2020b) term sheet
use: Confirming by Wed 1 Dec 2027 gives 22 trading days before Mon 3 Jan 2028 (Keel arithmetic; NUMBERS 5's first trading day): about twice the notice that the most demanding private funds' investors accept
critique: A fund asks; Laura tells. The fund pays a seller on the due date; Laura's plan pays no one from this money until Jan 2033. Bracketed figures in the model are fill-ins
note: Mon 16 Nov: Table 3 row 1 and 3e; 22 trading days from 1 Dec 2027 is about twice ILPA's 10-business-day floor for a capital call: a month is generous by practice.

idea: ILPA pairs a short hard notice with a long soft one: "at least 10 business days" to answer a call, plus "estimates of quarterly projections on capital calls"
use: Q15's draft row for the deposit (watch 2027 earnings quarterly, confirm in December) has the same two speeds as the investors' own standard

note: Mon 16 Nov: Table 3 row 1 store; ILPA pairs a hard notice with soft quarterly projections, the two speeds of Q15's draft row (a quarterly 2027 look, then the December confirmation).

sources: ILPA (2020c) subscription-line guidance, recommendation and note 4
use: Laura's 2028 deposit is one call of 100% of what she still owes ($150,000 of $150,000; Keel arithmetic), four times ILPA's line: the 2027 look matters more than the 1 Dec date

use: Laura's confirmation can be "at least $X": anything received runs the same order (ASK_HUMANS Wed 11 Nov), and "most" still buys the floor down to a $76,565 deposit (NUMBERS 5)

where: This run: ilpa.org (subscription lines guidance, June 2020)
note: Mon 16 Nov: Table 3 row 1 store; a confirmation can be 'at least $X'; $76,565 matches NUMBERS 5(c); never state a confirmed amount to co-sponsors before it is owned.

idea: In cost engineering a contingency is a narrow thing. It "usually excludes: a) Major scope changes such as changes in end product specification, capacities, building sizes, and location ...; b) Extraordinary events ...; c) Management reserves; and d) Escalation and currency effects", and it "is expected to be expended". Money "for discretionary management purposes outside of the defined scope of the project" is a MANAGEMENT RESERVE, sized by risk tolerance
sources: AACE RP 10S-90 Cost Engineering Terminology, https://library.aacei.org/terminology/welcome.shtml and https://library.aacei.org/pgd02/pgd02.shtml ; RP 44R-08 contents PDF https://web.aacei.org/docs/default-source/toc/toc_44r-08.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In AACE's own words the kept half is a management reserve, not a contingency: it covers overruns, currency and a funding gap, and nobody expects it to be spent
critique: Laura is the owner, not a project manager; the terms come from industrial projects

note: In cost engineers' terms the kept half is a management reserve, not a contingency, and they price overruns, escalation and currency on separate lines while the IPS gives one pot three jobs; carries Q5-007 and Q5-015.

critique: NASA's reserve was budgeted for that project; Laura's flexibility may never reach the facility
verified: VERIFIED: excerpts of the policy PDF
note: Released only on approval.

note: Risk recorded (A31, card Q24): one pot, three uses; tested one at a time.

idea: Held reserves are breached often: of 53 major NASA projects that completed development or are in its final phase since 2009, 30 stayed under the statutory reporting threshold (development cost not 15% or more over baseline); three Artemis projects account for "nearly $7 billion of the total overruns—or almost half"; in 2019 portfolio cost growth was 27.6% over baselines

critique: Space projects with new technology, not a residency building; whether all 53 had confidence-level baselines is UNVERIFIED (the policy began in January 2009, GAO 2019). Percentages only (case l.164-165)
verified: VERIFIED: GAO 2025 Highlights read in full; GAO 2019 read in part
note: Defence: reserves get used (23 of 53 major NASA projects overran by 15% or more).

idea: A sponsor-held contingency used up: Crossrail's £14.8 billion (2010) was "including contingency"; by November 2016 risks exceeded Crossrail Ltd's own contingency and it forecast it would need "the £600 million of remaining contingency funding available to the programme, which was held by TfL"; its contingency fell from £1,857 million to £84 million; funding rose to £17.6 billion (December 2018) and the middle estimate to £18.9 billion (2021)

critique: The sponsors were governments that kept paying; Laura's contribution does not rise with overruns (SKELETON 3d) and her flexibility is promised to no one
verified: VERIFIED: NAO report, summary and 2021 update read at the source in part
note: Store: Crossrail's sponsor-held £600m was needed.

idea: Budget slack on purpose: a company "purposefully budgeted additional financial resources", while "the empirical literature has interpreted it as being dysfunctional"
use: Weak: a firm's slack hidden inside a budget. Laura's flexibility is outside her figure and named
critique: Abstract only
note: Store only.

idea: Norway, 215 finished public buildings from three public owners (2003-2020; 90% under 11,000 m²), final cost against the budget at the investment decision. Smallest-area quarter: P10 -5% / P50 12% / P90 42% (n=48). Middle half: -12% / 4% / 30% (n=94). Largest quarter: -13% / -1% / 19% (n=48). Area is significant (p<0.01): "Smaller projects tend to have higher cost overruns than larger ones"
sources: Mæhlen, Bekkevold, Welde & Olsson (2024), Table 1 and sections 3-4
use: The nearest published distribution for a small building measured from an approved budget: a middle of 12%, and 1 in 10 above 42%
critique: Norwegian public owners. Size is measured by floor area; the quarters' m² cut-offs and a P80 are not published
clash: no; "near P50" needs "from an approved budget"
note: 3b or 3e: small buildings overrun by more; Norway's smallest quarter P50 12%, P90 42% from an approved budget (n=48).

idea: Same data, by investment type. Renovation: P10 -6% / P50 11% / P90 52% (n=54). New build: -11% / 4% / 30% (n=135). New build with refurbishment: -15% / 6% / 27% (n=26). "P90 is far higher than for new buildings, which means that the largest overruns are often renovation projects", though the regression rejects chance only "to a small extent"
use: If the residency reuses an old building, as many in Taiwan do (Q9c), the risk is the tail, not the middle
critique: The renovation effect is not significant in the regression; the gap between medians is small
note: Renovations have the fattest tail (P90 52%); a residency often reuses an old building.

idea: Same data. Lowest quarter of estimated price per m²: -4% / 13% / 43% (n=48). High distinctiveness: -8% / 10% / 34% (n=87), against low: -11% / 3% / 28% (n=128). The authors read a low price per m² as possibly "underestimated ... elements have been omitted, documentation is immature"
use: A modest, one-off community building is likely cheap per m² and distinctive: both classes overrun more
critique: The classes overlap, so their effects do not add up. Price per m² is the estimate itself (row 21)
note: The same data by price per m² and distinctiveness.

idea: Why small overruns more: owners may make "an investment decision on a more immature basis for a smaller project because, at the portfolio level, there is a lower risk in absolute costs". The model explains 19.4% of the variation (R² 0.194)
use: Laura announces in 2031, before any investment decision on the building, so the immature-basis point applies to her twice over
critique: A hypothesis the paper does not test
note: Store: why small projects overrun more (decided on a less mature basis).

idea: Placing the shares on rows 1-3 (lognormal fits to each class's P50 and P90). P80 is about 31% for small buildings, 32% for a low price per m² and 37% for renovations (a straight normal reading gives 32%, 33% and 38%). 18.6% sits at about P60-62 and 25.9% at about P70-74. NUMBERS 8j's 13% and 17% sit at about P52 and P59 of the small class
sources: Keel arithmetic on Mæhlen et al. (2024)
use: The claim's "short of P80-P90" holds; "near P50" does not
critique: Two-point fits: the true shape is unknown, and P80 is not published
clash: yes: NUMBERS 8j's label "early-stage norms" (line 1000) fits middle odds; a label risk
note: Placement, Keel arithmetic, illustration only (A31): 18.6% about P60 and 25.9% about P70-75 for small and renovated buildings from an approved budget; Laura is earlier. 8j's label fixed today ('overrun allowances', not 'early-stage norms').

idea: England's 15 major Arts Council lottery capital projects, each with a grant over £5m. 13 went over budget; the total overrun was £93.9m (16.9%). By project: Cambridge Arts Theatre -7.9%, RADA -1.9%, Royal National Theatre 1.7%, National Glass Centre 5.9%, the Globe 8.9%, National Centre for Popular Music 11.2%, Royal Exchange 11.4%, Malvern 11.8%, Royal Opera House 12.1%, Dovecot 20.0%, Royal Albert Hall 22.2%, Milton Keynes 26.7%, Royal Court 36.5%, Victoria Hall 38.2%, Sadler's Wells 58.0%. Keel arithmetic: median 11.8%, P80 about 27%-29%, P90 about 37%; 9 of 15 at or under 18.6%, 11 of 15 at or under 25.9%
sources: House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts (2004), HC 253, Figure 1
use: Arts buildings, measured from the original estimate at grant: the same middle (about 12%) as Norway's small class, and a similar 80th
critique: None of the 15 is small. The 1990s lottery boom. The baseline is the estimate when the grant was made
note: England's 15 arts lottery buildings: 13 over budget, 16.9% in all; the closest arts reference class.

idea: Within those fifteen, the smaller ones overran less. Six had implied original budgets of about £7m-£17m (Malvern, Dovecot, Cambridge, Glass Centre, Popular Music, the Globe), and they ran -7.9% to +20.0%. The tail sat in theatres: Sadler's Wells 58.0%, Victoria Hall 38.2%, Royal Court 36.5%

note: The smaller six ran -7.9% to +20.0%.

idea: Same report. ACE's programme contingency of 5% was not enough and was raised to 7%. Supplementary grants met about 35% of the overrun, so about two thirds fell on the organisations. The two projects under budget had cut their scope

idea: Heritage Lottery Fund. 17% of completed projects cost more than expected, and 26% were late. "The likelihood of cost increases rises with grant size, with 39% of projects awarded over £2 million going over budget." About half of the overrunning projects got grant increases (8.5% of all projects), which took 3% of total funding (£114m). Over a quarter of the overruns were due in part to poor planning. NAO: average overrun £293,000; 6% of projects got increases averaging £176,000

use: Overruns become more frequent as projects get bigger; most small heritage projects finish within budget
critique: Measures how often, not by how much. Baseline is the grant, after HLF's own development stage

idea: Same hearing: "Once you take the roof off a historic building, you tend to find things that you were not necessarily expecting" (HLF's chief executive); overruns "compare pretty favourably with average construction sector figures"

critique: One witness's view

idea: Australia, 276 projects (161 building, 115 civil engineering), measured from contract award: mean 12.22%, SD 20.65, skewness 5.5; no significant difference in the mean by size. Building projects under A$1m: n=14, mean 24.90%, SD 64.81. A$1m-10m: n=70, mean 10.30%, SD 17.10

Under A$1m: over 10%, 0.19; over 20%, 0.09; over 30%, 0.06. Keel arithmetic: 18.6% sits at about P79 and 25.9% at about P89 for A$1m-10m; about P90 and P93 under A$1m

(CONFLICTING, card Q51 row 23, Mon 16 Nov: the report gives these two figures both ways round; do not quote either until read again) Challenges named: "finding unforeseen issues in the building", "managing historic building improvements", "managing cost overruns". No overrun percentages

note: Store: Canada Cultural Spaces Fund overrun top-ups.

idea: UK construction KPIs 2011, cost predictability (on budget or better). Projects of £5m or more: 60%; under £1m: 55%. For non-housing there is "little disparity across project values"; housing ranges from 49% (under £1m) to 73% (£5m or more)

critique: Contract stage; measures how often, not by how much

idea: Norwegian road contracts: 74% overran, by 17% on average. When they overran, small contracts did so by 32%, medium by 25%, large by 14%: "Contract size increases the probability of overruns, but the size of the overruns is smaller"

critique: Roads, not buildings; slides only

idea: Smaller projects overrun more in percentage terms. Norwegian roads: mean 7.9%, with smaller projects overrunning more (Odeck). Dutch transport: small projects show the largest percentage overruns (Cantarelli et al.)
use: Supports rows 1 and 19
critique: Transport, not buildings

critique: Public works measured from contract
note: Counter-evidence kept: larger projects overrun more often.

critique: Contract stage; other countries
verified: Shehu: search excerpt only; Shrestha & Zeleke: abstract only

idea: Taiwan, a small heritage renovation: the Control Yuan's repair of the roof and facades of its own national-monument building. Approved at NT$74.0m (including NT$3m of air conditioning) and awarded at NT$66.071m, it went through three change orders to NT$90.627m: "增幅達 22.47%、37.03%" (+22.47% on cost, +37.03% on time). The auditor's reason: "如屋頂未拆解前，無法詳細預估桁木損壞數量" (until the roof is taken apart, the damage to the trusses cannot be estimated in detail). The work also needed NT$7.839m from the second reserve fund
use: Taiwan's own "roof off". A project of about US$2.3m (Keel arithmetic at NT$32.768) overran by about a fifth of its approved budget, inside the band of Norway's renovation class between its middle and its 80th
critique: One case; a public owner. Against the award, Keel arithmetic gives about +37% if the totals are on one basis (UNVERIFIED)
verified: VERIFIED (section text read in search excerpts of the ly.gov.tw page and PDF)
note: Taiwan heritage roof repair: +22.47% on cost from rot found when the roof came off; store only (density cut, no NUMBERS 0 entry); carries Q10c-035.

idea: Taiwan, Kinmen County's monument and historic-building repairs: some were delayed "因解體調查後須辦理變更設計" (the design had to change after the dismantling survey) or by failed tenders. In 2023, NT$83.5m of a NT$147.58m budget was spent (56.58%)
use: In Taiwan, the costs of reusing a heritage building surface mid-project
critique: No overrun figures
verified: VERIFIED (search excerpt of the audit report)
note: Store: Kinmen's heritage repairs and the dismantling survey.

idea: Taiwan, C-LAB (空總臺灣當代文化實驗場, a site that supports cross-disciplinary artists' experimental work). In June 2023 its phase-2 budget rose from NT$755.838m to NT$1,024.079m, about +35.5% (Keel arithmetic). The rise was mainly for newly added monument repair, the demolition of a nearby building and "營建物價上漲" (rising construction prices). A cultural-heritage review had added monuments and cut the buildable area
use: In Taiwan, a heritage review can change an artists' site's scope after the budget is set
critique: Large (about US$31m) and public; mostly added scope, not overrun on a fixed scope
note: Store: C-LAB's phase 2 budget +35.5%.

idea: Taiwan's local arts venue programme (地方藝文場館及文化資產多元活化計畫, to the end of 2024, extendable to 2025). Grants are as a rule at most NT$3m per venue, with the rest raised locally. "如有特殊原因致編製預算或變更設計後超過原核定預算者，由地方政府自籌" (anything over the approved budget after budgeting or design changes is self-funded by the local government)
use: In Taiwan, as in England, the grant is capped and the overrun is the owner's
critique: A public programme. The office hosting the extract was not identified (UNVERIFIED)
note: Taiwan's own rule: anything over the approved budget is raised by the owner; with Q5d-008, why the flexibility is Laura's (3b, 3d).

idea: In bad markets. The half kept at the house model's 1-in-20 low is $9,881, 8.6% of $115,000: about P41-46 in Norway's small and renovation classes, and only 4 of England's 15 overran by that little or less. Its median if shares fell over 2031-2033 is $15,423 (13.4%; about P51-53). The half kept plus the excess is $16,193 at the 1-in-20 low (14.1%) and $23,201 at the median if shares fell (20.2%)
use: In the years it is smallest, the half kept covers about a typical small-building overrun, not a bad one; in a median fall the excess brings it back to a fifth
critique: House model; the figures are MODEL
clash: yes, partly: the three uses share one pot, smallest when co-sponsors are most likely to fall short (Q5 row 2; NUMBERS 8f, "the honest line"); a risk to record
note: Honest limit (3e): in a 1-in-20 bad market her flexibility is about the small-building middle overrun.

idea: The denominator, which extends Q5 row 33 with rows 8, 9, 17 and 28. Suppose funders cap their grants, Laura carries overruns alone, and her $115,000 is a share s of the project's budget. Then the half kept covers an overrun of 18.6% times s of the budget: 9.3% if s is one half (below the small-building middle of 12%), 6.2% if s is one third
use: Whether a fifth sits "above the middle" depends on who pays overruns, which the 2031 talks decide
critique: s is unknown, and the case says not to estimate the building's cost (l.164-165): s is a parameter, not an estimate
clash: yes, partly (Q5 row 33): a risk to record
note: Risk (Q5 row 33): if her $115,000 is only part of the budget, her flexibility covers less of the building's overrun; never a cost estimate.

idea: In the year shares fall, building costs more often rise: same-year correlation of yearly cost changes with share returns is negative in every series (Taiwan index vs TAIEX -0.34, n=34; Turner vs S&P -0.31, n=61; BEA structures vs S&P -0.31 since 1950, n=76)
sources: Keel arithmetic on DGBAS (2026), TWSE (2009-2026), Turner (2013-2026), U.S. Census Bureau (2003), BEA via FRED, Shiller (repo)
use: If an overrun bill arrives while her flexibility is still in VT, the same-year relation is the one that applies, and it is wrong-way
critique: Yearly data, small n (95% interval for Taiwan -0.61 to -0.00); Spearman agrees (-0.26 to -0.28); partly a timing artefact (costs are late-cycle)
verified: VERIFIED (Keel arithmetic on primary series, method below)
clash: risk: IPS l.15 holds her flexibility in shares; already recorded in NUMBERS 8f's honest line
note: Guard: never 'partial natural hedge'; in the year shares fall, building costs more often rise (-0.31 to -0.34 in three series).

idea: One year after a share move the sign turns weakly right-way: Taiwan index +0.18 (TAIEX), +0.27 (S&P); Turner -0.02 since 1965 but +0.34 since 1990; BEA +0.12 since 1930
use: The lagged help the claim describes exists in the data, but it is small and only clear in the US since 1990
critique: Only Turner since 1990 (95% interval +0.01 to +0.60) excludes zero
note: One year later the sign turns weakly right-way.

idea: Over two-year windows (shares 2031-33, costs 2033-35 in Laura's terms) the relation is about nothing: -0.33 to +0.25 across four series and two methods
use: The window that matters to Laura shows no dependable hedge and no dependable harm from building costs
critique: Overlapping windows inflate apparent n; separate windows leave 16-48 points
note: Over Laura's two-year windows the link is about nothing (-0.33 to +0.25); store and defence.

idea: Laura's actual pair (world shares, Taiwan building costs) leans wrong-way: Taiwan index vs S&P over the next two years -0.15 (overlapping), -0.33 (separate windows); after five two-year S&P falls, Taiwan costs rose +8.4% on average over the next two years against +4.6% after rises

critique: S&P stands in for VT; n=5 falls; the 2004-05 steel boom drives the gap
note: World shares against Taiwan costs lean wrong-way.

idea: Regime decides the sign: US years with inflation of 4% or more: Turner -0.51 same year, -0.39 a year later; BEA -0.30, -0.28. Under 4%: Turner -0.11, +0.22; BEA +0.02, +0.31
use: The same flip as stocks and bonds (store H3-104, H4-167): the help comes in demand slumps, the harm in inflationary falls
critique: US only (Taiwan's index starts 1991, too few inflationary years); 19-25 inflationary years
clash: risk: the inflationary fall is the case to name in 3e
note: 3e clause: an inflationary fall (1974, 2022) is the case that hits her flexibility and building costs at once; named as a limit, no trigger (CANON A34).

idea: After big falls (over 20%), costs rise in the crash year and ease the next: Turner after the S&P's 1974, 2002, 2008 falls +8.2% then -1.1% (all-year mean +4.8%); Taiwan after seven TAIEX falls over 20% +6.1% then -0.3% (after rises +3.5%)
use: The claim's lagged form holds on average after large crashes, with the crash year itself wrong-way
critique: n=3 and n=7; averages hide 1974 (inflationary) against 2009 (deflationary)
note: After big falls costs rise in the crash year.

idea: Taiwan's index follows the S&P by about six months, then rebounds: monthly r +0.25 at 3 months, +0.28 at 6, +0.09 at 12, -0.20 at 18, -0.31 at 24 (n=417 months; +0.22 and -0.32 without 2021-23)
sources: Keel arithmetic, DGBAS monthly + Shiller monthly
use: A building priced six months after a slump gets cheaper inputs; one built over the following two to three years meets the rebound
critique: Overlapping yearly changes: effective n about 35, so +/-0.33 is noise-level; a pattern, not proof
note: Store: Taiwan's index follows the S&P by about six months, then rebounds.

idea: Cost surprise against trend (yearly change minus its own five-year mean) is wrong-way the same year and right-way the next: Taiwan vs TAIEX -0.43 then +0.41; Turner -0.20 then +0.20; BEA -0.27 then +0.05
use: An overrun is cost above the budgeted drift (NUMBERS 8d's 3.0%); its timing against shares is the same split
critique: Trend definition is Keel's choice
note: Cost surprise against trend.

idea: Taiwan 2008-09: the index peaked in Jul 2008 (92.10) with shares already falling, rose 14.0% on the year as TAIEX fell 46.0%, then fell 15.1% to May 2009 and 8.9% on 2009's average as TAIEX rose 78.3%
use: The strongest right-way move on record, but driven by steel and other materials falling with the world, not by bids
critique: Annual averages make 2008 look wrong-way; Dec-to-Dec 2008 was +1.2%
verified: VERIFIED (DGBAS table read in full; Kaohsiung report excerpt)
note: Store: Taiwan 2008-09.

idea: Taiwan's contractors named low-price bidding their main 2009 difficulty, yet their net margin rose to 4.3% from 2.4% in 2008
sources: Construction and Planning Agency (2011), abstract items 16 and 24
use: In Taiwan the 2009 bid discount was smaller than the materials fall (Keel inference): owners got less than the index's -8.9%
critique: One survey year; margin is the industry's, not tender prices
note: Store: Taiwan's contractors in 2009.

idea: Taiwan's public works contracts pass index moves during the build to the owner: a three-level price adjustment (single items, sub-groups, total index); typically changes beyond +/-2.5% of the award month, monthly from start to completion
use: For a build under such a contract, the cost path through the build, not the tender price, reaches the project; the same-year relation (row 1) matters
critique: Laura's residency's contract form is unknown and out of scope; private contracts may differ
note: Store with Q10c-016: Taiwan's public contracts pass index rises during the build to the owner.

idea: 2022, the inflationary counter-case: TAIEX -22.4%, S&P -16.3%; Taiwan index +7.4% (materials +8.51%), Turner +8.0%, BEA +16.3%
sources: Keel arithmetic; Legislative Yuan Budget Center (2023)
use: The year her flexibility would be small is a year building costs ran well above NUMBERS 8d's 5.0% band top
critique: One year; Taiwan's index flattened from May 2022 (-1.0% to December)
verified: VERIFIED (DGBAS; LY report read in part)
clash: risk: Table 3 row 7 has no building-cost trigger
note: 2022, the inflationary counter-case.

idea: In 2022 Taiwan's large public tenders (NT$50m+) awarded only at the third or later try rose to 26.32% (15.71% in 2017); first-try awards fell to 21.96% (39.87% in 2017)
use: When costs run, Taiwan tenders fail before they award: delay is the first form an overrun takes
critique: Public works only; failed tenders also reflect budgets set below market (PCC's own finding)
note: Failed tenders in 2022.

idea: Of 98 major projects (NT$1bn+) revised in 2021 to Jul 2023, 41 raised their budgets for construction prices and wages; Kinmen Bridge: four revisions, 7 years 6 months longer
use: Budget revisions bunch in an inflationary run, not after a share crash
critique: Percentages for Laura only; no cost read across
note: The 98 revised projects.

idea: Taipei found failed-tender rates for large works highly correlated with the index's yearly change (2012-2021)
use: The overrun signal in Taiwan is the cost index itself, not the share market
critique: Taipei only; the correlation figure not read
note: Taipei's failed tenders and the index.

idea: Markups are procyclical: Austrian construction auctions, markups of all bids -1.5 points and of winning bids -3.3 points in the crisis; without the stimulus the fall would have been larger
use: The mechanism in the claim ("contractors bid low when work dries up") is real and measured
critique: Austria, public works, stimulus muddies it; a few points of margin, not a collapse
verified: VERIFIED (PMC full text read in part: abstract, data, results)
note: Store: markups fall in slumps (Austria).

idea: Texas highway bids fell from 1.05 to 0.93 of the engineer's estimate in the recession and stimulus; contracts drew "nearly two additional bidders"; lower costs and lower markups both explain it
use: A 12-point swing against the estimate is the size of the discount a slump can bring
critique: Roads, not buildings; Texas; 2006-2010 only
verified: VERIFIED (NBER paper read in part; Digest read)
note: Texas bids in the recession.

idea: US 2009: every state's bids 5-12% below estimates (AASHTO); New Jersey schools 15-39% below; a Texas contractor bid 17% under estimates against 9% over in 2006, margins cut 20-25%; NYC school bids drew 7-12 bidders against 2-4
use: The discount is visible at tender within a year of the crash
critique: Press reports; selective examples
note: US 2009 bids.

idea: Selling-price indices fell hard, sticky indices barely: Turner -10.8% y/y (Q3 2009), RLB -3.5% (Q2 2009), 14 of 15 indexes down; BLS's new-school-building PPI only -2.9% from its Mar 2009 peak
use: How much the "fall" is depends on the index; any 3e wording names the index
critique: Indices differ in method; CONFLICTING sizes
note: Store only (sources disagree).

idea: Low bids come back as claims and failures: RLB carried "a contingency for claims for change orders, which are on the rise because of unrealistic low bids"; "risky bids could cause contractors, especially smaller ones, to fail"
use: A slump-time tender can raise the overrun risk her flexibility covers (Taipei Performing Arts Center, store H9-097)
critique: Anecdote, no rate of failure measured
note: Defence: low slump bids come back as claims and failures; a cheap tender is not a saving to count on.

idea: Construction is late-cycle: backlogs carry prices 12-18 months; competition "could intensify even more as non-residential building contractors work off their backlog"; "Backlogs fall and competition rises"
use: Explains rows 1 and 2: same year wrong-way, next year right-way
critique: Mechanism, not a measured lag
note: Store only.

idea: UK after 2008: BCIS tender prices -12.6% in the year to Q2 2009, -3.7% to Q2 2010; seven quarters of falls to Q3 2009; social-housing tender prices still 13% below their Q2 2008 peak in Q3 2012
use: A third country shows the lagged fall and how long it lasts (four years below peak)
critique: Not tested against the FTSE (gap); secondary for BCIS
note: Store only.

idea: The share index is not a reliable leading indicator of construction prices: UK "all share index ... produced inconclusive results"; ENR and Hong Kong forecasting models use the real economy and construction workload, not shares
sources: Akintoye et al. (1998); Ashuri et al. (2012); Wong et al. (2010)
use: The link from shares to building costs runs through the real economy; sometimes it does not run at all
critique: Abstracts only
note: Guard: share prices do not lead building prices.

idea: Hedge less when cash and needs move together ("even without hedging, the supply of internal funds tends to match the demand for funds"); with no correlation "it is optimal to hedge fully"; hedge ratios above one "when investment opportunities are negatively correlated with current cash flows"
use: The test for her flexibility: no use earns the "hedge less" credit; co-sponsors argue for more
critique: Firms with investment needs, not a donor's reserve; equations not rendered
note: Theory: hedge less only when funds and needs move together (Froot, Scharfstein and Stein, 1993); hers do not, so her flexibility is a reserve, not a hedge.

idea: Sharpe-Tint's surplus objective rewards assets that move with liabilities: E(r_A) - (lambda/2)var(r_A) + lambda cov(r_A, r_L); "If the assets are uncorrelated with the liabilities ... standard mean-variance"
sources: Sharpe & Tint (1990), via Ang, Chen & Sundaresan (2013) eq. (3)
use: VT earns about zero credit against building costs; its case in the plan is expected size, never hedging
critique: Sharpe-Tint's own paper is a scan, not read
note: Store only (not read at source).

idea: Downside matters more than average co-movement: Sharpe-Tint counts downside "symmetrically with upside"; with a downside penalty the equity weight falls from 84% to 48%, "exactly the opposite of the Sharpe-Tint advice"
use: Her flexibility is judged in the bad states, and the bad state (an inflationary fall) is where building costs turn wrong-way
critique: Pension calibration (liability-equity correlation 0.35 from LKB); not Laura's numbers
note: Store: downside matters more than average co-movement (Ang, Chen and Sundaresan, 2013).

idea: The classic surplus calibration assumes pension liabilities correlate 1.00 with bonds and 0.35 with equities; Keel finds building costs about 0 to -0.3 with shares
sources: Leibowitz, Kogelman & Bader (1992), via ACS (2013) note 5
use: Against building costs, shares are a worse hedge than pension theory assumes for pension claims
critique: LKB not read; different liability
note: Store only.

idea: The uses take turns: slump 2008-09, giving fell and building costs fell a year later; inflationary 2022, building costs rose while giving held in dollars; stagflation 1973-75, both (giving -9.2%; Turner +17.2% in 1974); NUMBERS 8f's 1973 start leaves her flexibility $13,832 ($22,036 with the excess)
sources: This card; store H8-112, H9-013, Q4b-007; NUMBERS 8f, 8j
use: One sentence for 3e: which use calls on her flexibility depends on the kind of fall; only a stagflation brings two at once
critique: 1973-75 is US-only; Taiwan's index starts 1991
verified: VERIFIED (each part at its source; the pattern is Keel's reading)
clash: risk: the stagflation case, to record
note: 3e: the uses take turns (a slump hits giving; an inflationary fall hits building costs; the Taiwan dollar is unlinked, 8j); 1973-75 hit two at once, recorded.

idea: The part of her flexibility that does not move with shares is the excess above the stated top: median with it $23,201 where shares fell over 2031-33, against $15,423 without (house); $23,987 against $16,164 (history)
use: The plan's own answer to wrong-way timing is Treasury money, already in the design
critique: MODEL; the excess exists only when the funds pay above the top
note: The steady part of her flexibility is the excess above the top (median $23,201 with it, $15,423 without, where shares fell; 8f): why $29,800 is always said with its two parts.

idea: Write the pass mark down before the test, then pass a message only if the low end of the 95% interval clears it; every key message must pass, not the average
sources: FDA (2010) Label comprehension studies guidance: success "only when the lower limit of the two-sided 95 percent ... confidence interval for the comprehension rate is above the predefined target level"
use: Before each blind round Keel writes each check's target (for example "co-sponsors count the bottom: 85%, no critical confusion") and reports the interval beside the count
critique: Built for drug labels read by hundreds; FDA's 2023 slides call thresholds "targets, not hard pass/fail"
note: Mon 16 Nov: Keel's method (voice rounds, aha cold tests, exhibit reads): write each check's target before the round and report the interval beside the count; serves no report part directly, so F 3.

idea: Pass marks by field, from strict to loose: FDA labels about 90% (choosing the right product 85%); ANSI safety symbols 85% with at most 5% opposite readings; Health Canada 80%; five-second "main message" 80%; ISO symbols about 67%; cloze 60%
sources: FDA 2023 advisory slides; Wogalter et al. (2006) on ANSI Z535.3 and ISO; Health Canada consumer-use studies; Lyssna guide; Nielsen (2011)
use: Set the bar by what a miss costs: the figure co-sponsors count (3d) at 85-90%; a voice or aha read is a finding test, not a pass rate
critique: The bars are conventions: an ERIC review of cloze cut-offs calls "these criteria ... quite arbitrary"
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 16 Nov 2026; ANSI and ISO bars as reported by Wogalter et al. and the Greenwich supplement, the paywalled standards not read)
where: This run: fda.gov; safetyhumanfactors.org; canada.ca; lyssna.com
note: Mon 16 Nov: method only; the bars are conventions (ERIC calls them arbitrary) and the ANSI and ISO figures are second-hand; useful only to set the 3c and 3d check targets by what a miss costs.

idea: Small counts need small-sample intervals: add about two right and two wrong answers, then compute (the adjusted Wald method); 4 of 5 right is anywhere from 36.5% to 98.3%
sources: Sauro & Lewis (2005), HFES, Table 1 and conclusion ("add two successes and two failures")
use: Keel arithmetic (z = 1.96): Caplet's own reflections 18/18 = 79-100%; plain passages 20/24 = 64-94%; one-turn conceit 2/24 = 1-27%; a 3-reader check 3/3 = 38-100%
critique: Readers each judge many passages, so judgements are not independent; the intervals are too narrow if anything
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for every blind round (adjusted Wald interval beside each count); the ROUND3-4 intervals check at z 1.96; recheck the 4-of-5 example against Sauro and Lewis Table 1 (z 1.96 gives about 36-98%).

idea: Small rounds can kill but not crown: a big gap shows with few readers, a small one never does
sources: Keel arithmetic on ROUND3-4 counts with Sauro & Lewis (2005) and ISO 4120:2021
use: The conceit verdict (2/24 against Caplet's 18/18) stands at any sensible sample; "plain reads as Caplet's" (20/24, one-sided Fisher p about 0.10 against 18/18) is "no gap found in 24 reads", never "indistinguishable"
critique: Caplet decided the conceit stays; tests shape how it is used, not whether
verified: VERIFIED (counts from ROUND3.md and ROUND4.md; Keel arithmetic)
clash: None (Caplet's call on the conceit, Books 19-20)
where: This run: Keel's voice files; Keel arithmetic
note: Mon 16 Nov: voice programme: the conceit's 2 of 24 stands, plain 20 of 24 is no gap found in 24 reads, never indistinguishable; one-sided Fisher p 0.095 checks; Keel arithmetic, so S 3.

idea: Readers needed before a rate can be claimed: every reader right needs 19 reads to show 80% or better, one miss needs 27; showing 90% with none wrong needs 42
sources: Keel arithmetic on the adjusted Wald method (Sauro & Lewis 2005)
use: A rate in a test note ("co-sponsors read the bottom 90% of the time") needs dozens of reads; three-reader rounds report findings, not rates
critique: A pass rate from fresh model readers is not a pass rate from Wharton judges either
note: Mon 16 Nov: method; the 19, 27 and 42 reads check by Keel arithmetic; mostly restates row 4: three-reader rounds report findings, not rates.

idea: Proving two things are alike takes about twice the tasters of proving they differ: ISO's triangle test uses 24-30 assessors for a difference and "approximately 60" for similarity, and advises against fewer than 18
sources: ISO 4120:2021 Sensory analysis, Triangle test (sample pages), clause on number of assessors and Table A.1
use: "Heard as Caplet's" is a similarity claim, so 24 reads cannot certify it; Table A.1: 6 assessors need 5 right, 12 need 8, 24 need 13 at the 5% level
critique: Food tasting, not prose; chance there is 1 in 3 because one sample of three differs
note: Mon 16 Nov: voice programme: heard as Caplet's is a similarity claim, so ISO 4120's about 60 assessors bounds what 24 reads can say; from another field.

idea: A forced choice is a cleaner voice test than a confidence scale: show a known Caplet passage, then two new ones, one Caplet's and one Keel's, and ask which matches (a duo-trio test, chance 1 in 2)
sources: ISO 10399 Sensory analysis, Duo-trio test (sample pages; fewer than 24 assessors not recommended)
use: Replaces "surely / probably" with a yes-or-no score that has a known chance rate; Keel's existing positive checks (Caplet's reflections) become the reference
critique: Readers who know the test may hunt for style tells rather than read for voice
note: Mon 16 Nov: voice programme: a duo-trio forced choice with Caplet's reflections as the reference replaces the surely/probably scale; a concrete change for rounds 5-6.

idea: Problems found by n readers = 1 - (1 - L) to the n, with L about 31% for a typical problem; 5 users find about 85%; five is for finding problems, not for measuring
sources: Nielsen (2000); Nielsen Norman Group (2021) "5 test users: qual vs quant"
use: Keel arithmetic: 3 readers find about 67% of problems of average visibility, 5 about 84%, 9 about 96%; add rounds rather than readers per round
critique: L varies by task; a rare misreading (seen by 10%) is found by 3 readers only 27% of the time (Keel arithmetic)
note: Mon 16 Nov: method; Nielsen's five-user formula is textbook UX; Keel's 67, 84 and 96% and the 27% for a rare misreading check.

idea: Five readers can be a lucky or unlucky draw: from 60 users, random sets of 5 found anywhere from 55% to 99% of the problems; sets of 10 never fewer than about 80%, sets of 20 at least 95%
use: A clean round with three readers may be luck; before 27 Nov the key passages (3c, 3d) get a second round with new readers
critique: One software task, not a written report
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for the 3c and 3d reader panels: a clean three-reader round may be luck, so the key passages get a second round with new readers before 27 Nov.

idea: Cognitive interviewing runs in rounds of 5 to 10 ("as few as four interviews may be sufficient"), "seldom" more than 12-15 before changes, usually 3-4 rounds, each after a fix
sources: Willis (1999) Cognitive interviewing: A "how to" guide, RTI
use: Keel's voice rounds already iterate; make the rule explicit: fix, then re-test the fixed passage on readers who never saw the old one
critique: Survey questions, not paragraphs; Willis (2005) book not read
note: Mon 16 Nov: method; the voice rounds already iterate; makes the rule explicit: fix, then re-test on readers who never saw the old version.

idea: Spread the reading: "three interviewers each conduct three interviews apiece" beats one interviewer doing nine
use: Keel's three readers each read 13 passages: 39 reads but only 3 minds; more readers each reading fewer passages gives more independent judgements
critique: Willis means interviewers; the same logic applies to readers and to scorers
note: Mon 16 Nov: method: Keel's rounds give many reads but only three minds; more readers each reading fewer passages; a real fix for the voice and aha tests.

idea: A problem found once is still a problem: count "discoveries ... even if they occur in only a single interview"; cognitive testing has "very little in the way of 'truth in numbers'"
use: One reader hearing "ink" as "signed" is a fix, not a vote lost 2 to 1
critique: Gives no rule for telling a real problem from one reader's quirk
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for every blind read: one reader hearing owned as signed is a fix, not a vote lost 2 to 1; feeds the critical-confusion list (row 22).

idea: Size the panel by its job: German survey practice runs 5-30 interviews a round, 10-20 typical, and more interviews kept finding new problems (Blair and Conrad 2011); the US health statistics centre uses 20-50 to learn how questions are read, not to estimate rates
sources: GESIS Guide 049 Cognitive pretesting; National Center for Health Statistics, CCQDER Cognitive interviewing page
use: The panels that judge 3c and 3d (the figure co-sponsors count) earn larger samples than a voice spot-check
critique: Blair and Conrad read only as reported by GESIS
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 16 Nov 2026; Blair and Conrad 2011 as reported)
note: Mon 16 Nov: same cognitive-interview sample-size point as row 10 (size the panel by its job); Blair and Conrad only as reported by GESIS.

idea: US plain-language practice: "Plan to test at least twice"; three readers are enough for a usability look; for a side-by-side comparison, "know what results you will consider a success" before running it
sources: Plain Language Action and Information Network (2011) Federal plain language guidelines; Digital.gov plain-language testing pages
use: Before a round comparing two versions (words against chart in the aha test), Keel writes which result would change its call
critique: The guidelines give no numbers for comparative tests
where: This run: ies.ed.gov copy of the guidelines; digital.gov
note: Mon 16 Nov: method; test twice and fix the success rule in advance, mostly carried by row 1; applies to the aha test's words-against-chart comparison.

idea: Saying you understood is not understanding: the Bank of England's layered summary raised self-rated understanding by 0.71 on a 1-5 scale (more than an economics degree's 0.55), but on direct questions the old summary scored 2.02 of 5 and the best new one 2.85
sources: Haldane & McMahon (2018), AEA P&P 108; Bholat et al. (2018), BoE Staff Working Paper 750 ("frequently overestimate their understanding")
use: Never score "did you follow it?" or "how clear was it 1-5"; score only what the reader says back or does with it
critique: Different samples and measures across the two papers; the direct test is the follow-up, not a re-run
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for every reader panel: never score did-you-follow-it or a 1-5 clarity rating, only what readers say back or do; the BoE gap (0.71 self-rated, 2.02 to 2.85 of 5 tested) is the proof.

idea: What the BoE scored: five direct multiple-choice questions, two applied ones (a grocery budget, a salary) and trust 0-10; the "relatable" version raised correct applied answers by 32 points; 4-5 right for about 1 in 8 readers of the old summary and 1 in 3 of the relatable one
sources: Bholat, Broughton, Parker, ter Meer & Walczak (2018); Bholat et al. (2019) JME 108 (abstract)
use: Each Keel check gets one direct question and one applied question in Laura's world ("what does the residency have for its first ten years of running costs?")
critique: About 500 per condition, pre-registered: far bigger than Keel's rounds
note: Mon 16 Nov: method: one direct and one applied question in Laura's world per check; the relatable version's 32-point gain on applied answers also backs concrete wording in 3a and 3d.

idea: Check questions must not borrow the passage's words: the BoE admits its questions "more closely mirrored language" in the new summaries, "A fair challenge is whether the phrasing ... biased our results"
use: Never ask "what does owned mean?" after a passage that says "owned"; ask an applied question in other words, or the reader matches words, not meaning
critique: Some overlap is unavoidable for figures ($95,000)
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for all check questions (voice, aha, exhibits): never borrow the passage's words; the BoE's own footnote is the warning.

idea: Test the questions before the readers: a BoE pre-trial of over 100 people answered £5,200 (52 weeks times £100) to a question meant otherwise, so the wording was fixed; the FTC's notice designers ran their pretest as a dry run of the method
sources: Bholat et al. (2018); Kleimann Communication Group (2006)
use: One reader answers Keel's check questions first, so a failure points to the passage, not to a muddled question
critique: Adds a step to a 24-hour schedule; one pilot reader is enough to catch the worst
note: Mon 16 Nov: method: one pilot reader answers the check questions first so a failure points at the passage; small cost on 27 Nov's schedule.

idea: Reading grade beat pictures: in a 4,521-adult test the comprehension gain was "driven by the material's reading grade, rather than visuals or word count" (Flesch-Kincaid grade about 15 against about 7)
sources: ter Meer (2019), Bank of Canada workshop slides
use: In the aha test (words against chart) hold the reading grade level fixed, or the chart's win may be the plainer caption
critique: Slides, not a paper; one country, one kind of text
note: Mon 16 Nov: aha test and exhibit designs: hold reading grade fixed when words face a chart, since grade beat visuals for 4,521 adults; slides, not a paper, so S 4.

idea: Ask about a third party: label tests use "scenario questions based on a hypothetical third party", because "Understanding does not always translate to behavior"
sources: FDA (2023) Nonprescription Drugs Advisory Committee slides
use: "A co-sponsor's board must put one figure from Laura's letter into its budget: which, and why?" Key: the stated bottom (3d: co-sponsors count the bottom)
critique: A scenario tests applying, not what a real funder would do
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for 3d's reader test: a third-party budget question (which figure does a co-sponsor's board count?), keyed to the stated bottom as SKELETON 3d says.

idea: Score open answers in five boxes (correct, wrong, opposite of the meaning, don't know, no answer), with two scorers working apart; ANSI calls multiple choice "typically less accurate than open-ended testing"
sources: ISO 9186-1 categories and ANSI Z535.3 (2022) contents note; Wogalter et al. (2006); CPSC (2021) symbol report
use: Keel's one-sentence meaning is scored by two scorers blind to which version the reader saw, with "opposite" counted on its own
critique: Two scorers double the work; agreement must be reported too
verified: VERIFIED (read at source, 16 Nov 2026; ANSI's change note read in its published contents pages)
note: Mon 16 Nov: method: five-box scoring by two blind scorers with opposite readings counted apart; doubles the scoring; ANSI's wording read only in its contents note.

idea: Pre-list the critical confusions, the opposite readings that do harm, and allow none (ANSI allows at most 5%)
sources: Keel proposal from ANSI Z535.3's critical-confusion limit and Blastland et al. (2020) "Anticipate misunderstandings"
use: For the range: the top owned before the 2031 move; the gift able to fall below the bottom, or to land above the top; co-sponsors' money or the ten payments paying it; "owned" heard as "signed" or "promised"
critique: The list is Keel's; a reader may find a new confusion, which goes on the list (row 12)
verified: VERIFIED (sources read at source, 16 Nov 2026; the list is Keel's design)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c and 3d: the pre-listed confusions (top owned before the move, gift outside the range, who pays it, owned heard as signed) are what the text must pre-empt as well as what tests score; Keel's list, so S 4.

idea: Count an answer only if the result and the reasoning are both right ("double check: outcome and process"), from readers' written working
use: A reader's "$95,000" counts only if their reason names the Treasuries she owns, not a guess at the middle
critique: Needs a written "why" from each reader; slower to score
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for the 3c range check: count a reader's figure only with the right reason (the Treasuries she owns), which stops lucky guesses at the middle.

idea: A free test: the reader thinks aloud, then summarises the text "to someone else, being explicit enough for a subject-matter expert to evaluate"; an expert's fuller account then shows what surprised; the aim is "active mastery", the reader drawing inferences
sources: Fischhoff, Brewer & Downs (Eds.) (2011), Communicating risks and benefits, FDA
use: Keel's meaning sentence becomes "explain it to a co-sponsor in two sentences", graded by a reader who knows the plan
critique: A summary rewards fluent readers; the same chapter warns that scenario questions can "frame problems"
note: Mon 16 Nov: explain-it-to-someone-else with expert grading is paraphrase testing (Q22-035, with Q31-033 teach-back); the co-sponsor framing can go into that row's use.

idea: Test whether readers can use the point, not just recall it: the FTC scored "judgment quality" (pick the better of two banks from their notices) apart from "perceptual accuracy", with 1,032 shoppers and four notice designs
sources: Levy & Hastak (2008), FTC quantitative research report
use: Show two one-paragraph plans side by side (Laura's and a growth-first one) and ask "which one has the residency's first ten years paid whatever markets do?"
critique: A rigged pair would test nothing; the other plan must be one a real adviser might offer
note: Mon 16 Nov: method for the aha tests: judgment quality (pick the plan that pays the ten whatever markets do) over recall; the rival must be a real plan, such as the team's growth-first first plan.

idea: Opinion panels are not comprehension tests: focus groups "do not tell the researcher what a consumer will actually do with a notice"; the FTC's notice took 66 readers over 8 rounds
sources: Kleimann Communication Group (2006) Evolution of a prototype financial privacy notice
use: A reader's "this is persuasive" is noted but never scored; only what they say back counts
critique: Focus groups still find what readers want included
note: Mon 16 Nov: same point as row 15 (what readers say they like or understand is not evidence); the FTC's 66 readers over 8 rounds stay findable here.

idea: Shorter saved time but not choices: Harvard staff choosing funds with real money read the summary prospectus in 22.5 minutes against 31.2, with no evidence of better choices; the authors' first look in 2008 had reported lower fees
sources: Beshears, Choi, Laibson & Madrian (2009), NBER w14859; their comment letter (SEC file S7-28-07, item 116)
use: A shorter passage that reads faster is not proof it lands better; and an early good result needs a re-run before Keel trusts it
critique: 186 readers, one task
note: Mon 16 Nov: method: faster reading is not better choosing, and an early good result needs a re-run; Beshears et al. are known in behavioural finance.

idea: Order of returns breaks a CLAT that beats its rate on average: $10m, 10 years, 6.0% rate, $1.36m a year, 9.3% compound growth; S&P 1993-2002 order leaves about $8.0m; the reverse order leaves zero with "inadequate assets to pay out the year 9 and year 10 annuities"

idea: Walton v. Commissioner: two GRATs of $100,000,023.56 in Wal-Mart stock (Apr 1993), annuity 49.35% then 59.22% of value, $108,570,025.58 due; each paid $94,104,550.57, "a $14,465,475.01 shortfall", "no property to be delivered to the remainder beneficiary"; stock $27.6875 at funding, $26.1875 at the last payment (13.3% short after a 5.4% fall, Keel arithmetic)

idea: No CLAT exhaustion test and no payout limits: "No probability of exhaustion rules; contrast CRATs: Rev. Rul. 77-374"; "No minimum or maximum"; IRS: "no minimum or maximum payout rate limitations"; SOI: not "constrained by minimum or maximum payout restrictions"

idea: The only exhaustion rule for a lead annuity is a valuation rule at the assumed rate: an annuity "is expected to exhaust the fund" is valued for fewer years; "if the amount of the annuity payment ... is less than or equal to the applicable section 7520 interest rate ... the corpus is assumed to be sufficient to make all payments"

idea: The regulation's own example deems a one-stock trust sufficient forever: $1m of one corporation's non-dividend stock, 6% annuity, 8.2% rate: "the trust corpus is considered sufficient to pay this annuity for the entire 10-year term of the trust, or even indefinitely"

idea: The investing rule scales with the charity's share: if the charity's annuity is worth more than 60% of the trust (after liabilities), the deed must bar acquiring, and "the retention of assets which would give rise to a tax under section 4944" (jeopardizing investments); at 60% or less this condition does not apply

idea: That guard is a standard of care, not an ability to pay: jeopardy means managers "failed to exercise ordinary business care" in providing for "long- and short-term financial needs"; "No category of investments shall be treated as a per se violation"; judged "as of the time ... and not subsequently on the basis of hindsight"

A trustee power to "commute and prepay" the charity early at a discount disqualifies a CLAT

idea: The Which-Outcome effect: asked to complete "It is certain that ... [amount]", 78.7% / 74.5% / 76.7% chose "at least" and 0% "exactly"; with "It is possible", 72.3% / 72.9% / 79.5% chose "up to" (three products); people call the bottom of a spread "certain" and the top "possible" even when those values occur only 5-10% of the time
sources: Juanchich, Teigen & Gourdon (2013), JDM 8(3), Experiment 1 table and text
use: "Certain" pulls listeners to a minimum and "possible" to a maximum; Laura's confidence word decides which end co-sponsors hear
critique: Lab vignettes about batteries, diets and jeans, not pledges; respondents completed sentences rather than reading Laura's
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c confidence sentence, the evidence under row 2; Table 1 checked at source (78.7 / 74.5 / 76.7% at least, 0.0% exactly); it is a sentence-completion task by 50 MTurk workers, so say chose, not read as (the card's verdict 1 says read as and should not).

idea: The same authors' advice: "one should perhaps avoid the terms certain and possible in a context of magnitudes. Certain is problematic because it may be unclear whether the associated outcome value should be given an 'exact' or an 'at least' reading"
use: Never "certain to be $115,000": it is heard as "$115,000 or more", and the contribution is never above the top (NUMBERS 4; CANON D12); put "certain" or "guaranteed" on the Treasuries that pay, not on the sum
critique: Book 19 allows "guaranteed" and "certain" for Treasuries; this row moves where the word sits, not whether it is used
clash: None; guards the ban on a contribution above the stated top
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c, certain goes on the Treasuries, never on $115,000 (SKELETON 3c already carries it); quote checked at source in section 7.6, which opens If verbal probabilities are reported; heard as at least is the authors' inference, not a listener test; fits Book 19: it moves the word, never drops it.

idea: A Norwegian corpus count found "will" goes with "at least" and "can" with "up to"; used together, "certain" and "possible" act as "worst case—best case estimates"
sources: Juanchich, Teigen & Gourdon (2013), introduction and discussion
use: "She will give $95,000 and can give $115,000" would be heard as worst and best case, which is wrong after the move: she gives the top in every tested path (NUMBERS 4)
critique: Corpus is Norwegian; English use is assumed similar by the authors, not shown here
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d guard against a will give / can give pairing, heard as worst and best case; the corpus count is Teigen and Filkukova (2013) as reported by Juanchich et al.; the worst case-best case line checked at source.

idea: A bare number in a gain frame is read as "at least" by most (58% and 54% in the standard Asian Disease task); given a reason that caps it ("only 200 vaccines"), 71% read "200" as "at most"
sources: Mandel (2015), Frontiers in Psychology 6:537, reporting Mandel (2014) General Discussion
use: Give the reason with the top ("what the Treasuries she owns pay") and listeners read $115,000 as exact or at most, not as a floor with more to come
critique: One reported experiment, in a classic textbook task, not money pledges
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c and 3d, give the top with its reason; 58% and 54% checked at source but 54% is the loss frame, so drop in a gain frame; add Mandel (2014) Exp. 3: spelling out what is and is not saved raised exactly to 59% and cut at least to 24%, the stronger lesson for naming each end.

idea: Overstatements are judged more inaccurate than understatements of the same size, and optimistic statements more than pessimistic ones; false reports are judged as deviant from truth "with less importance attached to the magnitude"
sources: Teigen & Filkuková (2011), Scand. J. Psychol. 52(1), abstract
use: A top missed by $1 costs more goodwill than a bottom beaten by $20,000; the reason nothing is stated before the move (a top stated a month early is not yet owned in 2.9% of house paths, NUMBERS 4)
critique: Vignettes on prices and amounts; abstract only
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c, why nothing is stated before the move (aha 7; 2.9% a month early, NUMBERS 4); abstract only; sits beside Q25-001 (Gneezy and Epley), which carries the promise point.

idea: Listeners prefer the limit that is worst for them: travellers want maximum distances and durations, buyers (not sellers) maximum prices; mistaken maxima are judged more "wrong" than mistaken minima; advisers, "concerned about being blamed if wrong", do not share the preference
sources: Halberg, Teigen & Fostervold (2009), Acta Psychologica 132(3), abstract
use: Co-sponsors are the listeners here, and their worst case is the bottom; Laura, as the speaker, should not choose for them which figure they hear, so name both
critique: The worst case for a buyer is a high price; for a co-sponsor it is a low gift, so the mapping is by analogy
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3d, why both ends are named: co-sponsors as listeners lean to their worst case, the bottom; abstract and introduction only; the buyer-to-funder mapping is by analogy, as recorded.

idea: Japan's state arts fund counts only money already spent: costs must be "自ら支払った経費であることが証拠書類（銀行振込明細書等）により確認できる" (proved by bank records to be paid by the group itself) in the fiscal year; "未払いの経費は計上できません" (unpaid costs cannot be counted); prepayments before the year and payments in another name do not count

idea: In China a promise to give becomes legally owed when it is public: under Art. 41 a charity may demand payment and go to court if the donor "通过广播、电视、报刊、互联网等媒体公开承诺捐赠的" (pledged publicly through broadcast, TV, print or internet media), or if the gift is for poverty, the elderly, orphans, disability or disasters under a written agreement; "文化" (culture, Art. 3(4)) is not on that second list
