idea: "A simple rule with an escape clause strikes a better balance between credibility and flexibility"; "Flood and Isard (1989) have shown that a rule with an escape clause always dominates pure discretion and, if supply shocks are sufficiently volatile, it also dominates a simple rule"
sources: Persson, T. & Tabellini, G. (1997) Political economics and macroeconomic policy, NBER WP 6329, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w6329/w6329.pdf
use: Supports a rule with named exits over "we will decide when it happens"
critique: "Dominates" is within a model of one policymaker and one shock; nothing measured
verified: VERIFIED in part (survey read in part; 1990 book not read)

idea: "Escape-clause models were developed by Flood and Isard (1989), named and extended by Persson and Tabellini (1990)"; "the policymaker is tempted to treat all situations as extraordinary ones. Hence, a higher political authority must impose a cost on the policymaker every time the standard rule is violated"
sources: Flood, R.P. & Marion, N.P. (1997) Policy implications of "second-generation" crisis models, IMF WP/97/16, https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/wp9716.pdf
use: The temptation cannot arise in l.17: neither reason is a judgement that something is "extraordinary"; each is a payment that arrives or does not (row 33). The missing "higher authority" before 2031 is the weak test (row 35)
critique: Laura has no higher authority over her own money; co-sponsors are an audience from 2031, not an authority

idea: Under the gold standard, rules were set aside "only under exceptional circumstances, which can be unambiguously identified both by monetary authorities and by the public, and are reinstated whenever the reasons for the suspension are gone, or ... after a reasonably predictable length of time"
sources: Giovannini, A. (1993) Bretton Woods and its precursors, in Bordo & Eichengreen (eds.), A retrospective on the Bretton Woods system, University of Chicago Press, pp. 109-154, https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c6868/c6868.pdf
use: Both of Laura's reasons can be identified by her and by any co-sponsor (a bank record; the Treasury's own payment record). Reinstatement: a late deposit runs the same order (card Q34)
critique: A national monetary convention among many actors; hers is one household's plan

idea: Lohmann's model: the government can override the central banker at a cost; in equilibrium it never does, and the possibility makes the banker accommodate extreme shocks; the full-commitment case is the limit of an infinite cost. A secondary account: Lohmann observed that New Zealand's legislature can repeal the central-bank law at any time, so the commitment is "political, rather than legal"
sources: Lohmann, S. (1992) AER 82(1): 273-286, https://www.jstor.org/stable/2117615 (text not read); read through Eijffinger, S. & de Haan, J. (1996) Princeton SP19, https://ies.princeton.edu/pdf/SP19.pdf ; Debelle, G. & Fischer, S. (1994) Boston Fed conference 38, https://www.bostonfed.org/-/media/Documents/conference/38/conf38f.pdf ; a UNLV handbook chapter, https://smiller.faculty.unlv.edu/HANDBOOK_CHAPTER_FINAL.pdf
use: Laura's plan has Lohmann's shape de facto: she can always override (sell), and from 2031 the cost is her word to co-sponsors. The override is never meant to be used
critique: Before 2031 the cost is close to zero (a sale), so the shape exists but has no weight (row 35)
verified: UNVERIFIED at source (four secondary accounts agree; the AER text is behind JSTOR)

idea: "Real world escape clause rules suffer from the problem that it is not possible to precisely define the state that triggers intervention. There is unlikely to be agreement over what constitutes, for example 'extreme economic circumstances'. This admits the possibility that opportunistic governments will override the central bank in less than extreme circumstances"
sources: Mihov, I. & Sibert, A. (2002, July) Credibility and flexibility with monetary policy committees, working paper, https://igier.unibocconi.eu/sites/default/files/media/attach/241002.pdf
use: Laura's two states can be defined precisely, which is the property these authors say real-world clauses lack: a deposit received or not by 31 March 2028; a payment more than five business days late or not
critique: Their worry is a government with its own aims; Laura's adviser has none apart from her plan

idea: Reputation can partly stand in for a rule: "reputational forces can substitute for formal rules", but the outcome is a weighted average of rule and discretion and looks "more like ... discretion when the discount rate is high"
sources: Barro, R.J. & Gordon, D.B. (1983) Rules, discretion and reputation in a model of monetary policy, Journal of Monetary Economics 12(1): 101-121, https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(83)90051-X ; NBER WP 1079
use: From 2031 Laura's reputation with co-sponsors does the binding. Before 2031 no one outside knows the plan, so reputation does nothing
critique: Their game repeats every period; her co-sponsor meetings are one round, so reputation is thinner than in their model

idea: Escape clauses can backfire: "While well-designed escape-clause rules can raise society's welfare in principle, limited credibility makes it difficult to implement such rules in practice", and they "can also produce equilibria far inferior to an irrevocably fixed exchange rate"; when the trigger depends on expectations, the "circularity creates the potential for multiple equilibria"
sources: Obstfeld, M. (1997) Destabilizing effects of exchange-rate escape clauses, Journal of International Economics 43(1-2): 61-77, http://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/inecon/v43y1997i1-2p61-77.html ; Obstfeld (1994) The logic of currency crises, https://eml.berkeley.edu/~obstfeld/ftp/currency_crises/cc.pdf
use: Laura's triggers do not depend on what anyone expects: no one's belief about the plan can make a deposit missing or a Treasury payment late
critique: A debt-limit standoff is partly about expectations, but it is Table 3's look-closer row, not a reason (and it never forces a sale)
verified: VERIFIED in part (abstracts; 1994 paper in part)

idea: Being tough can cost credibility: "following a tough policy ... may lower rather than raise the credibility of a no-devaluation pledge" when its costs persist
sources: Drazen, A. & Masson, P.R. (1994) Credibility of policies versus credibility of policymakers, Quarterly Journal of Economics 109(3): 735-754, https://www.nber.org/papers/w4448
use: Holding through a long fall is not a persistent cost for Laura's payments; it is borne by her flexibility (the kept half), which no one is promised
critique: Their cost is unemployment that mounts with time; Laura has no mounting cost from holding

idea: The UK keeps a political override of the central bank for "extreme economic circumstances", but the order lapses unless Parliament approves it within 28 days and ends after three months
use: A named override with its own time limit and its own approver. Laura's exits need no time limit, being events, not periods
critique: Its trigger ("extreme economic circumstances") is the kind of vague state row 11 warns against; it is limited by procedure, not by definition

idea: A trigger that asks for an explanation, not an exemption: a letter if inflation moves "more than 1 percentage point in either direction"; "The thresholds do not define a target range"; "over 30 letters" since April 2007; the letters are "a communication tool", not a sanction; the test is "whether the explanations we give are judged to be reasonable or not"
sources: HM Treasury (2025) Remit for the MPC, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/monetary-policy-remit-budget-2025/letter-from-chancellor-of-the-exchequer-to-govenor-of-the-bank-of-england ; Bank of England 2026 remit, https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/letter/2026/mpc-letter-remit-2026.pdf ; Research handbook on inflation ch. 26, https://splloyd-econ.github.io/RHandbookInfl_BoE.pdf ; Treasury Committee (2007) HC 299, https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm200607/cmselect/cmtreasy/299/29909.htm ; Treasury Committee evidence 1 Mar 2011 (King), https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm201011/cmselect/cmtreasy/798/11030102.htm
use: Table 3 already uses this second design: its five non-reason rows (X-date, fund notices, trade dates, yields and prices, her flexibility) ask the team to look and explain, never to change the plan. Two designs in one table: two exits, five letters
critique: Frequent letters suit a target hit only on average; Laura's payments are owned outright, so her signals should fire rarely
verified: VERIFIED (remit letters and 2007 report read at source in part); handbook chapter's author not confirmed

idea: Breaking a rule outside its clauses damaged it: in Nov 2003 the Council held the excessive deficit procedures for France and Germany "in abeyance"; the ECB said this "risks undermining the credibility of the institutional framework"; the Court annulled the Council's conclusions: "the Council cannot break free from the rules ... which it set for itself in Regulation No 1467/97"
sources: European Central Bank (2003, Nov 25) statement, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2003/html/pr031125.en.html ; Court of Justice (2004, Jul 13) press release 57/04, Case C-27/04, https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2009-02/cp040057en.pdf ; European Commission (2004, Dec 14) communication, http://ec.europa.eu/economy_finance/economic_governance/sgp/pdf/30_edps/communication_to_the_council/2004-12-14_de_fr_communication_on_budgetary_situation_en.pdf
use: The failure l.17 is written against: a reason not on the list used anyway. CANON A34 (never add a rule or trigger) is the report's version of the Court's sentence
critique: Twelve governments and a treaty, with large economies outvoting the rule; Laura's plan has no voters
verified: VERIFIED (ECB statement and Court press release read in full; Commission communication in part)

idea: After the breach the clause was widened: the 2005 reform made "severe economic downturn" mean "any negative growth rate, or even a period of positive but very low growth"; in Nov 2003 "many critics claimed that the Pact was dead"; the ECB was "seriously concerned"
sources: European Central Bank (2005, Oct 13) The reform of the Stability and Growth Pact: an assessment [speech], https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/key/date/2005/html/sp051013.en.html ; ECB (2005, Mar 21) statement, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2005/html/pr050321.en.html
use: Widening after a breach is the second way rules die. Laura's text cannot be widened in the competition (frozen) and the report adds nothing (A34)
critique: The original definition before 2005 was not read at source (gap 7)

idea: A narrow clause used once and closed: the EU general escape clause was activated "for the first time ever" in March 2020, kept through the energy shock, and "deactivated at the end of 2023"; the 2024 rules add a one-year limit per activation, extensions, and an independent fiscal board's opinion (Art. 25: "severe economic downturn in the euro area or the Union as a whole")
sources: European Commission (2023, Mar 8) press release IP/23/1410, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_1410 , and remarks, https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/speech_23_1542 ; Council working document WK 9891/2023, https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-9891-2023-INIT/en/pdf ; Regulation (EU) 2024/1263, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF?uri=OJ%3AL_202401263
use: Shows a well-defined exit can be opened and closed on the record. Laura's reason 1 has its own closing date built in (31 March 2028), and after it only reason 2 remains (Q7 row 31)
critique: The 2020-23 activation was extended once for a second shock; a time limit can be renewed, which is its own widening
verified: VERIFIED (press release in full; regulation Arts 25-26 and Council note in part)

idea: The national escape clause, written for "exceptional circumstances outside the control of the Member State", was used for defence by 15 states on 8 Jul 2025 and reached 19 activations by Nov 2026 (up to 1.5% of GDP for four years), and was then extended to energy security for Greece (9 Oct 2026) and Italy (9 Nov 2026); critics: a clause "originally designed for country-specific temporary emergencies rather than continent-wide structural defence needs, creates particular concerns about the integrity of the newly reformed economic governance framework"; it "would de facto unplug the rules for a long time"
sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 Art. 26, as row 19; Council of the EU (2025, Jul 8) press release, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2025/07/08/council-activates-flexibility-in-eu-fiscal-rules-for-15-member-states-to-increase-defence-spending ; Council timeline, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/national-escape-clause-for-defence-expenditure-nec/timeline-national-escape-clause-for-defence-expenditure ; European Parliament EGOV (2025) PE 764.381, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/IDAN/2025/764381/ECTI_IDA(2025)764381_EN.pdf ; Guttenberg, L. & Redeker, N. (2025, Feb 21) Bertelsmann Stiftung and Jacques Delors Centre policy brief, https://www.bertelsmann-stiftung.de/fileadmin/files/user_upload/20250221_Policy_Brief_Defence_Spending_Fiscal_Rules_Lucas_Guttenberg_Nils_Redeker.pdf
use: Scope creep: a clause for emergencies used for a planned, lasting need. Laura's equivalent risk would be calling a planned use (say a building overrun) a "reason"; l.17 has no such door, and the overrun is her flexibility's job
critique: Defence spending may be a real emergency; the critics are think tanks and a Parliament research unit, not a court
verified: VERIFIED in part (press releases and EGOV read in part; Bertelsmann brief in excerpt)

idea: The Swiss debt brake: the ceiling may rise only for "extraordinary developments outside of the control of the Confederation", only if the extra need is at least 0.5% of the ceiling, by a qualified majority of both chambers, and shortfalls are offset within six years; the business cycle is handled by a cyclical factor, not by the clause; adopted 2 Dec 2001 with about 85% yes
sources: Federal Act on the Federal Budget (FHG), Arts 15 and 17a-17b, via Federal Finance Administration, https://www.efv.admin.ch/en/federal-governments-debt-brake ; Bundestag Wissenschaftliche Dienste (2024) WD 4-014-24, https://www.bundestag.de/resource/blob/996708/WD-4-014-24-pdf.pdf
use: A threshold stops trivial use (0.5% of the ceiling); Laura's reason 2 has one too (five business days, so a one-day holiday slip is not a default; Q30-029). The cyclical factor is the design point of row 4
critique: A constitution with a referendum behind it; Laura's rule has no legislature

idea: Even a narrow clause has its way back stretched: about CHF 30bn of COVID spending was booked as extraordinary; the offset deadline moved to end-2035, with 2039 possible for "besondere, vom Bund nicht steuerbare Entwicklungen"; CHF 26.3bn was still outstanding at end-2025; only three episodes have been recognised as extraordinary (UBS 2008, COVID 2020-21, Ukraine 2022); a commentator calls the broad wording a possible gateway
sources: BBl 2022 2409 (FHG Art. 17e), https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/fga/2022/2409/de ; EFD, Bundesschulden, https://www.efd.admin.ch/de/bundesschulden ; Open Legal Commentary, Art. 126 FC, https://openlegalcommentary.ch/en/bv/art-126 (citing Stauffer 2001)
use: Rare use kept the Swiss rule credible, while the repair stage was where it bent. Laura's exits have no repair stage to stretch: a late deposit runs the same order on arrival (card Q34), and a default is restated on what was paid
critique: Laura has no debt to repay after an exit; the analogy is to the rule's shape, not its numbers

idea: Germany's court voided EUR 60bn of credit moved to a climate fund under the emergency clause: the clause needs a causal link between emergency and borrowing, and "impairments of the financial and economic situation fall outside the provision's scope of application if they are mere upswings and downswings as part of a cyclical economic trend"; "not every economic crisis situation constitutes an unusual emergency situation"; the longer the emergency, the fuller the justification must be
sources: Federal Constitutional Court (2023, Nov 15) Judgment, 2 BvF 1/22, https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Entscheidungen/EN/2023/11/fs20231115_2bvf000122en.html ; press release 101/2023, https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/EN/2023/bvg23-101.html
use: Table 3's "Never" column is this causal test written in advance: a missed deposit changes the range and 2033's payment, "Never: a sale"; a default changes payments and range, "Never: a forced sale"
critique: A court enforces Germany's clause; nothing enforces Laura's column but the adviser's word
verified: VERIFIED (press release in full; judgment in part, incl. para 151)

idea: Chile's structural balance rule, admired for credibility, began with no escape clause "to bolster credibility"; the cycle is removed by design (long-term copper price); yet the target changed in 2008, 2009, 2010 ("de facto suspended in 2010 because of the earthquake"), 2014 ("even though Chile did not undergo major economic perturbations") and twice in 2020; debt about 4% of GDP in 2007, about 40% in 2023; a clause and a 45% debt ceiling were added in 2022, "applicable only starting in 2026 to promote credibility"
sources: IMF (2011) WP/11/17, https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/2011/wp1117.pdf ; IMF (2021) Country Report 21/241, https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/cr/2021/english/1chlea2021005.pdf ; IMF (2023) Country Report 23/249, https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/cr/2023/english/1chlea2023004.pdf ; González, H. (2024) World Bank, https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/066f80bf77301b1f5933386d1c234a4c-0360012024/related/Hermann-Gonzalez-Fiscal-Councils-the-Chilean-experience-vf.pdf ; IDB (2013) Ten years, ten lessons, https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/The-Structural-Balance-Rule-in-Chile-Ten-Years-Ten-Lessons.pdf ; UDD CIES (2026) La regla fiscal en Chile, https://negocios.udd.cl/cies/files/2026/09/v2_080926_dp_rs_regla-fiscal.pdf
use: A rule with no named exit got exits improvised by whoever held the pen. l.17 names its exits before any shock, which is what Chile added in 2022
critique: Debt rose for many reasons (pandemic, social spending); the link to the missing clause is the sources' judgement, not a measured effect (gap 6). Store row H5-076 was UNVERIFIED and is now read at source
verified: VERIFIED in part (five sources agree on the absence of a clause and the target changes)

idea: A rule with no exit, rewritten in the crisis: Argentina's 1991 convertibility law gave "credible assurances of nonreversibility"; in 2001 the government announced a dollar-euro basket (14 Apr), passed Ley 25.445 (June) and a zero-deficit law (30 Jul); the measures were "perceived by the markets as desperate or impractical, and served to damage market confidence"; convertibility ended on 6 Jan 2002
sources: IMF Independent Evaluation Office (2004) The IMF and Argentina, 1991-2001, https://ieo.imf.org/-/media/ieo/files/evaluations/completed/07-28-2004-report-on-the-evaluation-of-the-role-of-the-imf-in-argentina-1991-2001/07292004report.pdf , and Appendix 9, https://www.imf.org/external/np/ieo/2004/arg/eng/pdf/app9.pdf ; Ley 25.445, https://www.argentina.gob.ar/normativa/nacional/ley-25445-67456/texto
use: Writing the exits before the storm is what lets l.17 say "A fall in the market is not one of them" without having to improvise in the fall
critique: A sovereign currency board under a debt crisis; nothing in Laura's plan can run out of reserves the way a currency board can

idea: People bind themselves "by removing certain options from the feasible set, by making them more costly or available only with a delay, and by insulating themselves from knowledge"; the devices "have to be set up ahead of time rather than being left to the discretionary control of the agent"
sources: Elster, J. (2000) Ulysses unbound, Cambridge University Press, sample chapter, https://assets.cambridge.org/97805216/62130/sample/9780521662130wsn01.pdf
use: The plan uses none of the four devices strongly before 2031: no option is removed, a sale is cheap and same-day, and the plan does not hide the market from her; it makes market news harmless instead (TNA l.15, "ignore price noise"). It is set up ahead of time (IPS submitted before the Jan 2027 purchase)
critique: Elster's subject is one person fighting a later self; Laura's plan is built for co-sponsors who must rely on it (Q7 row 10)

idea: Elster's five conditions for binding oneself (1979, pp. 37-47): (i) a decision now raises the chance of a later one; (ii) the act does not change the later options "in such a way that the new feasible set includes the old one"; (iii) it sets up "some causal process in the external world"; (iv) resisting now is easier than resisting later; (v) it is an act, not an omission
sources: Hubin, D.C. (1986) Of bindings and by-products: Elster on rationality, Philosophy & Public Affairs 15(1), https://www.oocities.org/hmelberg/elster/HUBIN86.HTM ; Elster, J. (1979) Ulysses and the sirens, Cambridge University Press (not read)
use: Keel inference: the Treasuries meet (i), (iii), (iv) and (v): they pay through an outside process (maturity) with no later decision, and buying in calm January 2027 is easier than holding firm in a crash. They fail (ii): after buying, selling restores her old options, less a sale's cost and the day's price. So the plan is carried by the assets, not bound by them
critique: Hubin argues (iv) and (v) are not necessary conditions; the verdict rests on (ii) and (iii) only
verified: UNVERIFIED at source for Elster 1979 (Hubin's paraphrase read)

idea: Personal rules rest on self-reputation, which "transforms lapses into precedents"; a "bright line" rule "admits no excuses" and makes "lapses more salient"; a contingent rule, "persevering except under very adverse circumstances", is harder to keep "when the veracity of excuses and ex post rationalizations is difficult to ascertain"
sources: Bénabou, R. & Tirole, J. (2004) Willpower and personal rules, Journal of Political Economy 112(4): 848-886, https://www.princeton.edu/~rbenabou/papers/JPE2004.pdf
use: l.17 is their contingent rule with excuses that can be checked: a bank record and a Treasury payment record. "A fall in the market is not one of them" is the bright line, so a sale in a fall would be a visible lapse, not a judgement call
critique: Their agent doubts her own willpower; the case never says Laura does, and the report must never imply it. The rule is for co-sponsors' reliance, not her self-control
verified: VERIFIED in part (introduction and sections on rules read)

idea: Defaults stick: under automatic enrolment one firm's 401(k) participation among new hires rose from 37% to 86%, and most stayed at the default contribution rate; inertia, not preference, explained it
sources: Madrian, B.C. & Shea, D.F. (2001) The power of suggestion, Quarterly Journal of Economics 116(4): 1149-1187, https://doi.org/10.1162/003355301753265543 ; NBER Reporter (2024, no. 3), https://www.nber.org/reporter/2024number3/influencing-retirement-savings-decisions-automatic-enrollment-and-related-tools ; U.S. Department of Labor CLEAR review, https://clear.dol.gov/study/power-suggestion-inertia-401k-participation-and-savings-behavior-madrian-shea-2001
use: Keel inference: Laura's plan runs on the same force: once the Treasuries are bought, doing nothing keeps the plan, and only three dated steps need anyone to act (Jan 2027, Jan 2028, before the 2031 meetings)
critique: One firm, employees not a client with an adviser; CLEAR rates the study's causal evidence low (a before-after comparison)
verified: VERIFIED in part (abstract, NBER Reporter, CLEAR)

idea: Self-binding directives (research only): experts agree they must specify in detail the circumstances for activation and for termination, criteria that can be "assessed reliably", a person of trust, a neutral party, "legal provisions stating clear criteria for the validity, content, activation and revocation", an expedited procedure and regular updates
sources: Scholten, M., et al. (2023) Implementation of self-binding directives: recommendations based on expert consensus and input by stakeholders in three European countries, World Psychiatry 22(2): 332-333, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10168143
use: The design lessons transfer without the setting: detailed activation (Table 3's "Act when"), termination (a late deposit runs the same order; payments restated), a named person ("Who"), a quick test (a date; five business days)
critique: Research only: medicine imagery is banned in the report (INSTRUCTIONS I85; EXPECTATIONS l.545; store H2-052 already notes the "rehab" reading Ray rejected)

idea: Dutch law (research only): self-binding directives are legally binding (since 2008; under the Wvggz from 1 Jan 2020) and "cannot be revoked in the circumstances for which they are written"; but uptake is very low and use rare, and the procedure takes over four weeks
sources: Scholten, M., van Melle, L. & Widdershoven, G. (2021) International Journal of Law and Psychiatry 76: 101699, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0160252721000285 ; van Melle, L., et al. (2023) BMC Medical Ethics 24: 38, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12910-023-00915-y
use: The crash is the circumstance l.17 is written for, and l.17 does not let it count; same structure. The low uptake warns that a rule too slow to use is not used: Table 3's tests are a date and a count of days
critique: Research only (row 30). Laura's rule has no legal force; the Dutch one does

idea: Those bound mostly want the binding (research only): 463 of 565 (82%) respondents with bipolar disorder endorsed self-binding directives, 65 (12%) rejected them; users in a systematic review prefer directives "revoked only when users are competent to consent"
sources: Gergel, T., et al. (2021) Lancet Psychiatry 8(7): 599-609, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8211565 ; Psychiatric Services (2023) systematic review, https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ps.202200003
use: Only as a check on the idea that binding is imposed: the people bound chose it, as Laura's plan is her choice made in calm
critique: Research only (row 30); a survey of patients, nothing to do with money

idea: Keel inference: Laura's two reasons are exits for when the plan cannot be carried out (no deposit to complete it; Treasuries that do not pay), not exits for when keeping it would be painful; so the literature's main worry (calling every bad year extraordinary, row 8; vague states, row 11; self-fulfilling triggers, row 13) has nothing to work on, and a market exit has no job to do (row 6)
sources: Rows 6, 8, 11, 13; IPS l.11, l.13, l.17; CANON A8, A34; SKELETON 3e ("the only two events that can remove a layer the payments rest on")
use: The literature's reason why "only these two" is enough: fiscal clauses exist because keeping a rule in a recession hurts; keeping Laura's in a crash costs the payments and the floor nothing. SKELETON 3e's one clause on "why only these two" now has its theory
critique: It holds for the payments and the floor; a crash before the 2031 move still lowers the top and her flexibility (Table 3 row 6), which the range rule absorbs, not an exit
note: Day 8 lead: the two reasons are exits for when the plan cannot be carried out, not for when keeping it hurts; theory under 3e's 'why only these two'.

idea: Keel inference: before 2031 nothing binds the plan in Elster's strict sense; the Treasuries carry it (it runs unless someone acts), the sentence names the only two acts that would be justified, and from the 2031 meetings co-sponsors make breaking it costly
use: Change the note "bound by the assets" to "carried by the assets, named by the sentence, bound from 2031 by her word". 3a can say the payments need no later decision, which is IPS l.13's meaning
critique: "Carried" is Keel's word, not a literature term; the report may use plain words only
note: Day 8 lead: carried by the Treasuries, named by the sentence, bound from 2031 by co-sponsors; 3a or 3e. Never 'Ulysses' in the report.

idea: Keel inference: IPS l.17 with Table 3 against twelve tests from rows 1-25: met 7 (few and set in advance; checkable; ordinary swings absorbed; not expectation-driven; change limited by "Never"; a way back for reason 1; one exit nameable to co-sponsors), partly 3 (outside the holder's control; who invokes; protection from widening), weak 2 before 2031 (a check on the invoker; a cost of reversal)
sources: Rows 1-25; Table 3; card Q34; CANON A34
use: Answers the question: on design l.17 is at the strict end of the practice read; its weakness is enforcement before 2031, which is Q7's "soft before 2031" seen from the fiscal side. 3e states it as a limit, adds no rule

idea: Keel inference: "owed, not owned". A foundation's unconditional pledge is a booked liability against a risky pool; a conditional one (matching, milestones) is not booked; a building set-aside is a book entry. Laura's floor is the reverse: the Treasury fund first (January 2028), the figure after (2031)

critique: Laura is not a foundation and is not under 4942; the contrast is about order, not law
note: Day 8 lead: 'owed, not owned' for 3d; never say foundations count pledges as owned.

idea: The oldest version of "before, trigger, after, with the reason": reflective thought runs "(i) a felt difficulty; (ii) its location and definition; (iii) suggestion of possible solution; (iv) development by reasoning of the bearings of the suggestion; (v) further observation and experiment leading to its acceptance or rejection"
sources: Dewey (1910), How We Think, ch. 6 "The Analysis of a Complete Act of Thought" (Mead Project, Brock University)
use: Claim 1's shape predates every rubric; the strongest moments have all five, step (v) above all: K (the dated curve test), T (the 27 Sep test, then the 29 Sep pricing), C (the bar of 30 Sep, then the runs)
critique: A philosopher's account of thinking, not a scoring rule; the page itself does not name book or year (the Mead Project's index does)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f, the oldest source for belief, test and after; its step (v), verification, is why each moment ends on a dated test (K curve, T 27 and 29 Sep runs, C the 30 Sep bar), all facts as in RANKING_5 and BLIND_POOL_3.

idea: What starts it: "the perplexity or problem", which in a new case "is likely to present itself at first as a shock ... of something queer, strange, funny, or disconcerting"; and what ends it: "The concluding and conclusive step is some kind of experimental corroboration, or verification, of the conjectural idea"
use: The trigger is a fact that surprised, told plainly (K: the ten cost more than $300,000 on 173 of 185 closes; T: readers who put the plan first still called it too timid); the reflection is worth most where it ends on a test, not an opinion
critique: Same
note: Mon 16 Nov: same Dewey chapter as row 1; the felt-difficulty trigger and step (v) verification are already inside row 1's five steps, so one Dewey row in the store.

idea: Reflection has three depths: on the content of a problem, on the process used to solve it, and on its premises; "Reflection on presuppositions is what we mean by critical reflection", because it questions "the justification for the very premises on which problems are posed"
sources: Mezirow, "How critical reflection triggers transformative learning", in Fostering Critical Reflection in Adulthood (University of Colorado course copy)
use: The three moments reach different depths, which the closing paragraph can use: K is process (how the ten were priced); T is premise (should fixed promises rest on shares at all?); C is premise (why one world fund at all?)
critique: Adult education theory; no scoring data; year not shown on the copy read
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f closing paragraph, the moments reach different depths (K process, T and C premise); adds Mezirow's content-process-premise split, which Q27's levels lack; year of the chapter still to be found before any citation.

idea: What sets it off: "Anomolies and dilemmas of which old ways of knowing cannot make sense" are "trigger events"; one becomes critically reflective "by challenging the established definition of a problem being addressed"
use: T's trigger is exactly this: readers who ranked the plan first still called it too timid, which the plan's own frame (payments first) could not answer without pricing the critics' view
critique: Personal transformation (divorce, job change) is the chapter's main case
note: Mon 16 Nov: same Mezirow chapter; the trigger-event idea adds little beyond Dewey's felt difficulty (row 1), and exactly overclaims for T, where the team priced the critics' view and kept its frame rather than redefining the problem.

idea: REFLECT's top level asks for "Exploration and critique of assumptions, values, beliefs, and/or biases, and the consequences of action (present and future)"; the dilemma is scored there for "multiple perspectives, exploring alternative explanations, and challenging assumptions"
sources: Wald, Borkan, Taylor, Anthony & Reis (2012), Academic Medicine 87(1), 41-50, Supplemental Digital Content (worked, scored example)
use: C: the copout scores at the top only if the objection is put as an alternative explanation with its reasons, and the team's own assumption (a world fund is the sensible default) is examined; T: "too timid" challenges the plan's central assumption from outside
critique: The SDC is one scored student narrative, not the whole rubric table; medical students' personal essays
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f copout, REFLECT credits the objection put as an alternative explanation and the team's own default examined, which matches BLIND_POOL_3 E1's before and after (VT a sensible default, then why it suits Laura); one scored example, not the rubric table.

idea: In REFLECT's own scored example, "The evidence for transformative learning is in the commitment to applying the understanding in the future": the writer is credited for what the lesson commits them to, not for the event
use: Each moment ends on the part of the plan it still governs (K: the completion rule; T: the floor and the order of claims; C: the world fund and the two reasons to change), which is the report's version of a commitment carried forward
critique: Personal commitments in medicine against a team's rule in a plan
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f closing paragraph, the credit goes to what the lesson commits the writer to, so each moment ends on the part of the plan it still governs (RANKING_5's own rule); one scored SDC example, so cite as an example, near Q27-006 (DEAL's last step).

idea: Reviewers of reflection assessment warn that assessors see only "interpretative descriptions" they cannot check: written reflections "do not allow assessors to verify information related to the reflections reported"; the "dependency on a person's interpretative description is a serious threat to the validity" of the assessment
sources: Koole, Dornan, Aper, Scherpbier, Valcke, Cohen-Schotanus & Derese (2011), BMC Medical Education 11, 104
use: Caplet's moments are unusual in being checkable: each carries a date and a register figure (173 of 185 closes; 0.8991 against 0.90; 3.2% of markets), so the judge can verify what most reflections only assert
critique: Medical education, individual learners
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f every moment; re-read at source today (assessors see only interpretative descriptions, a serious threat to validity; their guideline: objective information about the triggering situation to verify); Caplet's dated register figures answer the marker's main doubt.

idea: Their remedy: assess "generic process skills rather than the subjective content of reflection", and give assessors "information about the triggering situation"
sources: Koole et al. (2011), abstract and recommendations
use: Each moment states its trigger as a fact a judge can see (the dated curve; the blind readers' verdict; the objection on 5 Oct), so the process is judged, not the feelings; RANKING_5's "names a belief, the dated test" matches
critique: Advice to assessors, not to writers
note: Mon 16 Nov: Koole's remedy (process skills, objective information about the triggering situation) is the basis of row 7's use; quote re-read at source today; one Koole row.

idea: The same review notes that hindsight and limited introspection go undetected in written reflection, and that writing it takes "skills other than pure reflective skills"
use: Tell a reason found later as "what we understand now" (standing order 21; Q13 row 3), so a judge does not have to guess which reasons were held at the time
critique: Medical education; a review's warning drawn from earlier studies, not a new test with assessors
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f, research basis for standing order 21's rule that a reason found later is told as what the team understands now (Koole: hindsight and introspection bias go undetected; re-read at source today); evidence for an existing rule, not a new one.

idea: Readers average, writers add: "perceivers' judgments show a weighted averaging pattern, which results in less favorable evaluations when mildly favorable information is added to highly favorable information"; across seven studies "presenters do not anticipate this averaging pattern"; in study 1 presenters paid more to make a bundle look costlier and "cheapened its value" in evaluators' eyes
sources: Weaver, Garcia & Schwarz (2012), Journal of Consumer Research 39(3), 445-460
use: The strongest support for claim 2: a fourth, weaker moment (buying it scored 17.7 against 20.7-21.7) would lower the judge's view of the three, not add to it; RANKING_5's move of buying it to 2.5 is what this predicts
critique: Products and gift bundles, not essays; the averaging holds for items judged together as one set
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (VTechWorks record, 16 Nov 2026; full PDF listed there, not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f set, evidence for three moments and for moving buying it to 2.5 (17.7 against 20.7-21.7, RANKING_5); abstract re-read today (weighted averaging, presenters do not anticipate, seven studies), full paper unread so S 3; holds for items judged together as one set.

idea: The "rule of three" in persuasion is contested: Shu and Carlson (2014) found three claims beat two or four when the audience knows it is being sold to ("Including a fourth claim was shown to increase skepticism"), but a test with 198 business students found four positive claims liked more than two, and the number of claims did not move scepticism
sources: Nordmo & Selart (2015), Frontiers in Psychology 6, 1324 (their report of Shu & Carlson 2014, Journal of Marketing, and their Experiment 1)
use: Do not defend "three moments" with a magic number; three is right for 3f because 600 words hold three moments told with before, test and after, and Wharton names no count
critique: Advertising claims about a company, not a reflection; Shu and Carlson's own paper could not be opened (robots block), so its figures are second-hand
verified: VERIFIED for Nordmo & Selart (PMC full text, 16 Nov 2026); UNVERIFIED for Shu & Carlson's own figures (site blocks fetching)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard only, never defend three moments with a rule of three; Nordmo and Selart re-read today (198 students; four claims liked more than two; claim count did not move scepticism) but Shu and Carlson second-hand, so S 3.

idea: The three moments already cover all six words of Wharton's criterion: research (K: every close priced; C: four alternatives tested against a bar), collaboration and disagreement (C: the teammate's objection; T: outside readers' verdict), decision-making (all three), uncertainty (K: the fills were timing; T: the price of the critics' view; C: which fund does better is unknown), learning (all three); a fourth moment adds no word
sources: Keel inference on `experience/BLIND_POOL_3.md` fact sheets E1, E3, E4, E6 and Wharton's criterion (`WHARTON_NORTH_STAR.md` section 0)
use: Claim 2's practical test: depth is affordable because breadth is already met; the closing paragraph can say which recommendation each moment changed or held without listing the five words
critique: Inference, not a finding; "collaboration" rests on roles the record supports, never names (SKELETON 3f)
verified: Keel inference on VERIFIED inputs (fact sheets and filed criterion read, 16 Nov 2026)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f, the practical case for depth over breadth; the six words match WHARTON_NORTH_STAR l.145-146 exactly, but the use column then says five words: say six (the Team Reflection paragraph's own list, l.129-130, has five, without uncertainty); Keel inference, so S 3.

idea: The pratfall at source: 48 male students heard a taped quiz contestant (92% right, or 30% right); a spilled coffee made the able one the most liked of all (composite 30.2) and the average one the least liked (-2.5); ability x blunder F(1,40) = 10.33, p < .01; the blunder alone did nothing
use: Claim 3 holds only after competence is shown: 3f comes last, after Sections 2 and 3 have shown the plan working, which is where an admission helps; an admission in the report's opening would cost
critique: Liking, not trust or credibility; one tape, 48 men, 1966; a clumsy accident, not a wrong judgement; the store's version (H5-015) was second-hand
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f placement, an admission helps only after competence is shown, so 3f last; re-read at source today (48 male sophomores, 30.2 and -2.5, F=10.33 df 1/40, the pratfall alone insignificant); replaces H5-015's second-hand version; liking, not credibility.

idea: The authors' account: an able person "may be viewed as superhuman and, therefore, distant", and the blunder makes him "more human and more approachable"; for an average person it "should lower his attractiveness"
use: 2.5: the mis-click is a pratfall of this kind: one harmless slip, told once in a clause after the curve check has shown care, reads as human; told as a pattern or early in the report it reads as the average contestant's spill
critique: Speculative explanation offered by the authors, not tested
note: Mon 16 Nov: the authors' untested explanation of row 13 (quotes re-read today); its 2.5 use is weak, since the mis-click is told without attribution (Book 18), so it is not a competent person's blunder; harmless is not in the record (the order was cancelled, then re-placed at 15:22).

idea: Owning up to a mistake of skill repairs trust better than denying it; for a mistake of honesty it is the reverse: rated integrity after a competence lapse 5.32 with an apology against 4.27 with a denial, after an integrity lapse 2.73 against 4.39 (200 students, a filmed job applicant)
sources: Kim, Ferrin, Cooper & Dirks (2004), Journal of Applied Psychology 89(1), 104-118, Study 1
use: T: the first plan's failure is a lapse of judgement about markets, a competence matter, so saying it plainly helps; K: the headline "fits inside $300,000" dropped is the same kind. Nothing in the record is an integrity lapse, so the reverse case does not arise
critique: Job candidates on video, not teams' reports; trust in a person, not a plan; the "apology" admitted fault for a tax error
verified: VERIFIED (accepted manuscript read, SMU repository, 16 Nov 2026)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f T, which kind of mistake, not whether; checked at source today, Table 3 Study 1 (N=200, 7-point scale): perceived integrity 5.32 apology against 4.27 denial after a competence lapse, 2.73 against 4.39 after an integrity lapse; say rated integrity, since rated competence barely moved (4.56 against 4.46).

idea: The reason, in the authors' words: people "weigh positive information about competence more heavily than negative information about competence", and "negative information about others' integrity more heavily than positive information about integrity"
use: Why one admitted slip does not sink a team that shows skill everywhere else in the report; and why nothing in 3f may look like hiding (an integrity cue outweighs any number of good ones)
critique: Asymmetry inferred from earlier schema research, tested here only indirectly
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard, why one owned slip does not sink a report that shows skill elsewhere and why nothing may look like hiding; the reason for row 15, kept as a separate guard.

idea: When later evidence settles the matter, the wrong response costs more: evidence of guilt hurt denials against apologies, evidence of innocence hurt apologies; "trust may be further damaged if the response is ultimately found to be untrue" (444 students, Study 2)
use: Every admission in 3f must match the dated record a judge can check against the IPS and TNA: the copout told as a decision kept, not as a mistake; the fills as luck, not as a lapse or a skill. Over-admitting is also a mismatch
critique: Lab vignettes with a State Board ruling as the evidence
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard, every admission must match the dated record a judge can check (the copout a decision kept, the fills told as timing, as E1 and E3 say); Study 2 N=444 confirmed at source today.

idea: Firms whose shareholder letters blamed bad results on their own decisions had higher share prices a year later than firms that blamed outside forces: 14 companies in three industries, 21 years of letters; the five most self-blaming beat the five most other-blaming by "14 percent to 19 percent" in a hypothetical portfolio
sources: Lee, Peterson & Tiedens (2004), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, as reported by the University of Michigan (5 Apr 2004)
use: Investors are the audience Wharton's judges stand in for: an admission tied to the writer's own decision (T: the first plan dropped after the team's own test) reads as control, not weakness
critique: Read through the university's release, not the paper; 14 firms; correlation, not cause; the 14-19% is a paper portfolio
verified: VERIFIED for the release (read at source, 16 Nov 2026); the paper's own tables UNVERIFIED (not reached)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f T, owning the first plan's drop as the team's own decision reads as control; release re-read today (14 firms, three industries, 21 years, 14 to 19 percent), paper unread, correlation only, so S 3.

idea: The mechanism, in the lead author's words: "Claiming personal responsibility for negative events makes the organization appear more in control"; external attributions "did not positively predict future outcomes"
sources: Lee et al. (2004), via the University of Michigan release
use: Control is the quality a co-sponsor and a judge are buying; each moment's admission ends on the rule the team then controlled (completion rule, floor, bar for switching)
critique: Same as above
note: Mon 16 Nov: the release's mechanism quote (more in control; outside attributions did not predict outcomes), re-read today; same source and use as row 18, so one row carries both.

idea: In performance reviews, telling your own mistake first helps: managers rated employees who disclosed a prior mistake before the manager learned of it ("stealing thunder") significantly better; the result held "after controlling for mistake severity"; and with disclosure, "acceptance of responsibility resulted in significantly better performance evaluations than blaming others"
sources: Guchait, Guzzo, Wang & Abbott (2023), International Journal of Hospitality Management 115, 103582 (three between-subjects experiments with hospitality managers)
use: The closest test to Wharton's setting found: an evaluator scoring someone's performance. The report discloses before the judge could find it in the IPS (l.9's switch; the TNA's frozen notes): T tells the first plan's failure in its own words and owns it
critique: Hospitality employees, not written reports; sample sizes not on the record page
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (PolyU research portal, 16 Nov 2026; full text not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f T; abstract only (re-read today), so S 3; stealing thunder needs a risk the evaluator learns it elsewhere, and the 27 Sep failure appears nowhere a judge could find it while IPS l.9 already tells the switch, so use only the second finding: accepting responsibility beat blaming others.

idea: Negative claims are read harder: "negative claims are weighted more heavily, given more attention, and elaborated on more thoroughly, than positive claims"; negative persuasion raised scepticism far more (F = 26.31, p < 0.001)
use: Each admission in 3f (the first plan's 3.2% misses; the dropped headline) will be read more closely than any boast, so its figure and date must be exact and register-sourced
critique: Their negatives were claims against a company, not a writer's admissions about itself
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard, each admission's figure must be exact and register-sourced; re-read today (F=26.31 is negative against positive persuasion on scepticism), but the paper's degrees of freedom do not fit N=198 and its negatives were claims against a company, not self-admissions.

idea: A small flaw added after praise can raise a product's appeal ("a small dose of negative information"), but only when the reader processes "effortlessly rather than effortfully" and the negative "follows rather than precedes positive information" (four studies, lab and field)
sources: Ein-Gar, Shiv & Tormala (2012), Journal of Consumer Research 38(5), 846-859
use: Where claim 3's shortcut fails: a Wharton judge reading a 12-page report against a rubric reads effortfully, so a token flaw earns nothing; only an admission that carries its cost and its consequence does (rows on Kim et al. and Lee et al.)
critique: Consumer products, not reports; the abstract implies, but does not show, the effect vanishing under effort
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (IDEAS/RePEc, 16 Nov 2026; full text not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard, a token flaw earns nothing from an effortful reader such as a judge; abstract only, consumer products, so S 3.

idea: Self-criticism can be a performance too: in assessed reflection "self-criticism and self-praise are two sides of the same coin", and "Both approaches can be used by students in reflective writing to performance manage"; the belief that "reflections that engage in greater self-criticism are more honest" is the target
sources: McGarr & O'Gallchoir (2020), Teaching in Higher Education 25(7), 902-908
use: Where claim 3 fails: an admission chosen to look humble reads as performance. The tell is purpose: each admission in 3f must be the cause of a rule still in the plan (K: the completion rule; T: the floor), never a confession for its own sake
critique: A short critical essay, not a test with readers
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (University of Limerick record, 16 Nov 2026; full text not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f guard, an admission chosen to look humble reads as performance, so each must be the cause of a rule still in the plan; abstract only, an essay with no readers tested, so S 3.

idea: Pension plan sponsors judge by outcome: 3,400 sponsors, 1994-2003, hired managers after large excess returns that did not continue; fired managers would have earned about what their replacements did
use: Kills claim 4 as a description: investors mostly judge by results; the reflection that names luck and the test is the rare one
critique: Abstract only; US institutional sponsors
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (IDEAS/RePEc abstract read 16 Nov 2026; full text not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f and 2.5, most institutional investors judge by results, the setting for row 31's contrast; abstract only, so S 3; near Q13-006 (outcome bias in the lab) and H9-175, but the first investor record in the store.

idea: The professionals who pick fund managers for pension plans weigh "soft" factors above past returns: "it is mainly the fund managers' non-performance attributes that drive recommendations"; a move from bottom to top on soft factors brought slightly under six extra recommendations a year, on past returns about half of one
sources: Jenkinson, Jones & Martinez (2016), Journal of Finance (accepted manuscript dated Sep 2014; Greenwich Associates surveys 1999-2011; consultants with about 91% of the US market, funds of about $3 trillion)
use: Claim 4's real-world test: the investors who say they judge the manager and the process, not the last return, do exactly that
critique: "Soft factors" are the consultants' own survey ratings of the manager, not a measure of process quality
verified: VERIFIED (accepted manuscript read, all but the last 6% of its text, Berkeley course copy, 16 Nov 2026)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f C context; re-read at source today (non-performance attributes drive recommendations; slightly under six extra recommendations against half of one; 91% of the US consulting market, about $3 trillion); the paper itself says its soft investment factors relate to the investment process.

idea: And the process judges did not pick better: recommended funds returned 6.31% a year net against 7.43% for the rest, equal-weighted (-1.12%; three-factor alpha -0.97%, four-factor -0.92%, significant at 5%); value-weighted, no significant difference; "We find no evidence that these recommendations add value"
use: Judging by process is right only when the process is the kind that can be checked against a dated record; the copout moment shows a bar written before any number ran, which is checkable, unlike a manager's "philosophy"
critique: US active equity only; consultants may add value elsewhere (asset allocation, fees)
note: Mon 16 Nov: checked at source today: 6.31% against 7.43% (-1.12%) is equal-weighted only and, in the authors' words, fund scale seems fully to explain it (it disappears with size controls); value-weighted, no significant gap; the paper finds recommendations in general add no value and never tests process-based picks against performance-based ones; never say judging by process cost 1.12% a year.

idea: Pension money moved by plan sponsors went the wrong way: over 80,000 yearly observations, 1984-2007, products that received contributions then underperformed products that lost money, a shortfall of $56.2 billion over 22 one-year periods and "-$170.2 billion" on five-year windows, before trading costs; "Plan sponsors could have saved hundreds of billions of dollars in assets had they simply stayed the course"
sources: Stewart, Neumann, Knittel & Heisler (2009), Financial Analysts Journal 65(6), 34-51
use: C and the IPS's "only two reasons" (l.17): the copout objection asked for a switch with no new evidence; a plan that changes only for a missed deposit or a Treasury default cannot make the sponsors' mistake. One sentence at most, as what the team understands now (never as the reason on 5 Oct)
critique: US institutional products; the abstract does not show that sponsors chased past returns, only that new money went to later losers
verified: VERIFIED at abstract level (IDEAS/RePEc, 16 Nov 2026; full text not read)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f C, at most one sentence on what switching on returns costs investors, told as what the team understands now (RANKING_5); abstract only, and it shows new money went to later losers, not that sponsors chased returns, so S 3.

idea: Judging only by process has its own failure: process accountability "can readily ossify into bureaucratic rituals and mutual backscratching"; judging only by outcome breeds "risk-averse consensus forecasts" and "escalating commitment to initially off-base forecasts"; Tetlock and Mellers favour "experimenting with process-outcome hybrids" that weigh "rigor and accuracy"
sources: Tetlock & Mellers (2011), "Structuring accountability systems in organizations", in National Research Council, Intelligence Analysis: Behavioral and Social Scientific Foundations, pp. 249-270
use: Claim 4 changed: a reflection is judged on both, a dated process and an honest result. C passes both (a bar set first, then the runs); K names the result that was luck; T prices the outcome the critics wanted
critique: Written for intelligence agencies; a framework, with no new data of its own
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f, claim 4 changed to a hybrid of a dated process and an honest result; quotes re-read at source today (ossify into bureaucratic rituals; process-outcome hybrids; rigor and accuracy).

idea: Outcome judging, properly done, protects dissent: it "sends a much-needed signal to beleaguered dissenters"; but "a large body of work shows how easily outcome-accountability systems can be corrupted" (Heinz managers shifting shipments to hit targets)
use: C: the teammate who called one world fund "a copout" is the dissenter, never the fool (RANKING_5); the bar of 30 Sep was already in place when the objection came on 5 Oct, so the answer rested on a standard set before anyone's view was known, never told as a test written to settle the objection (dates in `experience/BLIND_POOL_3.md` E1)
critique: Same
note: Mon 16 Nov: quotes re-read today, but the source says outcome accountability protects dissenters by judging accuracy, while C was settled by a process bar set before the objection; keep the moment's guard (the teammate never the fool, bar of 30 Sep before the 5 Oct objection, both E1) and drop the claim that this finding supports it.

idea: The lab result Tetlock and Mellers cite for outcome pressure feeding "escalating commitment" (Simonson and Staw 1992) failed to replicate: a two-study replication found "no effects of accountability", the second study with a stronger manipulation and a larger sample
sources: FORRT Replication Atlas (FLoRA) entry for Simonson & Staw (1992), Journal of Applied Psychology 77(4), 419-426, citing Schulz-Hardt et al. (2021), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied
use: A guard on how claim 4 is argued: the case for telling process rests on Wharton's instruction and on the investor record (Goyal and Wahal; Jenkinson et al.), not on the escalation experiments, which do not replicate
critique: The atlas gives no sample sizes and does not split process from outcome accountability; the replication itself was not opened
verified: VERIFIED for the atlas entry (read at source, 16 Nov 2026); the replication paper UNVERIFIED (not opened)
note: Mon 16 Nov: guard on how claim 4 is argued, never rest it on escalation experiments; atlas re-read today (outcome recorded failed; no effects of accountability; a stronger manipulation and larger sample), replication itself unopened, so S 3.

idea: Wharton tells its own evaluators to judge process, twice: the Final Report instructions say "WInS gains and losses are not treated as evidence of the quality of the strategy", and the Guide says a strategy "should not be rewritten simply because markets move or hindsight reveals a different outcome"
sources: Wharton Global Youth Program (2026), Final Report instructions l.146 and Competition Guide p.5 (filed texts; context, never a reference)
use: Claim 4's aha: most investors judge by outcome (Goyal and Wahal), but this one audience is instructed not to, so a reflection that names luck and the dated test meets the reader on its own terms. K: the fills near the cheapest close are told as timing
critique: Wharton's words bind the judges' scoring, not their instincts; outcome bias survives instructions (card Q13 row 6)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f K and 2.5 aha beside row 24; both quotes match WHARTON_NORTH_STAR (l.143-144 criterion; l.197-198 Guide p.5), but only the first is addressed to evaluators, the Guide line tells teams not to rewrite, so drop twice and tells its evaluators for the pair; near H9-175 (Guide p.3), this row is the stronger current wording.

idea: Wharton credits change that comes from learning and bars change that comes from results: "The strategy may evolve as you learn more" (Guide p.2) against "you may not redesign your strategy after observing the results" (p.5)
sources: Wharton Global Youth Program (2026), Competition Guide pp. 2 and 5 (filed text; context)
use: All three moments changed or held the plan before any order (K, 28-29 Sep; T, 27-29 Sep; C, 30 Sep-5 Oct), so each is the change Wharton invites, not the one it bars; say the date, because the date is what makes it learning
critique: p.5's half is already card Q27 row 4; the pairing with p.2 is the new point
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3f closing paragraph, learning not results, all three moments dated before any order (E1, E3, E4, E6); fix the page: may evolve as you learn more is Guide p.1, not p.2 (filed Guide text), and it is not in WHARTON_NORTH_STAR; p.5's half is Q27-004 and quoted accurately.

idea: Schon in his own words: reflection in action "is closely tied to the experience of surprise"; "When performance leads to surprise-pleasant or unpleasant-the designer may respond by reflection in action", "reframing the problematic design situation in such a way as to redefine, interactively, both means and ends"; reflection on action is "pausing to think back over what she has done"
sources: Schon, interviewed by J. L. Bennett, "Reflective conversation with materials", ch. 9 in Winograd (Ed.), Bringing Design to Software (1996), Stanford HCI copy
use: A surprise can be pleasant: K's surprise was unpleasant (the ten did not fit on 173 of 185 closes); T's was a pleasant surprise with a sting (first place, "too timid"); both reframed means and ends (the 2028 deposit's first job; the floor's size priced against the critics' view). 3f is reflection on action, told after the fact, so reasons found later are labelled as now

idea: Speaker control is what turns a conditional into a promise: "the speaker of an inducement is normally seen to have control over the consequent event", and people drew "many more conditional inferences of all kinds for high control than for low control conditionals" (Evans and Twyman-Musgrove 1998); "Crucially, if q is a potential action of the speaker, then it is a promise; but if q is not a potential action of the speaker, then it is a tip", and "promises tend to be perceived as pragmatically 'stronger' than tips" (Haigh et al. 2011)
sources: Evans and Twyman-Musgrove (1998), Cognition 69(1); Haigh, Stewart, Wood and Connell (2011), Acta Psychologica 136(3)
use: This is why the RBA's forecast became a promise while a weather forecast never does: the RBA sets the rate it was forecasting. Laura sets her own contribution, so co-sponsors will hear her figure as a promise however she phrases it. It settles claim 2: a co-sponsor hears it as Odyssean. Judge's note
critique: Lab conditionals ("if you do p, I will do q"), not dollar ranges
verified: VERIFIED (Evans: abstract read at source on PubMed; Haigh et al.: author's copy read at source, 16 Nov 2026)
note: Mon 16 Nov: 3c and 3d, the mechanism from the psychology of reasoning: a conditional about the speaker's own action is heard as a promise; it bridges central banks to Laura, whose contribution is her own act; Evans read in abstract only.

idea: Florida let a printed pledge die with its donor: two $50,000 pledges signed in 1968 on a card reading "In consideration of and to induce the subscriptions of others, I (We) promise to pay"; $20,000 paid; the donor died on 18 Nov 1969 with $80,000 unpaid; the hospital's claim failed: "A mere gratuitous promise of a future gift, lacking consideration, is simply unenforceable as a nudum pactum"; "To ascribe consideration where there is none ... is to approve fiction"

idea: Even a binding gift in Taiwan gives only the gift: a gift is a contract the recipient accepts (art. 406, 「他方允受之契約」); where it cannot be withdrawn (notarised, or for a moral duty, art. 408 para 2), the recipient may claim the gift, or its value if the giver's fault made delivery impossible, but 「不得請求遲延利息或其他不履行之損害賠償」 (no interest for delay and no other damages) (art. 409 para 2); art. 407 is deleted

idea: Black Mountain College (North Carolina, 1933-1957), the best-known US arts community, had no endowment and raised its running money year by year
sources: "Black Mountain College: Open Form in American Education", RSA Journal (University of Turin), 2017, https://ojs.unito.it/index.php/rsajournal/article/download/8570/7090/27987 (accessed 9 Nov 2026): "There was no endowment, and the college had to annually raise funds for its own continuance"; a section titled "The Illusion of Self-Support" says it believed it "could survive financially on a year-by-year basis without an endowment or other reliable yearly source of income"

idea: Black Mountain ended in debt from running costs: loans secured on its land and unpaid salaries, while students fell to 9

Black Mountain College Museum, https://www.blackmountaincollege.org/bmc_idea_and_place/: land leased or sold, and "The money earned helped settle debts ... primarily paying off loans and back salary owed to faculty". Enrolment "35 students by 1953, then to 15, then to 9": book excerpt at https://www.appalachianhistory.net/2014/11/book-excerpt-black-mountain-college.html (all accessed 9 Nov 2026)

The NC State Archives finding aid dates the closure to 1956 ("student enrollment and available funds dwindled until the college was forced to close in 1956", http://appx.archives.ncdcr.gov/findingaids/PC_1580_Black_Mountain_College__.html), the RSA article to spring 1957
