idea: Raising the reserve after the building opens rarely works: "Continuing capital campaigns with the intention of raising reserve money or start-up funds after the building opens is often an exercise in futility"; campaign goals miss "the 'buckets of money' beyond project costs"
sources: Katie Oman, "Toward Sustainable Cultural Infrastructure", Grantmakers in the Arts, https://www.giarts.org/article/toward-sustainable-cultural-infrastructure (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The case already puts the reserve first ("before making the first operating payment or contributing to the facility", case p.3); Caplet's ladder is bought in 2027, six years earlier
critique: A funder's practice essay, not a study
note: Same GIA article and 'exercise in futility' quote as Q11b-025, which is fuller (this row names the author, Katie Oman).

idea: Reserves come before buildings: "Building working capital and creating operating reserves should be an organization's first capitalization priority"; groups that cannot raise money "over and above operating costs" "should not take on building ownership"
sources: Nonprofit Finance Fund and Helicon Collaborative, "Critical Steps Toward Capital Health in the Cultural Sector" (2014), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/critical-steps-toward-capital-health-cultural-sector.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The order of Caplet's plan matches the field's advice: running money (the ladder) first, building money (the floor and the shares) second
critique: Written for US arts groups that own buildings; Laura contributes money, she does not own the facility
note: Landed (3a): reserves before buildings, the case's order and Caplet's.

idea: Money not held apart gets spent on deficits: "Capital is episodic; revenue is forever"; capital is "typically not segregated from regular operating revenue"; and "capital, regardless of the purpose for which it is intended, will be used to cover structural operating deficits"
sources: Nonprofit Finance Fund, "Case for Change Capital in the Arts" (2011), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/Case-for-Change-Captial-In-the-Arts.pdf; Brown and Nacht, "Lessons Learned about Change Capital in the Arts" (2014, evaluation of NFF's $15m Leading for the Future initiative), https://www.giarts.org/sites/default/files/lessons-learned-about-change-capital-arts-reflections-four-year-evaluation.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The kept half protects only while it is named and held apart from running costs
critique: US arts groups' own capital, not a donor's private money
clash: no (the IPS names what the kept half is for: overruns, the Taiwan dollar, a co-sponsor falling short)
note: Unsegregated capital gets spent on deficits, so the kept half protects only while named and held apart, as the IPS names it; carries Q11b-024.

idea: Deficits often arrive after the opening: NFF warns of being "house rich and cash poor", with surpluses during a campaign followed by deficits after completion; Kresge-backed campaigns added reserves to their goals
sources: NFF, "Four Planning Considerations for Every Capital Project" (2018), https://nff.org/insights/four-planning-considerations-for-every-capital-project/; Francis, A. & Johnson, C. (2015) "Funding the extraordinary", Nonprofit Finance Fund, for the Kresge Foundation (REFERENCES_APA row 58), https://kresge.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Funding-the-Extraordinary-Final-NFF-Report.pdf: 36 grants 2010-2012; COCA added $3.9M to its campaign goal for operating reserves, building reserves and endowment; the East Bay Center for the Performing Arts had a structural deficit after its campaign (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Co-sponsors who know the field will look first for the running money; Laura's is already bought
critique: US cases
note: Same NFF report for Kresge and the same $3.9M COCA example as Q11b-023; the 'house rich and cash poor' line can travel with it.

idea: In ordinary years a third or more of US arts groups run a deficit: 34% (2018), 35%, 33%, 24% (2021), 37%, 41%, 41% (2024), 34% (2025, preliminary); average working capital went from 8.6 months (2018) to a 16.4 peak (2021) and back to 9.9 (2025)
sources: SMU DataArts, National Trends 2026 data tables, https://culturaldata.org/national-trends/national-trends-2026/data-tables; National Trends 2025, https://www.culturaldata.org/national-trends/national-trends-2025: 44% ran a deficit in 2024; median working capital fell from 6.75 months (2021) to 4.25 months (2024) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Deficits are ordinary, so founder money is most useful as running money that cannot shrink
critique: The two reports give different 2024 deficit shares (41% and 44%): different data vintages; averages are pulled up by large museums (row 13)
note: Two data vintages disagree on 2024 (41% and 44%); quote one dated figure with its source.

idea: The typical arts group holds very little: in 2019 the average was 5 months of working capital but the median only 1.5 months; dance groups about two weeks, art museums about 11 months
sources: SMU DataArts, "Working Capital" report and press release, https://culturaldata.org/reports/working-capital (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Laura's ten payments, bought ahead, hold ten years of her $50,000 commitment from 2033: a different scale from the field's 1.5 months (Keel arithmetic; her payments are not the residency's whole budget)
critique: Data before 2020; working capital is not the same thing as a dated reserve
note: The typical arts group holds about 1.5 months of working capital while Laura's commitment is bought a decade ahead (say it is her $50,000, not the whole budget).

idea: Thin reserves and thin margins predict closure: the Tuckman-Chang measures "show substantial promise for predicting the closure" of some arts nonprofits, were the best predictor of distress for performing arts groups, and predicted survival through the Great Recession
sources: Hager (2001), Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, "Financial Vulnerability among Arts Organizations: A Test of the Tuckman-Chang Measures", https://consensus.app/papers/details/7a00f4aa74965de9a88f7d58762de7a8/; Tevel and others (2014), Voluntas, https://consensus.app/papers/details/5cccadc22da35a09a32a0a75dcd179fe/ (implications for "surplus accumulation"); Graves and others (2023), https://consensus.app/papers/details/d203912fe25a5ffc9a059a28637b2e55/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Academic support for changing claim 1 to "thin reserves and thin margins"
critique: Abstracts only; Hager finds the measures work for some arts types, not all; that the measures are equity, revenue concentration, administrative costs and operating margin is Keel's description, not quoted from the abstracts
note: Academic support that thin reserves and margins predict closure; abstracts only.

idea: Depending on grants is the danger, more than having few sources: "Greater vulnerability is associated with dependence on grant funding, not overall concentration"
sources: Green and others (2021), Voluntas (UK charities), https://consensus.app/papers/details/f90495ee1066578098b3289a9cf391e2/ (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Taipei's public residencies run 71-86% on government grants (row 32); Laura's prepaid money is not a grant that can be cut
critique: UK charities in all fields
note: Dependence on grants, not having few sources, predicts vulnerability; Laura's money is not a grant that can be cut.

idea: One-founder cultural institutions are fragile: private art museums that closed had been open a median of 10 years; closure was "usually related to financial difficulties, rather than the founder's death"; staying open "usually requires either ongoing financial contributions of their founders, or the establishment of a large endowment"
sources: Velthuis and Gera, "The fragility of cultural philanthropy: why private art museums close", International Journal of Cultural Policy 31(6) 805-818 (2025; online 2024), full text https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/251502052/The_fragility_of_cultural_philanthropy.pdf; Velthuis and others, Beyond the Global Boom (2023), https://privatemuseumresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Private-Museum-Report_UvA_Beyond-the-Global-Boom_2023.pdf and https://privatemuseumresearch.org/report (76 closed, against 446 open) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The closest reference class for a founder-led residency: Laura's ten prepaid years cover the window in which these closed, without depending on her later income
critique: Collectors' museums, far bigger and richer; a median, not a rule; Laura's commitment ends in 2042 and the case says nothing about the years after
verified: VERIFIED (full-text PDF excerpts; report and site)
clash: no (the case fixes ten payments; note only that 2043 on is outside the plan)
note: Fri 20 Nov, attack day (ATTACKS.md D20; campaign 9, professor 16, plain 9): museums "that closed had been open a median of ten years", never "usually close within ten years"; never in 3d.

idea: UK museums close at about 1% a year (2% in the austerity years), are much more likely to close in their first 10 years, and privately run ones had the highest closure rate (37%)
sources: Museums Association, "What causes a museum to close?", Museums Journal, 20 Apr 2026, https://www.museumsassociation.org/museums-journal/analysis/2026/04/what-causes-a-museum-to-close/, reporting the Mapping Museums Lab study of 2000-2025 (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: The first decade is the dangerous one, which is the decade Laura's payments cover
critique: Museums, not residencies; the study's own report was not read
verified: UNVERIFIED at the study (trade press report read)
where: This run: search excerpt of the article
note: UK first-decade closure risk, read in trade press only; use only beside Q9-016.

idea: US residencies are financially weaker than other arts groups: 25-29% earned income and 4-13% public funding; about 500 US residencies; "It's not really about rational financial planning; it's about believing in these artists and risking everything"
sources: Mapping Residencies, New York (2013), http://mappingresidencies.org/mr-pdf/mr1_ny_en.pdf, citing the Alliance of Artists Communities, "From Surviving to Thriving: Sustaining Artist Residencies" (2012) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A residency has little earned income to fall back on, so founder money and gifts carry it
critique: The Alliance report is members-only and was not read
verified: VERIFIED that Mapping Residencies says it; UNVERIFIED at the Alliance report
note: US residencies earn little of their own income; the Alliance report itself was not read.

idea: Yaddo (founded 1900) pays about 57% of its running costs from its endowment, which is about 65% shares; its cash covers under 3 months
sources: The Corporation of Yaddo, audited financial statements 2025, https://yaddo.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/The-Corporation-of-Yaddo-2025-FS-Final.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026): expenses $4,695,285; endowment appropriated for spending $2,289,342 plus a board-designated draw of $377,610; investments $39,324,300 (equity securities $25.4M); cash $1,052,062; spending rule 5% of a 12-quarter average; its "ability to meet its cash needs is dependent on continued contributions and investment market performance"
use: The residencies that last are carried by large endowments that rise and fall with markets; Laura's operating money is the opposite, fixed and dated
critique: Keel arithmetic: ($2,289,342 + $377,610) / $4,695,285 = 57% (2024: 55%); $25.4M / $39.3M = 65%; cash about 2.7 months of 2025 expenses. Yaddo is meant to last forever; Laura's commitment is ten years
note: Yaddo's running budget leans on a share-heavy endowment, the opposite of Laura's fixed, dated money.

idea: Yaddo nearly ended before its first guest: after Spencer Trask died in 1909 "the Trasks' financial investments depreciated the following year, jeopardizing Yaddo's future"; Katrina Trask closed the mansion in 1916 "to conserve what was left of the endowment"; the first guests came in 1926, 26 years after the founding corporation
sources: New York Public Library, Yaddo Records finding aid, https://www.nypl.org/sites/default/files/archivalcollections/pdf/yaddo.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A founder's own investments falling is exactly what Caplet's plan keeps away from the payments: no payment depends on a share price
critique: 1910s; the finding aid does not say what the Trasks' investments were
note: Top-40: Yaddo nearly closed before its first guest when its founders' investments fell, the risk the plan keeps away from the payments.

idea: MacDowell (1907) lasted because its founder kept raising running money: Marian MacDowell funded it "through a series of piano recitals and personal appeals" and gave lecture-recitals until her death in 1956; its director made "frequent trips to New York City to fund increasing operating expenses"; an endowment drive began in 1937; it has closed only twice (after the 1938 hurricane and in 2020)
sources: Library of Congress, MacDowell Colony records finding aid, https://findingaids.loc.gov/repositories/19/resources/2205 and http://hdl.loc.gov/loc.mss/eadmss.ms996002; https://www.macdowell.org/about; annual reports 2019 and 2020, https://www.macdowell.org/assets/media-center/newsletters/documents/2019_AnnualReport_FINAL2comp.pdf and https://www.macdowell.org/assets/media-center/newsletters/documents/2020_AnnualReport_FINAL.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A founder's continuing effort is the norm; Laura's ten prepaid payments do once, in 2027, what Marian MacDowell had to do every year
critique: Marian MacDowell had no fixed sum set aside; a founder's age and health matter in both stories
note: MacDowell's founder raised running money every year; the ladder does that once, in 2027, for ten years.

idea: Even a large residency endowment can fall 15% in a year: MacDowell's went from $33.1M to $28.2M in 2022 (investment return -$5.6M, after +$7.0M in 2021), while it ran a $3.4M gap before investment return
sources: MacDowell audited financial statements 2022, https://www.macdowell.org/assets/about/financial-information/MacDowell-Audited-Financial-Statements-2022-2-1.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026): expenses $5,812,785; change in net assets before investment return -$3,358,401; spending 5% of a 36-month average; a $5M line of credit, undrawn; a mortgage covenant requiring $7M of unrestricted liquid assets; a board-designated building and equipment reserve of $1,924,403; cash $750,115
use: Why "a fall in the market" is not a reason to change Caplet's plan: none of the payment money is in shares, while MacDowell's running budget leans on a share-heavy endowment in a year like 2022
critique: Keel arithmetic: ($33,120,586 - $28,207,650) / $33,120,586 = -14.8%. Its FY2024 Form 990 (ProPublica, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131592242): revenue $8.44M, expenses $7.21M; the 990's endowment figure differs from the audit's (different definitions)
note: MacDowell's endowment fell about 15% in 2022 while it ran a gap: plain support for 'a fall in the market is not one of them'.

idea: For the residencies that last, "a reserve" means a perpetual endowment, mostly in shares, plus people who keep raising money; Laura's operating reserve is something else: ten dated payments already bought
sources: Keel inference from rows 19-22; case p.3 ("set aside a portion of the portfolio to fund the ten payments"); store H7-090 and H9-114 on reserve norms
use: Changes claim 2: running money that does not depend on each year's fundraising is what lasts; the famous survivors got it from endowments that fall in bad years, Laura's is built not to
critique: Her money stops after 2042, endowments are meant to last forever; the case says teams need not size an endowment (case p.3)
note: Keel framing built on Q9-019 to Q9-022: survivors' reserves move with markets, Laura's are built not to; a useful line for co-sponsors.

idea: Cost errors in big projects apply to arts buildings: Flyvbjerg lists "concert halls, museums, sports arenas, convention centers", and the American Planning Association (2005) endorsed reference class forecasting for "non-routine projects such as stadiums, museums, exhibit centers, and other local one-off projects"
sources: Flyvbjerg (2005), "Policy and Planning for Large Infrastructure Projects: Problems, Causes, Cures", World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 3781, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/824924ad-5b05-5980-a173-a8c184434df6/content (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A one-off cultural building is in the class that overruns; judge its budget from similar projects, not from its own plan
critique: Store H3-111 and H7-086 hold Flyvbjerg's general findings; this row adds only the arts-building scope
note: Adds only that arts buildings belong to Flyvbjerg's overrun class, already in the store.

idea: Buildings overrun by about 60% on average: "buildings have a 60% cost overrun on average. That's the middle ground"; his base-rate table gives buildings a mean overrun of +62%, with 39% of projects over +50% and those averaging +206%
sources: Flyvbjerg interview, Sydney Business Insights, 14 Apr 2023, https://sbi.sydney.edu.au/megaprojects-and-getting-big-things-done-with-bent-flyvbjerg/; table from Flyvbjerg and Gardner, How Big Things Get Done (2023), as given at https://budgetoverrun.com/studies/flyvbjerg-megaproject-database (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: "Building costs that overrun" in the IPS is not a hedge word: the expected overrun for a building is large and the tail larger
critique: The book table was read on a secondary site; "buildings" covers all kinds, mostly large
note: The 62% average overrun for buildings is verified at a gov.uk source in Q5-014; the book table here was read on a secondary site.

idea: Weiwuying (Kaohsiung) from primary records: first approved at NT$8.36bn for 2005-2009, revised six times to NT$10.7545bn (+28.64%), finished at the end of October 2017 instead of December 2009 (more than 7 years late), opened 13 Oct 2018; the Control Yuan censured the project, and the Legislative Yuan's budget office said its halls were greatly enlarged without first doing a financial analysis or a detailed assessment of operations and risk
sources: Legislative Yuan Budget Center, NPAC 2019 budget evaluation, https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/ashx/File.ashx?FilePath=~%2FFile%2FAttach%2F192476%2FFile_256518.pdf (「未詳實評估營運及風險管理、未先進行財務分析即決定大幅擴增該廳院規模」); LY evaluation of 2020 second reserve fund use, https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/ashx/File.ashx?FilePath=~%2FFile%2FAttach%2F208141%2FFile_1657576.pdf (in 2020 the Ministry still needed NT$8.521m from the first reserve fund and NT$20.796m from the second to pay the last contractor bills); National Development Council site check, 9 Jul 2015, https://ws.ndc.gov.tw/Download.ashx?icon=.pdf&n=6KGb5q2m54ef6Jed6KGT5paH5YyW5Lit5b%2BD6IiI5bu66KiI55Wr5p%2Bl6K2J5aCx5ZGKLnBkZg%3D%3D&u=LzAwMS9hZG1pbmlzdHJhdG9yLzEwL3JlbGZpbGUvNTY4Ny8yNDk3Ni9hNmFjOTIwOS1jNGQxLTRjYjgtYmI4NC1jM2Y2MWFjZGMzODgucGRm (the year's work 30 points behind plan; contract disputes "不斷", without end); Executive Yuan, https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/448DE008087A1971/8e70c5e5-6184-4785-9c09-0d86f9f481fa (opening date) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A Taiwan arts building whose bills kept arriving years after it opened: flexibility has to last beyond opening day
critique: Corrects store H7-086 ("NT$10.58bn, due 2014"): the first approved schedule ended in 2009 and the last approved total is NT$10.7545bn; 2014 may be a revised plan date (not checked). A national project, far larger than Laura's facility
verified: VERIFIED (LY and NDC PDFs, Executive Yuan page)
note: Top-40: Taiwan's own budget records on Weiwuying (+28.64%, more than seven years late) back 'building costs that overrun'; corrects H7-086.

idea: The National Taichung Theater needed three supplementary budget changes by 2009; its build time was revised from 37 to 58 months; completion approved for June 2014 was moved to the end of 2015; the main contractor won 274 more days in arbitration; the main structure contract settled at NT$2.990bn against NT$2.748bn budgeted
sources: Taichung Cultural Affairs Bureau, special final accounts for the Taichung Metropolitan Opera House, 2018 and 2020, https://www.culture.taichung.gov.tw/media/859815/%E5%A4%A7%E9%83%BD%E6%9C%83%E6%AD%8C%E5%8A%87%E9%99%A2107%E5%B9%B4%E5%BA%A6%E4%BF%9D%E7%95%99%E5%9F%B7%E8%A1%8C%E5%A0%B1%E5%91%8A-%E4%B8%8A%E5%82%B3.pdf and https://www.culture.taichung.gov.tw/media/859814/%E5%A4%A7%E9%83%BD%E6%9C%83%E6%AD%8C%E5%8A%87%E9%99%A2109%E5%B9%B4%E5%BA%A6%E4%BF%9D%E7%95%99%E5%9F%B7%E8%A1%8C%E5%A0%B1%E5%91%8A-%E4%B8%8A%E5%82%B3.pdf (budget after changes NT$4,360,438,000; a legal adviser on contract disputes kept to 2022) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A second Taiwan case: cost grows through design changes, delay and disputes long after the first budget
critique: The first total budget was not found, so no overall overrun figure; Keel arithmetic: NT$2,990,201,962 / NT$2,748,486,000 = +8.8% on the main contract alone. Operations began 26 Aug 2016 (LY, row 26 URL)
note: National venues are the wrong reference class for a small residency; background only

idea: Taiwan's other public arts buildings ran years late too: the Northern pop music centre (Taipei) was planned for 2005-2008 and extended to 2019; the Kaohsiung marine and pop music centre was planned for 2009-2015 and extended to 2020 after failed tenders
sources: Legislative Yuan Budget Center, Ministry of Culture 2019 final accounts evaluation, https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/ashx/File.ashx?FilePath=~%2FFile%2FAttach%2F201251%2FFile_273947.pdf (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: With Weiwuying, Taichung and the Taipei Performing Arts Center (store H9-097), all five large Taiwan arts buildings checked ran years late
critique: Big government projects with public tendering rules; a small private facility may avoid failed tenders
note: National venues are the wrong reference class for a small residency; background only

idea: After opening, a national theatre still runs on government money and misses its sponsorship targets: the Taichung theater's 2026 budget has revenue NT$671.0m, expenses NT$699.3m and a NT$28.3m deficit, with NT$509.6m from government; in 2017 it raised NT$8.81m of sponsorship against NT$15m budgeted (58.74%), as central-Taiwan firms mostly gave small sums
sources: Presidential Office Gazette No. 7885 (30 Sep 2026), https://www.president.gov.tw/File/Doc/8323fd04-b8c2-4ce1-a3f1-1c1baf8579a7 (「營運仍高度仰賴政府資源」: operations still rely heavily on government resources); National Audit Office report on the 2017 accounts, https://auditreport.audit.gov.tw/ServerFile/Get/63796346196045545418542434c2e148e6a93e3c97b6e7bd6d; LY NPAC 2019 budget evaluation (row 26 URL): idle days in 2017 of 42, 99 and 159 in its three halls (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: "A co-sponsor falling short" (IPS) is the normal case in Taiwan, even for a national venue
critique: A theatre, not a residency; Keel arithmetic: (NT$433.092m + NT$76.556m) / NT$671.048m = 76% from government; the Audit Office gives idle days of 41, 100 and 159, a day off the LY's
note: Taichung's national theatre raised 58.74% of its sponsorship target, so 'a co-sponsor falling short' is the normal case in Taiwan.

idea: The money "promised to no one" sits in shares, so it is likely to be smallest in the years the IPS itself says co-sponsors cut: the IPS says that in a recession "shares fall and co-sponsors cut", and names "a co-sponsor falling short" as a use of the kept half
sources: FINAL IPS (`keel/final_report/FINAL_IPS_as_submitted.txt`), the income paragraph and the building paragraph; rows 10, 12, 29
use: Note for the Final Report: the payments and the floor do not depend on this; only the extra flexibility does
critique: Keel inference. Partly offset: building-cost inflation tends to run in strong economies, when shares are more likely to be up (Keel inference, not tested). The IPS does not say whether the kept half stays in shares after 2031
clash: yes (risk to note, never a change): the kept half is in VT, so it may be smallest exactly when a co-sponsor falls short
note: The risk that the kept half is smallest when co-sponsors cut is restated with measured lags in Q4b-033 and sized in NUM-011.

idea: Taipei Artist Village, Taiwan's first public residency (12 Oct 2001), was set up by the Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs in a converted former public-works office, run by the Taipei Culture Foundation from 2004 (which added Treasure Hill on 2 Oct 2010), hosted more than 500 artists from over 40 countries, and lost its site: designated for public urban renewal, it moved out by the end of November 2023, ahead of a planned October 2024 move, and its programme went to Treasure Hill
sources: Taipei Artist Village, https://www.artistvillage.org/about.php; Taipei Culture Foundation 2023 final accounts, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/5%E6%9C%AC-%E5%B8%83%E9%8A%85-%E6%96%87%E5%9F%BA%E6%9C%83_112%E5%B9%B4%E6%B1%BA%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_%E5%AF%A9%E8%AD%B0%E9%80%9A%E9%81%8E.pdf (room occupancy 38.06% in 2023 as it wound down) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: In Taiwan a residency can lose its building through no fault of its own; the IPS's three named risks do not include a lost site, but flexibility money is what would pay for a move
critique: A public site on public land; store H9-121 holds the founding (secondary)
note: A Taiwan residency lost its public site to urban renewal, a risk the IPS does not name that flexible money would pay for.

idea: Taipei's two public residencies run mostly on city money: the 2018 budget gave Taipei Artist Village NT$16.05m (city NT$11.17m, other government NT$0.20m, own income NT$4.67m, mostly rent; 5 staff) and Treasure Hill NT$37.05m (city NT$29.81m including NT$5.8m capital, other government NT$2.0m, own income NT$5.23m; 16 staff; staff costs NT$10.86m, security NT$3.43m, cleaning NT$2.40m)
sources: Taipei Culture Foundation, 2018 budget, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/107%E5%B9%B4%E9%A0%90%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_20230814175317.pdf (foundation-wide, government subsidy 67.28% of revenue); 2024 final accounts, https://www.tcf.taipei/taipeicultureSysUpDoc/financial/%E6%96%87%E5%9F%BA%E6%9C%83_113%E5%B9%B4%E6%B1%BA%E7%AE%97%E6%9B%B8_1140722_%E5%B8%82%E6%94%BF%E6%9C%83%E8%AD%B0%E7%89%88.pdf (Treasure Hill occupancy 73.38% in 2024, 72.95% in 2023) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Government share about 71% (Taipei Artist Village) and 86% (Treasure Hill); keeping a site guarded and clean was about 16% of Treasure Hill's budget: the building's running cost, not its construction (Keel arithmetic)
critique: Budgets, not actuals; 2018 prices; city-run, so not a model for a private residency
note: Taipei's public residencies run on 71% and 86% city money, budgets that are yearly and can be cut.

idea: Taiwan's national arts grant-maker never got its endowment: the law set a NT$10bn fund to be reached within 10 years; government gave its NT$6bn share by 2003, but the NT$4bn private share was never raised, and the fund is budgeted at NT$6.88bn at the end of 2025, under 70% of the target
sources: National Culture and Arts Foundation Act, https://law.moj.gov.tw/eng/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=H0000056; Legislative Yuan Budget Center, NCAF 2025 budget evaluation (11 Nov 2024), https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/ashx/File.ashx?FilePath=~%2FFile%2FAttach%2F246007%2FFile_19842001.pdf (「基金餘額仍未達法定數額」: the fund has still not reached its legal amount); LY evaluation page https://www.ly.gov.tw/Pages/Detail.aspx?nodeid=55923&pid=247583 (the 60% government, 40% private split; NT$2bn starting fund in 1996) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: Private money promised to Taiwan's arts did not arrive even for the national fund: a pledge is not money in hand
critique: A government foundation, not a residency
note: Top-40: the private half of Taiwan's national arts fund was promised in law and never arrived, plain proof that a pledge is not money in hand.

idea: A grant-maker living on investment income gives less in bad years: NCAF's revenue fell from NT$318.8m (2014) to NT$188.9m (2015) when its return was 2.42% against 3.59% expected (financial income 79.7% of 2015 revenue; fund about NT$2bn each in deposits, shares and fixed income); its 2027 budget pays NT$7.302m of regular grants from a special reserve kept "to keep regular grants steady" and holds a NT$300m "Act for the Future" reserve set aside in 2021
sources: NCAF 2015 annual report (English), https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/publishBookEn/20200623/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc/4fa69c5d236e4b53843284ca1e8553fc.pdf; NCAF 2027 budget, https://www.ncafroc.org.tw/files/informationBudget/20260903/b324c6ad9912453d98bffdaa6591b2d8/b324c6ad9912453d98bffdaa6591b2d8.pdf (『「穩定常態補助款」特別公積』) (accessed 9 Nov 2026)
use: A Taiwan grant-maker or co-sponsor funded by returns can give less in the same years shares fall; Laura's payments do not depend on returns
critique: Keel arithmetic: NT$188.86m / NT$318.80m - 1 = -41%; the 2014 figure may include one-off items (not checked)
note: Same NCAF income fall as Q4b-026, which settles its cause; the grant-steadying reserve fits Q4b-027.

idea: Laura's $50,000 a year is about NT$1.64m: roughly a tenth of Taipei Artist Village's 2018 budget and 4.4% of Treasure Hill's
sources: Keel arithmetic: $50,000 x 32.768 (USD/TWD on 6 Nov 2026, as in store Q10-023) = NT$1.638m; / NT$16.05m = 10%; / NT$37.05m = 4.4%; budgets from row 32
use: Context for co-sponsors: a strong base for a small residency, not a whole budget (agrees with store H9-119 for US residencies)
critique: 2018 budgets against 2033-2042 payments; city-run sites with large buildings; no estimate of Laura's facility
note: Keel arithmetic putting $50,000 a year at about a tenth of a small Taipei residency's 2018 budget; context, not a facility estimate.

idea: Yaddo's "reserve" is mostly a label its board can lift: board-designated $22,554,625 of a $32,402,204 endowment (69.6%) in 2025; "The board has the authority to modify or remove designations for cash unavailable for general expenditure, allowing the funds to be used for general operations if needed"
sources: The Corporation of Yaddo (2026), liquidity note (p. 10) and endowment note
use: Laura's operating reserve is also her own money held under her own rule; the IPS's two reasons (l.17, CANON A34) do the job of Yaddo's designation, and are narrower (two defined events, SKELETON Exhibits item 4)
critique: A designation is an accounting label, not a legal restriction. With every designation lifted, Yaddo's available money would be about 77 months of 2025 expenses instead of 19.4 (Keel arithmetic)
clash: risk: never call the operating reserve "restricted", "locked" or "irrevocable"; it is owned, dated and held under a written rule
note: Wording guard for 3a and 3e: a board's reserve is a label it can lift (Yaddo), so Laura's operating reserve is called owned, dated and held under the two reasons, never 'restricted' or 'locked'.

idea: Yaddo's running money did not cover its running costs in either recent year: operating cash flow -$1,067,071 (2024) and -$306,086 (2025); net assets rose $4,477,910 in 2025 only because investments gained $5,332,910 (about -$855,000 without them)
sources: Yaddo (2026), statements of activities and cash flows
use: The oldest US residency balances its year with market gains; none of Laura's ten payments depends on a share price (IPS l.11)
critique: Two years only; cash flow includes the timing of pledges; Keel arithmetic for the -$855,000
note: Store only: the oldest US residency balanced its year with market gains, the dependence IPS l.11 keeps out of the ten payments.

idea: Buildings reach Yaddo's running costs: depreciation $744,909 (15.9% of 2025 expenses) plus "Renovations, repairs, and purchases" $329,950 (7.0%), together 22.9%
use: Kills the "never paid for a building out of operating money" half of claim 1: upkeep is a running cost everywhere
critique: Depreciation is not cash; repairs are. A historic estate; Laura's facility is new and its cost is out of scope (case)
note: Store only: upkeep reaches every residency's running costs; never an estimate of Laura's facility's cost, which is outside the case.

idea: Yaddo paid capital work from gifts given for it: $465,191 released from its capital campaign and $50,891 for the physical plant in 2025
sources: Yaddo (2026), net assets released from restriction
use: The clean form of claim 1: building money from gifts given for buildings, as Laura's facility contribution is kept apart from the operating reserve (NUMBERS 8h)
critique: One year's releases; campaign total not read
note: Store only: Yaddo paid capital work from gifts given for it, the clean form of keeping building money apart.

idea: MacDowell's written two-pot rule (2017): budgets draw at most 5% of a 12-quarter average to cover operating deficits, and "To the extent the Colony's operating deficit exceeds the 5% level, the Board can designate an additional draw from unrestricted funds"; capital expenses are "covered by the Board Designated Building and Equipment Reserve Fund or special gifts designated for this purpose" (reserve $1,817,987 at end-2017, $1,603,442 at end-2016)
sources: The MacDowell Colony (2018), endowment and net-asset notes
use: The nearest written form of claim 1: one pot and one rule for running money, another for buildings; Laura's plan has the same shape in dated instruments
critique: The same rule lets the board draw past 5% when deficits are larger. Q9 row 22 holds the 2022 reserve figure; this row adds the policy
verified: VERIFIED (FS17 PDF: spending rule and net-asset table); the capital-expense sentence UNVERIFIED (search excerpt of the same PDF)
note: Store only: MacDowell's written two-pot rule, one for running money and one for buildings, the nearest written form of the plan's separation; the capital sentence is a search excerpt.

idea: MacDowell bought a New York unit in 2016 for $5.1 million with a 25-year, $2,550,000 mortgage; $2,081,897 was still owed at end-2023
sources: The MacDowell Colony (2018), mortgage note; ProPublica (n.d.), Form 990 data 2021-2023
use: A building bought half on debt leaves a fixed charge on running money for 25 years; Laura's plan borrows nothing
critique: A city office and event space, not the residency campus; the covenant is in Q9 row 22
note: Store only: a building bought half on a 25-year mortgage leaves a charge on running money, and Laura borrows nothing.

idea: Even MacDowell drew a line of credit secured on its investments: $495,000 owed at end-2017, $455,000 at end-2018, $0 at end-2019
sources: The MacDowell Colony (2018), balance sheet; The MacDowell Colony (2020), line-of-credit note
use: Gaps in running money were bridged by borrowing against shares; Laura's payments need no bridge, since each holding pays out before its payment date (NUMBERS 8h)
critique: Small against its balance sheet; reason not stated
verified: VERIFIED for 2017 (FS17 PDF); 2018-2019 UNVERIFIED (search excerpt of FS19)
note: Store only: even MacDowell bridged gaps with a credit line secured on its investments.

idea: Headlands spent on its campus while its running money drained: in 2023 it paid $757,854 for campus improvements and design work while operations used $474,399 of cash; cash fell from $1,499,588 to $262,351; money available within a year was $89,341, about 8 days of 2023 expenses
sources: Headlands Center for the Arts (2026), cash flows, Notes 4 and 9
use: The one clear breach of claim 1 in the filings read: capital work and programmes shared one cash pool. Laura's plan keeps them in different instruments
critique: Part of the work was paid from campaign gifts ($478,104 released in 2023); pledges may have been counted on. Keel arithmetic for days
note: The cleanest outside evidence for 3a's separate operating reserve: when Headlands paid campus work from the same cash as programmes in 2023, its available money fell to about 8 days; no number in prose.

idea: Headlands then cut programmes: "In January 2024, the Center reduced some of its programming and operational expenses and paused work on certain capital campus improvement projects"; expenses fell 36% ($4,324,043 to $2,778,522), artist stipends from $507,541 to $318,501; available money rose to $444,134 (about 1.9 months)
sources: Headlands (2026), Note 9, statements of activities and functional expenses
use: When capital and running money mix, residents' money is what gets cut: the outcome Laura's ten payments rule out for 2033-2042
critique: One residency; it also lost earned income in 2023
note: Store only, with Q9b-008: Headlands then cut programmes and artists' stipends, which is what mixing capital and running money costs residents.

idea: A reserve in policy is not a reserve held: Headlands' board-designated operating reserve was meant "to cover at least 90 days of operating expenditures" but held $281,690 (2019 and 2020), about 1.2 months of 2020 expenses (90 days was about $705,800); "Although the Center does not intend to spend from this reserve, these funds could be made available if necessary"; the 2024 audit shows no designated reserve
use: Laura's operating reserve is bought in full, not a target (NUMBERS 8h)
critique: The 2024 audit is silent; it does not say the reserve was spent. Keel arithmetic
note: Store only: Headlands' 90-day reserve held about 1.2 months, a policy target, while Laura's operating reserve is bought in full (NUMBERS 8h).

idea: Djerassi never set a running-money reserve: its board "has the ability to designate ... net assets for an operating reserve and board-designated endowment, but it has not opted to do so as of December 31, 2022 and 2021"
sources: Djerassi Resident Artists Program (2023), net assets note
use: Some well-known residencies hold no named reserve at all
critique: One residency
note: Store only: some well-known residencies hold no named reserve at all.

idea: Djerassi kept capital money apart by its source: a $2.2 million conservation easement sold in 1999 "created a land and buildings fund to support Djerassi's capital and land management needs"
use: Claim 1's "dedicated" form: building money from a one-time sale, never from running money
critique: Fund's later balance not shown; Q32 row 28 holds the 1999 gift of the land, this is the fund
note: Store only: Djerassi kept capital money apart by its source, a one-time easement sale.

idea: Djerassi's share-heavy endowment fell 38.7% in the 2022 period ($2,121,372 to $1,300,119): $414,911 drawn (about 30% of the period's $1,378,206 expenses) and a $404,229 investment loss; funds fell below their gift value, from "unfavorable market fluctuations ... and continued appropriation", and the shortfall ($301,121) was booked against unrestricted money
use: A small residency paying a third of its costs from shares in a falling year: the risk the operating reserve does not carry ("A fall in the market is not one of them", IPS l.17)
critique: The note calls the period "ten months", the statements "year"; percentages use the reported figures. Keel arithmetic
note: Store only: Djerassi's share-heavy endowment fell 38.7% in 2022 while paying 30% of costs, the risk IPS l.17 rules out for the reserve ('A fall in the market is not one of them').

idea: Djerassi after the 2020 shutdown: "forced to shut due to mandates" on 10 March 2020; positive cash flows "dependent upon the successful implementation of management's cost reduction programs and revenue targets"
use: Running money that depends on targets, against Laura's dated payments
critique: A pandemic shock, not a founder event
note: Store only: a pandemic shutdown, not a founder or funding event.

idea: Months of money available within one year, from audited liquidity notes: Headlands 4.1 (2020), 0.25 (2023), 1.9 (2024); Djerassi 8.7 (2021), 7.1 (2022); Yaddo 18.6 (2024), 19.4 (2025); MacDowell 34.8 (2021), 21.4 (2022)
sources: Yaddo (2026); Headlands (2021, 2026); Djerassi (2023); Marian and Edward MacDowell, Inc. (2023) liquidity table, with expenses from ProPublica (n.d.)
use: Sizes claim 3 from filings: small residencies hold weeks to months; only the two richest hold more than a year
critique: Keel arithmetic. Four US residencies, chosen because they publish audits (likely the stronger ones)
note: Store only: four audited residencies held about 8 days to 35 months of spendable money, so 3a carries no new number; residencies that publish audits likely flatter the field.

idea: At the richest, months of cover move with markets: MacDowell's available money fell from $15,049,020 to $10,388,628 in one year, 13.4 months of cover lost
sources: Marian and Edward MacDowell, Inc. (2023), liquidity table
use: Endowed "months" are market-priced; Laura's ten payments are dated
critique: Partly new designations, not only market loss; Q9 row 22 holds the endowment's fall
note: Store only: endowed months of cover move with markets (MacDowell lost 13.4 months in a year, partly from new designations), while Laura's ten are dated.

idea: Field survey, 2020: of 358 residency organisations, 9% were "forced to close indefinitely" and 12% "may have to close permanently"; most are "private not-for-profit or artist-run" and may not qualify for government aid; 71% of those hit financially lost artist-fee income; just over 20% got emergency government support
use: The field's normal state is thin: one shock closed about one in ten
critique: Self-selected online survey; a pandemic shock; not about founders
note: Store only: one shock in 2020 closed about one residency organisation in ten (a self-selected survey), the thin normal state of the field.

idea: Field survey, 2021: 61% of residency organisations could not access emergency funding, and of those, 66% said nothing relevant existed or they were ineligible
use: When income stops, outside money often does not come: co-sponsors cannot be the backstop for running costs, which is why IPS l.11 says the payments depend on "nobody else's money"
critique: Organisation sample size for Survey II not read
note: Store only: 61% of residencies could not reach emergency money in 2021, field evidence for IPS l.11's 'nobody else's money'.

idea: Jentel did not fail when its founder died: Neltje died on 30 April 2021 and "gifted her estate to the University of Wyoming, which includes both Jentel Artist Residency and the Neltje Center for Excellence in Creativity and the Arts"
use: Kills claim 2 as stated: the founder's money was placed by estate, at her death
critique: A wealthy heir; a university took it over, not co-sponsors
clash: risk: Q32 row 31 and its card text read Jentel as "fragile" (Gaps)
note: Corrects the store: Jentel did not fail, its founder's estate carried it to the University of Wyoming; store only, since 3d's one evidence clause is Taiwan's (SKELETON 3d), and it overturns Q32-031's 'fragile'.

idea: The university added its own money: "Along with an allocation of $1 million from UW's Board of Trustees, the Neltje gift is the cornerstone of the new center"; the residency is one of its two initiatives
use: A founder's placed gift drew a second funder: the order Laura's plan follows (her money owned first, co-sponsors after)
critique: Estate's size not given
note: Store only: a founder's placed gift was followed by a second funder ($1 million from the university), an order Laura's plan shares, never a match.

idea: Jentel at full size four years later: in December 2025 a new manager hosts "each group of six artists, writers and composers every month"
use: Continuity after the founder is possible when her money was placed
critique: University news release
note: Store only: Jentel runs at full size in 2025 under the university, the end point of Q9b-019.

idea: The founder's own foundation shrank because the residency moved: Jentel Foundation contributions $0 (year to June 2023) and $7,622 (year to June 2025); expenses $80,555 and $106,761, against about $599,000 in 2022 (store H9-119)
use: A filing alone can mislead: the money followed the residency to the university
critique: Figures from ProPublica's summary page; the 990-PF itself was blocked
clash: risk: H9-119's Jentel budget is the founder-era figure
note: Store only: the Jentel Foundation's $0 contributions after 2022 mean the residency moved, not failed, which is why H9-119's Jentel budget and Q32-031's reading are re-judged.

idea: Albee: the founder's will "made the Edward Albee Foundation the beneficiary"; the foundation says he died in 2016 "leaving resources and clear direction", and it has since rebuilt the Barn ("THE BARN: v2.0 (2024)")
sources: Konkle (n.d.), Edward Albee Society; Edward F. Albee Foundation (n.d.)
use: A second case of founder money placed at death, with the building renewed after
critique: No figures; the foundation's own page
note: Store only: Albee's will placed his money and his foundation renewed the building after his death; no figures.

idea: Dorland nearly closed with its land placed but no running money placed: the founders made "a gift-sale of their acres" to the Nature Conservancy in the early 1970s; the founder was "forced by ill health to leave" at the end of 1983; in 1985 "there was talk of temporarily closing Dorland, due to lack of funds"; it survived by replacing "two full-time positions (director and caretaker) with part-time help supplemented by considerable volunteer labor" and asking residents for money and chores
use: The sharpest contrast for claim 2: placing the property is not enough; the running money must be placed too
critique: A resident writer's first-person article; no figures
note: Store only: Dorland had its land placed but no running money and nearly closed two years after its founder left, the contrast with Laura's ten owned payments.

idea: Black Mountain's last two years: grant requests to the Guggenheim, Duke and Mellon foundations "soundly rejected"; three bank loan applications rejected; an Advisory Council including Einstein "boosted credibility but did nothing to boost credit"; an alumni letter for $25,000 "yielded $250"; electricity "turned off due to unpaid bills" before the closing was announced in October 1956
use: Famous names are not money: the co-sponsor lesson behind "money you already own" (IPS l.15)
critique: A college, not a residency; Q9 rows 1-3 hold the loans and the end, this row adds the failed asks
note: Store only: Black Mountain's famous council 'boosted credibility but did nothing to boost credit', the nearest outside echo of 'money you already own' (IPS l.15); 3d's one clause goes to Taiwan instead.

idea: Byrdcliffe after its founder died in 1929: his widow "survived the years between her husband's death and her own by selling real estate holdings in California ... as well as parts of the original Byrdcliffe tract"; today "the Woodstock Guild and private individuals own different portions of the property"
use: A founder-funded colony with nothing placed for running costs was sold off in pieces
critique: Its busiest years had ended long before 1929; family finance, not the colony's accounts
note: Store only: Byrdcliffe's founder placed nothing for running costs and the colony was sold in pieces.

idea: Bamboo Curtain (Taiwan) ended for site and pandemic reasons in the source now read: it decided to close at the end of 2021 because of COVID-19 and the planned Tamsui north-bank road, which would harm its setting; the founder's death on 30 August 2021 "也打亂了竹圍工作室原先規劃" (also upset its plans), including a city-backed archive project
use: The only Taiwan case does not support claim 2; it shows a residency's site is a risk of its own
critique: Student newspaper; no finances. Fills the cause gap in store H9-117 and Q11b's Gaps
note: Same Bamboo Curtain closure (the planned road and the pandemic) as Q9c-030, which reads three sources in full and adds the loss of senior staff.

idea: The pattern across rows 19-27: residencies that outlived a founder had the founder's money or property placed by deed, will or estate (Jentel, Albee; Yaddo and MacDowell in Q9 and Q32); those that nearly closed or broke up had the place but no running money placed (Dorland, Byrdcliffe, Black Mountain)
use: Laura's ten payments, owned in Treasuries and dated to 2042, are running money placed before the doors open, for one decade
critique: Small, hand-picked sample; survivors are easier to find; estates arrive at death, while Laura places hers in 2027-2028
clash: risk: after 2042 is outside the case (Q2c row 35); never imply the plan funds the residency past 2042
note: Keel inference from a small hand-picked sample: residencies outlived founders when running money, not only the place, was placed; Laura's is placed for one decade only, never past 2042.

idea: Laura's operating reserve in the same units: 120 months of her own $50,000 a year, owned and dated; about $444,545 on 1 Jan 2033 against $399,089 the ten payments are worth at today's forwards (MODEL)
use: The fair comparison with rows 15-16: residency months cover a whole budget and move with markets; hers cover her share only and are dated
critique: $50,000 is a base, not a whole budget (H9-119); never present 120 months as the residency's whole running cost
clash: risk: a comparison with endowments must not turn her flexibility (IPS l.15, about $21,300, NUMBERS 8k) into an endowment (CANON A31, D12)
note: Adapt: the $444,545 against $399,089 comparison belongs in Figure 1's note only (WORDS), 120 months must carry 'her share only' beside it, and her flexibility is never framed as an endowment (CANON A31, D12).

idea: The richest hold years in endowment, not in spendable money: Yaddo's $32,402,204 endowment is about 6.9 years of 2025 expenses, but $5,084,017 is held in perpetuity and the rest pays out by a 5% rule
use: "Years versus months" is the wrong contrast; "dated and spendable" against "perpetual and market-priced" is the right one
critique: Keel arithmetic; much of the endowment is board-designated and could be released (row 1)
note: Store only: the richest residencies hold years in perpetual, market-priced endowments, so the right contrast is dated and spendable against perpetual and market-priced.

idea: Checking a story at its source changed the claim (Keel's real work, 13 Nov): the brief expected Jentel to show a founder's residency failing; the university's pages and the filings showed a hand-over by estate
use: A real work event for the Articulation pool (I102), judged blind with Caplet's own
critique: Keel's event, not Caplet's experience
note: Team Reflection pool, judged blind beside Caplet's own events: a real work event in which checking Jentel at its source overturned the brief's claim.

idea: The Ministry's art-village grant is one year at a time: the plan must finish within one year ("以單一年度執行完畢為原則"), receipts by 30 Nov, and amounts "需俟立法院預算審議結果而定，本部得視實際情況酌減或停止補助" (depend on the legislature's budget; the Ministry may cut or stop them)
sources: 文化部 (2025c). 文化部藝術村營運扶植補助作業要點, points 4, 9, 10
use: A public co-sponsor's next year is never promised; the ten operating payments are owned before they fall due (IPS l.11; CANON A4). Lands: store; at most the half-clause in 3d of card 1
critique: Applies to the Ministry's village programme only; cities vote yearly too (rows 15-16)
clash: no; supports IPS l.9 ("co-sponsors cut their budgets") and l.15 ("a co-sponsor falling short")
note: 3d's half-clause, chosen in SKELETON: the Ministry's village grant is one year at a time and may be cut with the legislature's budget, so ten owned years are rare in Taiwan; no number or rule name in prose.

idea: It pays at most NT$3,000,000 per application (about US$91,600 at 32.768) for a yearly operating plan plus a space plan (equipment and facilities); the grant's living allowance is NT$800 per resident per day (NT$500 in the 2021 text), and a funded residency must last at least a month and pay residents at least that
sources: Same directions, points 5, 6, 8; 2021 text in Yunlin County's copy
use: The largest Ministry grant one village can get is below Laura's central contribution in NT$ (NT$3.77m, NUMBERS 8j). Lands: store only
critique: A cap, not what grantees get (2025 grants were NT$0.9m-2.0m, row 8)
verified: VERIFIED (current directions in full; the 2021 figure read in part)
note: Store only: the Ministry's village grant caps at NT$3m a year with a NT$800 daily allowance; scale only, never a facility estimate.

idea: Since the 28 Oct 2025 amendment only "依法設立或登記之法人、團體或組織" (legally established bodies) may apply; cities and counties, listed in the 2021 and Dec 2024 texts with Ministry shares of 50%-90% by fiscal tier, are gone from the list
sources: Same directions, point 3; 雲林縣政府文化觀光處 (2024) notice with the Dec 2024 directions
use: The matching formula belongs to local-government grants; a private residency applies on its own plan with no ratio
critique: Earlier texts read through Yunlin County's posted copies, in part; the Ministry gives no reason for the change
verified: VERIFIED (current text in full; earlier texts in part)
note: Store only, as the guard against 'match': the 50% to 90% shares were for cities, now off the applicant list, so a private residency gets no ratio; the Ministry's rules stay out of the report (SKELETON 3d).

idea: Multi-year help was withdrawn: the 2021 text let a body funded more than 3 years running apply for a plan of up to 2 years, and capped one applicant at 3 cases and NT$5m a year; both are gone from the Dec 2024 and Oct 2025 texts, and the 2025 call asked bodies funded in each of 2022-2024 for a self-improvement plan
sources: Yunlin County's copies of the 2021 and 2024 texts; its 18 Dec 2024 notice; current directions
use: Central residency money in Taiwan got shorter, not longer, after 2021; ten owned years stand out more now. Lands: store only
critique: Read through a county's copies; reasons not given
verified: VERIFIED (2024 notice read; earlier texts in part)
note: Store only: Taiwan's two-year option for residencies was withdrawn after 2021, so public residency money got shorter.

idea: The application must include an estimate of operating funds (營運經費概算), proof of ownership or right of use of the site, and proof of other bodies' resources (其他相關單位資源證明)
use: The nearest the rule comes to an "anchor": the funder checks what the owner and others already bring before paying a year of programme. Laura's owned bottom ($95,000, NUMBERS 4) and the ten operating payments are that kind of proof. Lands: store only (SKELETON 3d cuts the Ministry's rules)
critique: Proof, not a match: no ratio, and the grant is still one year
clash: risk: 3d must not say a Taiwanese funder "matches" or "anchors on" Laura's money; the rule says neither
note: Adapt for 3d: the rule asks for proof of operating funds before paying a year of programme, so Laura's money is proof the residency can run, never the 'anchor' this row's wording reaches for and never a match (SKELETON 3d).

idea: Money comes after the work: receipts by 30 Nov, a signed contract for NT$1.5m or more, and unspent money returned in proportion to the subsidy
use: The residency floats each year's costs before public money arrives; each operating payment is in hand at the start of its year (IPS l.17; CANON A33)
critique: Same pattern as NCAF (Q11d row 3)
note: Store only: Taiwan's grant money arrives after the work and its receipts, while each of Laura's payments is in hand at the start of its year.

idea: No second public grant for the same work (not if NCAF, a Ministry-supervised body or the Ministry already funds it), and equipment bought with the grant belongs to the village's owner
use: Public co-sponsors do not stack on one item, so the fundraising text should say which body funds which part; equipment stays with whoever owns the facility
critique: Adds the village rule to Q11d row 6 (NCAF and museum rules)
note: Same bar on double public money as Q11d-006, extended to the village grant; who keeps the equipment is a grant term the report does not need.
